Closes #2942. Follow-up to the basic macOS IORegistry support in #2360.

## Summary

The Mac Monitor can read GPU load and memory, but temperature, power and PCIe remain empty. Add opt-in Apple Silicon charts with rootless temperature/power readings and GPU frequency in place of the discrete-GPU PCIe card.

Enable with `STRATA_MACOS_TELEMETRY=1`; install optional `macmon` with `brew install macmon` for temperature, power and clock readings.

## What changed

- Read GPU driver allocations from IORegistry and label them as shared memory across all apps. Model sizing keeps using the existing Metal reader and working-set budget.
- Run one background `macmon pipe` process, discard readings after five seconds, recover from stopped/stalled helpers, and close the helper with telemetry.
- Adapt Apple dashboard labels, show unavailable samples as gaps, and label strata-mlx's expert-cache budget accurately.
- Document setup, metric meanings and limitations; add hardware-independent sensor, lifecycle, HTTP and chart tests.

## Extra Notes

The feature is off by default. Existing macOS `_Metal`, NVIDIA/AMD readers, Windows AMD notes and the default spark renderer are preserved; the original spark function is unchanged. Tests cover default reader selection, AMD precedence on macOS, unchanged default chart behavior, missing helpers and stale/invalid data.

Validation on upstream main `477ac13c`:

- `python -m unittest serve.test_server serve.test_monitor serve.test_apple_telemetry` — **356 tests passed**.
- `node serve/test_charts.cjs`, `node --check serve/web/app.js`, and `git diff --check` — passed.
- M3 Pro, 18 GPU cores, 36 GiB, macmon 0.10.0: real GPU load/allocation/temperature/power/frequency through the current-main mock HTTP server; browser rendering checked with no console errors. A streamed Flash Next generation was also verified in the earlier v0.1.40-based deployment.

No native engine sources or build files changed. Native Metal/CUDA/HIP/SYCL builds and physical NVIDIA/AMD/Intel Mac hardware were not tested. The extra sensors use OS-dependent IORegistry/IOReport/SMC interfaces and remain optional.

pulls.title: kv: mixed K16V8 (FP16 K, INT8 V)
pulls.author: iskamag
pulls.body:
## Title kv: mixed K16V8 (FP16 K, INT8 V) Issue: Resolves # (none) ## Summary Adds `--kv k16v8`, a KV cache format between `int8` and `fp16`: **FP16 K + INT8 V** (codes plus one FP16 scale per 64 values). It keeps FP16 precision for the attention scores while keeping the V-side memory saving: **1,552 B/cell** vs 1,056 for int8 and 2,048 for fp16. The format streams with `--kv-resident` (three runs: FP16 K, V codes, V scales), works with the MTP drafter (the drafter stays plain INT8, as under k8v4), and is independent of the SCR/suffix-reuse work. Full write-up and assets: [`docs/K16V8.md`](https://github.com/iskamag/Strata/blob/feat/k16v8/docs/K16V8.md) ## What changed - `include/strata/core/layer.hpp`, `src/core/layer.cpp`: `kv_f16k_q8v` state flag, format tag 4, pool sizing, elastic/streamed host allocation, zeroing, `qsa_attn_pools`, decode append. - `src/kernels/cuda/qsa_decode_attn.cu`: decode-attention mode 4 (FP16 K, INT8 V) across `step`, `batch`, `slots` and `rows`. - `src/kernels/cuda/kv_stream.cu`, `include/strata/kernels/kv_stream.hpp`: 3-run block movers and the folded K/V host helpers for appends. - `src/prefill/prefill.cpp`, `src/core/verify.cpp`, `src/core/mtp.cpp`: prefill/verify append paths; drafter forced to INT8 under k16v8. - `src/core/conversation_snapshot.cpp`: per-side K/V sizes and format tag 4 (modes 0/1/2). - `src/program/generate.cpp`: `--kv k16v8` parsing and help. - `src/kernels/kv_stream_parity.cpp`, `src/core/conversation_snapshot_test.cpp`: mixed-format coverage. - `docs/K16V8.md`, `docs/media/k16v8/`: results and the SVG output comparison. ## Extra Notes ### Performance Controlled A/B: same engine, IQ3_S, RX 6800 (gfx1030), HIP, `STRATA_HIP_PROMPT_F16=1`, MTP spec 4, 13,109-token prompt, fully resident KV. | KV | prefill tok/s | decode tok/s | bytes/cell | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | `int8` | 919.2 | 32.15 | 1,056 | | `k16v8` | 917.9 | 34.48 | 1,552 | | `fp16` | 906.6 | 33.90 | 2,048 | The three are within run-to-run/draft-acceptance noise. K16V8 is effectively int8 speed with FP16 K, and 24% smaller than fp16. At 96k context and 12 QSA layers: 1.71 GiB host KV (vs ~1.16 GiB int8 / ~2.25 GiB fp16); 32,768 resident cells use ~610 MB VRAM (vs ~415 MB / ~805 MB). The extra VRAM against int8 can reduce the expert cache by roughly 200 MB. ### Output length on the same prompt Prompt: `Make an animated SVG of an anthropomorphic cat holding a sword` | KV | output tokens | | --- | ---: | | `int8` | 37k | | `k16v8` | 29k | | `fp16` | 25k | On this workload, higher KV precision correlated with fewer output tokens: int8 produced the longest response, fp16 the shortest, and k16v8 sat between them — consistent with **less overthinking** when the cache is more precise. This is one observation, not a general quality or latency guarantee.
int8 — 37k output tokens
 k16v8 — 29k output tokens
 fp16 — 25k output tokens
Animated originals: [int8](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iskamag/Strata/feat/k16v8/docs/media/k16v8/int8.svg), [k16v8](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iskamag/Strata/feat/k16v8/docs/media/k16v8/k16v8.svg), [fp16](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iskamag/Strata/feat/k16v8/docs/media/k16v8/fp16.svg). ### Compatibility Exercised: `--kv-resident 0` and `32768`, `--mtp`/`--spec 4`, `--prompt-cache` prefix reuse, 96k context, vision, control vectors, `--adapt-async`, `--expert-cache auto`, HIP gfx1030. `--no-fast-attn` and `--native-flash-attn-short` fall back to the fused decode attention for k16v8; the gather/native path is not implemented for this format. Not yet exercised: `--batch`, `--layer-split`, `--pipeline-windows`, `--kv-grow` (elastic), and CUDA. Batch slots/rows and elastic allocation are implemented. On CUDA the prompt attention falls back to the decode kernel; gfx1030 already uses that path for most formats. `--cache-suffix-reuse` and `--kv-pool-tokens` are not in `main`, so this change is independent of SCR. ### Tests - `kv_stream_parity`: all five formats pass; k16v8 streamed-vs-resident is bitwise and the ring restore is identical. - `conversation_snapshot_test`: 4,872 checks pass, including k16v8 modes 0/1/2. - Live model: 13k and 63k-token retrieval prompts, 96k service profile, MTP drafts accepted.

pulls.title: [Engine] Calibrate: survive an engine dying mid-measurement; adaptive gate: say where the copies stopped (#1337, #2188)
pulls.author: dsenchankau
pulls.body:
Issue: extends #1337 (shipped in 0.1.41); diagnostics for #2188 (still open)

## Problem and result

--calibrate restarts the engine for every setting it measures. Since 0.1.41, a candidate whose engine won't start just skips that candidate and keeps what was measured so far (#1337). But an engine that starts fine and then dies during its own measurement still fails the whole calibration.

I hit this on a UD-Q4_K_XL run: --adapt-swaps 80 measured fine, then the --adapt-swaps 160 engine died at the adaptive tier's copy gate (the same error as #2188). About twenty minutes of --pcie-frac and --spec-min-p results were lost.

After this change a dead engine drops only its own candidate. The earlier settings survive and the winner is picked from what actually measured; in my run 80 swaps beat the default by 10% and was still written even though 160 died. The engine's timeout line for that gate now also prints how far the copies got, which is what's missing in #2188.

## Related discussion

#1337 (closed; this extends its rule from failed starts to mid-measurement deaths) and #2188 (open; the engine part here is diagnostics only, it fixes nothing). I don't think this needs a scope agreement first: a calibration where nothing dies behaves exactly as before, and the new C++ code only runs after a wait has already timed out.

## Approach

Steps 4, 5 and 6 (worker counts, expert tier, the AMD shared-expert fork) already had the failed-start rule through restart() and failed_starts. I routed a mid-measurement death through the same path and folded the three nearly identical blocks into one restart-and-measure helper. Step 6 had no mid-measurement protection at all and failed the whole run the same way. The first start (steps 1-3) still fails the run; nothing has been measured yet, so there is nothing to keep.

On the engine side, when the adaptive gate's wait times out the message now carries the gate's reached counter, its atomic, and the copy stream's pinned value, and says that the #267 release drains the window's own streams and never the tier's copy stream. With STRATA_VERIFY_TRACE=1 it also dumps the window's trace. Nothing changed for the case where the wait succeeds.

## Validation

Revision eb07e553. Ubuntu 24.04, i7-13700F, RTX 4080 SUPER (sm_89), CUDA 13.4 (nvcc V13.4.92, cuda_13.4.r13.4/compiler.38855100_0). I re-ran everything on the upstream main commit this branch is rebased on, as a baseline, and the failing lists below are the same on both.

**Passed:**

```
cmake -G Ninja -S . -B build-tests -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DSTRATA_ENABLE_CUDA=ON -DSTRATA_BUILD_TESTS=ON \
  -DSTRATA_Q6K_EXPERTS=ON -DSTRATA_MMQ_KQUANTS=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=89
cmake --build build-tests -j "$(nproc)"
ctest --test-dir build-tests --output-on-failure
```

Build is clean. ctest: "96% tests passed, 6 tests failed out of 149". expert_multi_test skips itself on this CPU (no AVX-512). The six failures (ple_parity, ggml_tq_overlay, native_hadamard_test, tq_cpu_parity, tq_cpu_parity_avx2, isa_guard_check) are the same six on the baseline, same command, same build dir. Nothing new fails on this branch.

```
PYTHONPATH=. .venv/bin/python tools/test_calibrate.py
```

33 tests, OK. The baseline has 30; the three new ones cover the cases above: a tier candidate dies and the faster candidate still wins, a worker count dies and the rest still measures, a fork candidate dies and the run still returns.

```
for t in tools/test_*.py serve/test_*.py bench/test_*.py; do
  PYTHONPATH=. .venv/bin/python "$t" >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "FAILED: $t"
done
```

Six failures, the same six on the baseline: test_iq_pack, test_nvfp4_local_pack, test_setup_download, test_setup_engine_hash, test_setup_golden, test_gfx906_qsa_query_swizzle_guard. All environmental, none caused by this change.

**Failed:** the ctest and python failures listed above. Every one of them reproduces the same way on the baseline, so none comes from this change.

**Not run:**

- HIP compile of src/core/verify.cpp, I don't have an AMD card. The new block is ordinary C++ in the file CUDA and HIP share, and it compiles on its own under -Wall -Wextra -Wformat=2, but that's a static check, not a HIP build. Could someone with a HIP setup compile this one file?
- Actually seeing the new timeout line. It needs the real #2188 stop (GPU + adaptive tier + STRATA_ADAPT_OVERLAP=1), and the STRATA_TEST_VERIFY_STALL hook stalls the window's flag waits, not the gate, so it can't fake it either. The #2188 reporters: a rerun on this branch with STRATA_VERIFY_TRACE=1 would give the evidence the thread needs.
- SYCL. The sycl tree has no adaptive gate at all (no adapt_gate_wait there), so this file is not built for SYCL.

## Limits

The python tests exercise calibrate.py against a fake engine; nothing crashes a real engine end to end in the tests. And this doesn't fix #2188, it only prints the values its diagnosis needs.

pulls.title: bench: community report, RX 7900 XTX on Windows 11, IQ2_XS and Coder IQ1_M at 262K
pulls.author: IREvil
pulls.body:
Adds `bench/results/2026-10-17-community-rx-7900-xtx/`: two Qwen3.8-Flash-Next quantizations at the model's native **262,144-token context** on an **RX 7900 XTX 24 GB under Windows 11**, with the prebuilt HIP engine (0.1.44.1), on a **64 GB** machine. The [existing 7900 XTX Windows report](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/blob/main/bench/results/2026-10-06-community-rx-7900-xtx/README.md) covers IQ3_S with 192 GB, so this one is the same card on a typical RAM size and a different pair of quants.

## What's in it

| | Chat decode | 4K prompt | 16K prompt | 32K prompt | Agent decode | HumanEval |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Flash-Next IQ2_XS | **80.2** tok/s | 1,198 tok/s | 1,367 tok/s | 1,279 tok/s | **90.2** tok/s | 81/82 |
| Coder IQ1_M | 65.6 tok/s | **1,568** tok/s | **1,631** tok/s | **1,567** tok/s | 83.4 tok/s | **82/82** |

- `iq2_xs/`, `coder-iq1_m/` — the stock `tools/strata_bench.py --long` suite, 3 runs per test, with the tool's own `results.json` and `engine-log-excerpt.txt`
- `long-context/` — a sweep past the suite's 32K ceiling out to **255K prompt tokens**, with the adapted `bench/bench_vs_llama.py` used for it included. Prefill stays within 10% of its 32K value and decode within 7-14% of its 4K value; a 255K prompt is ingested in **3.2 min (Coder) / 3.7 min (IQ2_XS)**
- `humaneval/` — an 82-problem execution-graded check per model, runner included

The two quants trade places: Coder ingests prompts 24-33% faster, IQ2_XS decodes 22% faster.

## The Windows-specific part

On a 64 GB machine the **commit limit (RAM + page file), not RAM or VRAM**, was what capped the GPU expert cache. With the 48 GB page file this machine came with, the engine dropped from its planned 11083 slots to **3667 (4.93 GiB)** — a symptom visible only in the log (`cudaMalloc ... commit left`) — and warned that it could exit silently at the ceiling (`0xC0000409`, #1607) while RAM was still free. Raising the page file to 64 GB removed the warning and the cache reached **9903 slots / 13.26 GiB**.

## Notes and limitations

- One session per model. Single decode runs vary widely; differences of a few percent between the two quants are not meaningful, the ~25-33% prefill gap is.
- The long-context sweep is a different session and prompt construction from the stock suite. Compare it within its own table, not across tables.
- No needle/recall or tool-calling test was run; HumanEval is the only correctness check here.
- Windows AMD currently can't do images (no image encoder in the Windows AMD engine), one card per model, no calibration, no `rocm-smi` telemetry.
- The dense-27B figures in the appendix are **llama.cpp**, not Strata, and are labelled as such.
- Results only: no engine, serve, setup or documentation code is touched.

pulls.title: Metal: hc matrices of any format quantized to Q8_0 at load; gemv for IQ3_XXS and IQ2_S
pulls.author: tolstenko
pulls.body:
## What it changes

Two related fixes in `metal/`, both hit while running **uncensored fine-tune GGUFs of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on Apple Silicon** (files whose hc/attention tensors are quantized differently from the original and the Unsloth releases). `metal/` only; the CUDA/HIP builds are untouched.

### 1. The hyper-connection read assumed BF16/Q8_0/F32 hc tensors

`Window::init`'s HC-Q8 step (metal/src/engine/window.cpp) only quantized `hc_` matrices that were already **BF16**; Q8_0 and F32 were read natively by `gr_down_8_8`/`gr_down_q8_8_8`/`gr_up*`. A fine-tune that re-quantized those tensors to **IQ3_S (down/inject) and IQ4_NL (up)** made the host pick the plain kernels, which read the bytes of a different format. The logits came out NaN on the first decode; the sampler's all-NaN path returned token **2147483647** (the `bi = 0x7fffffff` sentinel in sample.metal's `argmax_part`), the server surfaced it as `IndexError: token id 2147483647 is outside the vocabulary`, and the engine then segfaulted in `iq3s_grid` inside `mtp_encode` when the drafter gathered the embedding of that bogus token.

The fix is in the loader, not new kernels: the HC-Q8 step now takes `hc_` matrices of **every** quantized format (skips only Q8_0/F32, which the file's own kernels already read, and `*_norm`), dequantizes from the tensor's own type, and quantizes to Q8_0 once at load — the same treatment BF16 tensors already got. `gr_down_q8`/`gr_up_q8` then handle them unchanged.

### 2. `gemv.metal` was missing IQ3_XXS and IQ2_S

`moe.metal` instantiates both (expert gate/up), but plain `gemv` did not — so a model with an IQ3_XXS shared-expert gate (`ffn_gate_shexp`) or an IQ2_S attention projection failed with `no function gemv_18_16_1_4_1` / `gemv_22_16_1_4_1` (exit 3) before its first token. Added `GV_SET(T_IQ3_XXS)` and `GV_SET(T_IQ2_S)` to the default `GEMV_TYPES`.

## Measured (M2 Max, 96 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6.2)

With **RVN Uncensored IQ3_S** (88.9 GB merged GGUF, experts streamed from the SSD, `--spec 2` + MTP):

- Before: first request → `token id 2147483647 is outside the vocabulary (248320)`; direct CLI run → SIGSEGV in `iq3s_grid` (stack: `mtp_encode` ← `mtp_draft`).
- After: `/health` → `"loaded": true`; completions return real text; **decode 9.0-10.4 tok/s** (51-token story in 4.9 s), MTP drafting 19/32 accepted. The HC-Q8 step logs `290 matrices, 680 MB, made in 222 ms`.
- Same run, warm prompt (25 tokens): 107 ms/token prompt, 95.7 ms/token decode.
- The OrcaRouter Uncensored IQ3_XXS pack (2 shards, 85.2 GB) hits the same two failures on stock main; with this patch its remaining pipeline (metal_repack + iq_pack --compat-bf16) reaches a loaded server as well.

The HC-Q8 conversion is a one-time per-load cost (222 ms); resident and streaming modes both quantize only the hc matrices, everything else keeps the file's own kernels, so the validated packs' paths are unchanged. `STRATA_HC_Q8=0` still selects the exact-BF16 read for files whose hc tensors are BF16.

## What I did not test

- CUDA/HIP: the change is entirely under `metal/` (and the two files it touches are Mac-only paths).
- Intel Macs; other chips than the M2 Max.
- A full quality benchmark of the fine-tunes (the replies are coherent; the needles and KL numbers in docs/MAC.md were not re-run).

Happy to add anything else the review wants measured.

Fixes the failure mode behind: running a non-validated quantization of the model on the Mac engine — the engine refused with a missing-function error (clear) or silently produced NaN tokens (not clear) depending on which tensor hit first.

pulls.title: [Engine] serve: the drain's deadline bounds the whole drain again, not just each chunk header
pulls.author: ctr-137
pulls.body:
`_drain_body`'s docstring says what the drain promises:

> *What has not arrived DRAIN_SECONDS later is left unread: the limit is time, so that a conversation of many
> megabytes, at any speed the client has, still gets its answer.*

The timeout was armed **once per chunk**, at the header, and the chunk was then read with

```python
piece = self.rfile.read(min(left, 1 << 20))
```

which waits for that whole buffer inside one call, looping over socket recvs internally.  Each recv is bounded; the
call is not.  A client that keeps a byte arriving inside the window — comfortably inside it — holds the drain
**for ever**: one MiB announced at one byte every 0.25 s is about three days, and the announced size is bounded only
by `body_limit()` (256 MiB by default).

The route only has to answer *before* reading the body for the drain to run at all, which `GET /nope` (a 404) does.

### The change

The two things that make the bound real are the pair its sibling already uses, in `_drain_body`'s own
Content-Length loop:

- re-arm the deadline before **every** read (`armed()`), so it is checked per socket read and not per chunk;
- `read1`, so one iteration **is** one socket read — the sibling's comment says it: *"one socket read: read() would
  wait for it all"*.

I wrote the first of those two alone first, and it was not enough: the re-armed deadline still sat in front of a
`read()` that would not come back for days.  The test added here is what showed it, and it is what would catch a
regression of either half.

**Scope:** only the drain passes a deadline, and it reads with `keep=False`, so every added branch is inert on the
real body path — a chunked body from `_body()` and the control body both pass no deadline.  The connection is
HTTP/1.0 and ends with the answer either way, so ending the drain early can only ever drop a body that was going to
be dropped.

### How this was checked

Two cases added to `serve/test_chunked_body.py`.

The trickle case: a 404 route that reads no body, 1 MiB announced, one byte every 0.25 s, `DRAIN_SECONDS` 1.0.
**Without the fix it fails** — the client times out at 10.2 s because the drain never gives up — and with it the
connection is let go in 1.6 s.

The control: a complete 2 MiB chunked body is still read in full, and gets the answer that body deserves (a 400 about
the *context*, not about the framing).  That is there because the re-arming must be inert when nothing rushed the
body.

No regressions: `python -m unittest discover -s serve` → 850 tests, 2 failures and 1 error, and **all three fail on
unmodified `main` as well**:

- `test_winjob` — a `tasklist` invocation returns `None` in this environment;
- `test_keepawake` — waits on keep-awake callbacks with `wait_for`, fails alone on `main`;
- `test_responses` — counts threads named `(_loop)` globally, fails alone on `main`.

Both of those last two are load- and order-dependent, which is why the same pair of files failed *differently* in
each arm across runs; each fails on `main` on its own.

There is no issue for this; it came out of a static audit of the tree rather than a report.  Happy to file one if you
would rather triage it there first.



### Follow-up from review (midhatn)

The header/extension and trailer lines were still read with `readline()`, and the two-byte chunk terminator with `read(2)` — one call may make several recvs, and the timeout armed before it bounds each recv, not the call. With a 200 ms deadline and a byte every 40 ms that was 750 ms (header) and 765 ms (trailer).

`read_line()` / `read_exact()` now use `read1` and re-arm the deadline before every socket read when a deadline is set; with no deadline the original `readline()` / `read()` path is unchanged. Three regression tests cover a trickled header/extension, trailer and terminator.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

pulls.title: feat(sycl): opt-in fdinfo-only sampler for Intel GPU load and VRAM
pulls.author: pankleks
pulls.body:
## Summary

Refs #2921. Companion to #2924, **not** a replacement for the server-side idle-telemetry fix. The two PRs use separate branches off `main` and share no changed files.

Intel GPU load and resident VRAM come from `/run/gpustat.json`. The supplied root sampler can provide them, but its full mode also continuously reads temperature, energy, clock and PCIe sensors. Installing that full sampler can therefore undo the benefit of stopping the server's own sensor reads after idle unload.

This adds **opt-in `GPUSTAT_FDINFO_ONLY=1`** to the existing sampler:

- Reuse its DRM fdinfo parser to publish selected-card load and resident VRAM to the same JSON file. No hwmon discovery/reads, power/temperature/fan/frequency sampling, PCIe-link reads or `lspci` call on this path. Card discovery and VRAM-capacity detection still read static sysfs metadata at import.
- Filter by `drm-pdev` before deduplicating DRM client IDs, so another card's clients cannot supply the selected card's numbers in this mode. Existing no-argument `clients()` behavior is unchanged.
- Report unknown load for first/reset/stalled intervals rather than a fabricated zero; report zero load/resident VRAM with no clients. Clamp the sum of client duty cycles at 100%, as the existing sampler does.
- Keep the default full hardware sampler intact. Add a documented systemd override; no automatic installation/enabling, new dependency, public API or engine change.
- Document the existing `GPUSTAT_VRAM_MB` override for SR-IOV/ReBAR cases. On the tested 32 GiB B70, the largest-resource heuristic selected a 56 GiB VF reservation; specifying 32768 MiB fixes the display. **This PR does not change that default heuristic.**

## Validation

- Windows: `python -m unittest tools.test_gpustat_fdinfo tools.test_setup_sycl` â€” **22 passed**.
- Linux: `python -m unittest tools.test_gpustat_fdinfo` â€” **4 passed**.
- Tests cover counter intervals/empty clients/clamping, a complete fdinfo-only publish with hardware helpers forbidden, unchanged default full-sampler fields, and per-card filtering before client-ID deduplication.
- Compared the original full-sampler `main()` AST with the new body after its opt-in dispatch: identical. No C++/CUDA/HIP/Metal source or build change.
- Candidate upstream code on the B70: executed its real fdinfo-only idle publish into a separate test file, verified no clients/zero resident VRAM and 32768 MiB configured total, and verified the existing Intel reader consumes that file. Production service/output were not replaced by this PR test.
- An **equivalent small local wrapper** using the same upstream fdinfo parser and load calculation is already running in an unprivileged Linux container on an Arc Pro B70, Strata 0.1.45 / Linux 7.0.14-24-pve. It restored live load (up to 100% during a 512-token-cap inference) and resident VRAM (~28.3 / 32 GiB). After unload, fresh no-client JSON and paused Monitor GPU fields were confirmed; passive PM counters with the wrapper alive showed +65,646 ms suspended / +9,359 ms active over ~75 seconds, starting/ending suspended. **Those live inference/PM numbers are from the local wrapper, not the exact new upstream mode.**

The sampler option alone does not stop the server's separate hardware reader; #2924 addresses that. No independent wattage reduction, uninterrupted suspend, exact-candidate inference/PM run, multi-GPU hardware run or engine rebuild is claimed. Ready for review as an Intel/xe-only, opt-in Python sampler change; the exact-candidate hardware validation limits above still apply. No private configuration or credentials included.

pulls.title: fix(sycl): pause GPU telemetry while the model is unloaded
pulls.author: pankleks
pulls.body:
## Summary

Fixes #2921

Stop the SYCL Monitor's once-per-second GPU sensor reads while the model is unloaded. The HTTP server stays up, CPU/RAM/disk/server metrics continue, and the next inference still loads the model normally.

- `Telemetry` accepts an optional `gpu_active` predicate. Only SYCL supplies it (`Service.loaded`); CUDA/HIP/Metal and callers that omit it retain their existing sampling path.
- Paused GPU fields are absent/unknown, not a stale value or a fabricated zero-watt reading. The existing Monitor renders unavailable values as a dash.
- `_XeGpu.pause()` clears only its energy-delta baseline, so the first resumed power sample is not averaged over the unloaded interval.
- The explicit pre-load/free-VRAM reader is unchanged. No model/config/API/engine/kernel/firmware/power-policy changes and no new dependency.

## Validation

- Four focused regression tests cover service wiring (SYCL only), two-card pause/resume without hardware reads, CPU/RAM/server metrics while paused, backward compatibility with readers without `pause()`, and Intel energy-baseline reset.
- Linux: `python -m unittest serve.test_server serve.test_monitor serve.test_prometheus tools.test_telemetry_idle` â€” **357 tests passed**.
- Setup and existing AMD/Mac telemetry tests plus the focused tests â€” **30 passed**.
- Live Intel Arc Pro B70 / xe, Strata 0.1.45, IQ3_XXS / 262,144 context: streaming text, arithmetic, tool-call JSON, synthetic tool result and final answer passed; explicit unload followed by a fresh inference successfully auto-reloaded the model and resumed GPU telemetry. Config hash and 600-second idle policy stayed unchanged.
- Polling `/metrics` once per second for 120 seconds while unloaded: all 120 responses remained unloaded, GPU power/temperature absent, and CPU/RAM metrics available. Simultaneous passive PM counters recorded **+104,619 ms suspended / +15,384 ms active** over ~120 seconds, comparable to stopping the server in the original isolation test. An earlier equivalent run recorded +105,566 ms suspended / +14,437 ms active. The card still has transient wakeups (the final interval ended active/usage=0 and a later check was suspended); this is not a claim of uninterrupted suspend or that every wake source has been isolated.

This is not a claim of a measured wattage reduction: no independent power meter was used, and no GPU sensor reads were made by the PM observation. No CUDA/HIP/Metal GPU hardware run, engine rebuild, long-context benchmark, or sustained-load test was performed for this Python-only change. Inference sources and binaries are unchanged.

Ready for review: only SYCL enables the new pause predicate; other backends retain their existing sampling behavior. The hardware-validation limits above still apply.

pulls.title: [Engine] ple: no per-row MADV_WILLNEED on a locked table (#2281)
pulls.author: thc1006
pulls.body:
## Problem and result

With `--ple-io ram`, the PLE table is locked in RAM when it opens. On Linux and macOS, `PleTable::gather_batch` still calls `madvise(MADV_WILLNEED)` for every row it reads: 16 calls per token, on the prompt path and in the decode windows. Those pages are already resident. This change makes the POSIX branch of the hint return when the table is locked.

On ZFS, each of those calls becomes an ARC prefetch of the record that holds the row. When the record is not in the ARC, it is read from disk. #2281 has the trace and the source links.

Measured on 4x Tesla P100 with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ3_XXS, the root file system on ZFS and an 8 GiB ARC (details below):

| `--ple-io ram`, new ~16K-token prompts | prefill tok/s | disk reads per prompt |
|---|---:|---:|
| 0.1.45, default | 466-479 | 17.2-18.4 GB |
| 0.1.45, `--no-ple-prefetch` | 685-705 | 0.00 GB |
| this branch, default | 685-706 | 0.00-0.01 GB |

Each row is two fresh server starts with the same three prompts. Per prompt, this branch is within 0.3% of `--no-ple-prefetch`, and the answers were byte-identical in every run. Decode was 2.3% slower with the hint. This branch decoded 0.2-0.3% below 0.1.45 with `--no-ple-prefetch`, and so did this branch with the flag (run 7), which never reaches the new line.

I also copied the table to an ext4 file system in a loop file on the same ZFS pool. There the hint made little difference: 0.1.45 prefilled at 684-707 tok/s with and without `--no-ple-prefetch`, within 0.5% per prompt, and decoded within 0.4%. If your 2x A4000 machine is not on ZFS, this fits what you saw there.

ben0112's machine also has the model on ZFS (#2571). On POSIX, `--no-ple-prefetch` turns off only this hint, so on a locked table this branch skips the same calls as the flag that fixed it there. I have not run the branch on that machine.

## Related discussion

Issue: #2281 (closed). There, `--no-ple-prefetch`, the second toggle you suggested, brought ben0112's speed back, and @ben0112 suggested skipping the hint once `--ple-io ram` has locked the table. ben0112 also offered to test a patch build. This is that change.

## Approach

- `src/kernels/ngram.cpp`: the POSIX branch of `hint` in `gather_batch` returns when `impl_->locked` is set. On POSIX, `locked` is only set after `mlock` of the whole table succeeds, so a table whose lock failed keeps its hints. Besides configs that ask for `--ple-io ram`, setup writes it on Linux when the model is on a rotational disk and the RAM has room for the table on top of the model (#605).
- `src/ngram/ple_reader_test.cpp`: `format_round_trip` gets a third leg, "ram" (mmap with `lock`). It checks `read_row`, `gather` and `gather_batch` on a locked table against each format's dequantizer. If `mlock` is refused, the leg reads the table unlocked and prints a note. Values cannot show the hint, so on Linux with glibc the test also counts the `MADV_WILLNEED` calls (it defines `madvise` and passes each call on): `gather_batch` must make some on a mapped table that is not locked, and none on a locked one. A new check, `row_hints_follow_the_lock`, opens one small table with `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK` at 0 (the lock is refused and the hints stay), then locked (no hints, the same values), then again without the lock (the hints are back), and checks `locked()` against `VmLck`. Where `mlock` cannot succeed, the cases that need a lock print a note instead. Where it succeeds but locks nothing (ASan and TSan make it a no-op), `row_hints_follow_the_lock` prints a note.

## Validation

Re-run on 0.2.0-beta (`3d1fb48`) with this branch applied (it applies without conflicts), on Linux with glibc, as a user without `CAP_IPC_LOCK`. The selftest was built for the CPU only from `src/kernels/ngram.cpp`, `src/ngram/ple_reader.cpp`, `src/platform/direct_file.cpp` and `src/ngram/ple_reader_test.cpp` (g++ 11.4, `-std=c++20 -O2 -pthread`).

**Passed:**

- `ple_reader_test --selftest` on 0.2.0-beta with this branch, with `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK` at 7.85 GiB, 64 KiB and 0: every check OK, the NVFP4 format that 0.2.0-beta adds included. At 7.85 GiB: `ple row hints (Linux): kept on a refused lock, none on a locked table, back after reopening it without the lock: OK`.
- The same selftest with the `locked` check removed from `ngram.cpp` fails: `a locked table: gather_batch made 256 row hints, not 0`.
- Earlier, on 0.1.45 (`477ac13`):
  - With the `locked` check removed, `ple_reader_test --selftest` fails: "a locked table: gather_batch made 256 row hints, not 0". It also fails for six other wrong versions of `ngram.cpp`, among them one that checks whether the lock was requested instead of whether it succeeded, and one whose `close()` leaves `locked` set. These runs were on Linux with glibc, as a user without `CAP_IPC_LOCK`, with `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK` at 7.85 GiB and at 64 KiB. The versions and the output are in [`results/pr2918-mutants.diff.txt`](https://github.com/thc1006/strata-p100-deployment/blob/main/results/pr2918-mutants.diff.txt) and [`results/pr2918-test-mutants.txt`](https://github.com/thc1006/strata-p100-deployment/blob/main/results/pr2918-test-mutants.txt).
  - `ctest -R '^ple_reader_selftest$'` passes on `5c5aded` in the CUDA and HIP builds (the selftest runs on the CPU), with `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK` at 7.85 GiB, 64 KiB and 0. At 64 KiB only the 512-row table in `row_hints_follow_the_lock` can be locked, and at 0 none can.
  - Built on `5c5aded`, which differs from the head only in its commit message: the CUDA engine (CUDA 12.9.1, sm_60, the flags setup.py uses for a CUDA 12 build), the HIP engine for gfx1100 (ROCm 7.10.0a20251120 from TheRock's wheels, configured as setup.py does) and the SYCL engine (oneAPI DPC++ 2026.1.1 with oneMKL 2026.1.0, SPIR-V JIT, configured as `sycl/tools/build.sh` does). The HIP build shows no compiler warning in the two changed files, and the SYCL build, which does not build the test, none in `ngram.cpp`. The Mac engine is not built here; with clang 21 from zig 0.16.0 and `-Wall -Wextra`, both files compile without warnings for macOS (arm64 and x86_64).

**Failed:**

- none observed

**Not run:**

- On 0.2.0-beta: the engine builds (CUDA, HIP, SYCL), their ctest runs and the speed runs. The hint code this branch changes is the same in 0.2.0-beta as in 0.1.45.
- Windows, macOS, the HIP and SYCL engines on a GPU (I have no AMD or Intel GPU), this branch on ext4, a larger ARC, bare metal, and ben0112's machine.

## Limits

Not changed: the whole-table hint when the table opens, `--ple-io mmap`, `--ple-io direct`, `--no-ple-prefetch`, and Windows. On Windows the hint in `gather_batch` is one `PrefetchVirtualMemory` call per window of up to 4096 rows, and `gather`, `issue` and `prefetch_rows` hint there too; I have no Windows machine to measure a change on. With this branch and `--ple-io mmap`, the engine made the same 767,936 `madvise` calls in three prompts as 0.1.45 with `--ple-io ram`.

<details><summary>Where the time goes on ZFS</summary>

ben0112's last comment in #2281 puts the cost on the ZFS ARC, competing for disk I/O and memory bandwidth. The disk reads are ARC prefetch misses: 17-18 GB per prompt read into an 8 GiB ARC. Inside the hint, though, the threads almost never blocked. In a pass with kprobes on the engine's threads, the threads that issue the hints entered `zpl_fadvise` 768,192 times, slept there 3 times and were preempted 8,553 times. `arc_wait_for_eviction` never slept and took 1.0% of their time in `zpl_fadvise`.

The cost showed up as CPU time, including ZFS's work to complete the prefetch reads. System time on the whole machine (8 vCPUs) averaged 3-5 s per prompt without the hint and 37 s with it. At least 15.8 s of that was in ZFS's read-completion threads (`z_rd_int`). Under ftrace, `zpl_fadvise` averaged 39 µs a call counting only time on a CPU, and 95-96 µs counting time off the CPU too. I did not measure memory bandwidth.

</details>

<details><summary>Environment and method</summary>

- 4x Tesla P100 PCIe 16 GB (driver 535.230.02), VMware VM, 8 vCPUs (Xeon E5-2696 v4), 62.8 GiB of RAM.
- Ubuntu 22.04.5, kernel 6.8.0-138. Root on ZFS: OpenZFS kernel module 2.2.2-0ubuntu9.4, recordsize 128K, lz4. `zfs_arc_max` is 8 GiB, to leave RAM for the locked table and the experts.
- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next GSQ-RCO IQ3_XXS. The PLE table is in shard 2: 320,001,536 rows x 90 B = 26.8 GiB. `VmLck` was 28,125,136 kB in every `ram` run.
- 0.1.45 (`477ac13`) and this branch on top of it, built from two checkouts with the same flags. The engine measured here was built from `c1c9e57`, the first push, which has the same `ngram.cpp`.
- Server: 4 slots, layer split 13,26,38. Engine flags (abridged): `--max-context 32768 --kv int8 --expert-cache auto --prefill 2048 --pool-workers 6 --batch-groups auto --vram-reserve-mib 1536 --ple-io ram --spec 4 --spec-min-p 0.5 --resident-experts --trim-stage-weights --no-kv-grow --conversation-cache-mib 8192`.
- Raw data, the probe scripts and the build logs: [strata-p100-deployment](https://github.com/thc1006/strata-p100-deployment), in particular `results/AB-0.1.45-ple-hint.md` and `results/pr2918-*.txt`.
- Each run is a fresh server start under systemd with `LimitMEMLOCK=infinity`, one request at a time. Prompts are slices of Strata's own docs with a fixed nonce in front, so every run gets the same bytes. Nothing was reused: the engine logged 0 reused tokens for all 141 prompt reads. Temperature 0, thinking off. Three prompts of ~16K tokens with 32 tokens out, and three decodes of up to 512 tokens.
- Speeds are the engine's own figures. Disk reads are the sectors read in `/sys/block/sda/sda4/stat` (the pool's only partition, as the VM sees it) times 512 bytes, read before and after each request. System time is the `system` column of `/proc/stat`. No run that recorded steal time had any.
- The traced passes ran on other prompts, after the untraced ones: `perf stat -p <engine pid>` for the `madvise` counts, ftrace's function profiler (once more in run 3, counting only time on a CPU), and the kprobe pass in run 8. Tracing slows the hint, so none of the speeds in this description comes from a traced request.
- ext4: the PLE shard was copied to an ext4 file system on a loop file, itself on the ZFS pool. Shard 1 is a symlink back to ZFS, so that `--native` and `--ple-gguf` name the same directory. The locked table then comes from ext4's page cache.

</details>

<details><summary>Every run, in order</summary>

Prefill and decode are ratios to the first `--no-ple-prefetch` run on the same file system (run 1 on ZFS, run 9 on ext4). Each value is the mean ratio over the same three requests.

| # | file system | build | flags | prefill | decode | disk reads per prompt | engine `madvise`, 3 prompts |
|---:|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | ZFS | 0.1.45 | `--no-ple-prefetch` | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.00 GB | 192 |
| 2 | ZFS | branch | default | 1.000 | 0.997 | 0.01 GB | 192 |
| 3 | ZFS | 0.1.45 | default | 0.678 | 0.977 | 17.2-18.1 GB | 767,936 |
| 4 | ZFS | branch | default | 1.001 | 0.997 | 0.00-0.01 GB | 192 |
| 5 | ZFS | 0.1.45 | `--no-ple-prefetch` | 1.002 | 0.999 | 0.00 GB | 192 |
| 6 | ZFS | branch | `--ple-io mmap` | 0.293 | 0.812 | 17.2-17.8 GB | 767,936 |
| 7 | ZFS | branch | `--no-ple-prefetch` | 1.000 | 0.997 | 0.00-0.01 GB | 192 |
| 8 | ZFS | 0.1.45 | default | 0.675 | 0.977 | 17.8-18.4 GB | 767,936 |
| 9 | ext4 | 0.1.45 | `--no-ple-prefetch` | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.00-0.03 GB | 192 |
| 10 | ext4 | 0.1.45 | default | 1.000 | 1.002 | 0.00-0.01 GB | 767,936 |
| 11 | ext4 | 0.1.45 | `--no-ple-prefetch` | 1.002 | 1.000 | 0.00-0.02 GB | 192 |
| 12 | ext4 | 0.1.45 | default | 0.998 | 1.002 | 0.00-0.03 GB | 767,936 |

Run 6 only checks that the hint is still sent without a lock. Its page cache was not controlled, so its speed is not comparable.

</details>

pulls.title: [Engine] serve: the handler's connection has a deadline, so a peer that has stopped cannot own the server
pulls.author: ctr-137
pulls.body:
A client that has stopped — a silently dead one (no RST, no FIN), or one still connected that never reads its
streamed answer — can own a handler thread for good and, worse, the **engine's single turn**.  This gives the
handler's connection a deadline, and everything else that was needed was already written.

### What happens now

The SSE loop writes with `self.wfile.write()` while the generator is suspended inside the `ExitStack` that holds the
fifo (`Service.request`), so every later request queues behind a stream nobody is reading:

```python
with turn:                                     # holds the fifo while the generator is suspended here
    ...
for c in chunks:
    self.wfile.write(b"data: " + json.dumps(c, ...) + b"\n\n")   # blocks here, turn still held
```

The disconnect watcher (#430 #431) cannot see this.  It polls the socket for *readability* and treats EOF as a
hang-up, which catches a client that closed; a client that is connected and simply not reading is not readable, and
the watcher never closes or shuts down the socket, so it cannot release a write that is already blocked.

### The change

```python
PEER_STALL_S = _timeout_env("STRATA_PEER_STALL_S", 120.0)
...
class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    timeout = PEER_STALL_S        # socketserver applies it to the connection in setup()
```

`socketserver.StreamRequestHandler.setup()` does `if self.timeout is not None: self.connection.settimeout(...)`, so
this is the deadline for **every socket operation the handler makes** — the request line, the body, and the writes.
That covers three sites of one class at once, including one the audit did not have: a client that connects and sends
nothing at all, not even a request line, parked a thread just as well.

Nothing else had to be written, because the recovery already exists in two places:

- the SSE loop's `except OSError` notes the outcome, calls `cancel.set()` and `chunks.close()` — and closing the
  generator unwinds `with turn:`, which releases the turn;
- `BaseHTTPRequestHandler.handle_one_request` catches `TimeoutError` around the whole `do_<method>()` call —
  *"a read or a write timed out.  Discard this connection"* — as a backstop for anything that escapes the above.

It fires only when nothing has moved in either direction for that long, so a client that is sending or reading,
however slowly, is never cut off.  `0` switches it off (wait for ever, as before).

### How this was checked

**Measured against the real server**, as shipped versus with a 2 s deadline:

| | as shipped | with the deadline |
|---|---|---|
| a client that connects and sends nothing | still connected after 6 s; the thread is parked | connection ended after **2.0 s** |
| a client stops reading a stream; a second client asks a short question | **no answer within 30 s** — the turn is held | answered after **1.0 s** |

**`serve/test_connection_deadline.py`** (new, 4 tests) makes both of those regressions permanent: a silent client's
connection is ended at the deadline; a stream nobody reads no longer holds the turn; a reader *slower than the
writer* still receives the whole stream; and `0` switches it off.  All four need no GPU and no engine.

With the `timeout` attribute removed and everything else left in place, **two of the four fail** — the silent client
and the held turn — and the other two pass.  That is the pair of defects exactly.

**No regressions:** `python -m unittest discover -s serve` → 852 tests, one error, in `test_winjob.py`, which fails
the same way on unmodified `main` (a `tasklist` invocation returning `None` on this machine).

### What I left alone

Nothing about the body read.  `serve/test_request_hardening.py`'s case (#2814, pull #2910) gives the body its own
deadline and answers 408, because a body that stops arriving deserves an answer rather than a discarded connection.
With this in place that one is belt-and-braces: if you would rather have a single knob, `BODY_STALL_S` can fold into
`PEER_STALL_S`.

There is no issue for this; it came out of a static audit of the tree rather than a report.  Happy to file one if you
would rather triage it there first.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

pulls.title: [Engine] Conversation cache: park and restore conversations through session files
pulls.author: dsenchankau
pulls.body:
## Problem and result

I took this PR idea from [Maya](https://github.com/mw00/project-maya), a GLM5.3-Flash fork of Strata, where the disk conversation cache is on by default.

Right now the conversation cache has 2 options: keep it in RAM, or don't use it at all.

RAM is fine with a smaller quant (IQ3_S) and plenty of system RAM (96GB with that quant). It gets tight with a bigger quant like UD-Q4_K_XL, or with less system RAM.

UD-Q4_K_XL's experts are way bigger, and after startup the OS overhead + model + engine + coding harness have already eaten (almost) all the RAM. That leaves you two bad options: offload some experts to disk and lose decode and prefill speed, or skip the RAM cache and re-process the prompt over and over (slower the bigger the model gets).

For performance, the better move is to move the conversation cache to disk and keep more of the model's experts in RAM.

Without a cache, a conversation that comes back re-reads its whole prompt. With the cache on disk it's read back from its file and picks up where it left off. The re-reading gets worse the longer the session runs, but reading from the file stays about as cheap no matter how long it's been, so the disk cache pays off across a working session. You notice it most when you're using subagents a lot and bouncing between the main session and side ones. I measured the park/restore part (see Validation); I didn't run a reprocessing-vs-restore timing test, so I'm not putting a speedup number on it.

With this change, `--conversation-cache-disk-mib N` parks conversations into `conv-*.sess` files under `<pack>/conversation_cache`, and the budget counts the file bytes, so a lot more stay parked than would fit in RAM. A conversation that comes back on a later turn (same run, or after a restart) is read back from its file and continues from its own state instead of re-reading its prompt. It's off by default, the way the repo wants new features.

## Approach

- `include/strata/core/conversation_cache.hpp` - disk mode: `enable_disk`, `put_disk` (budget counts file bytes), the slim folder-index entry, and the budget check that refuses an oversized entry before it touches anything already parked.
- `src/core/conversation_file.{hpp,cpp}` - meta-only read (`session_file_read_meta`) and the startup folder scan (`conversation_cache_index`) that keeps this model's fresh `conv-*.sess` and deletes foreign, stale or unreadable files. Reuses the session-file format that's already there.
- `src/program/generate.cpp` - the park and restore calls in the serve loop, plus the guards that skip parking (snapshot bigger than the whole budget, and RAM admission).
- `include/strata/core/{conversation_snapshot.hpp,session_save_reclaim.hpp}`, `src/core/conversation_state.cpp` - the meta/checkpoint plumbing the index and restore need.
- No `serve/` change: the engine flags go straight through the run-config `args`, so `server.py` is untouched.
- Tests: a disk-mode budget-refusal check in `conversation_cache_test.cpp`; `conversation_file_test.cpp` already covers the meta-only read and the folder scan.
- `docs/DETAILS.md` - the flag and the measured numbers.

## Validation

Revision `1aa35f01`. Environment: Linux `home-pc 7.0.0-38-generic #38~24.04.4-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC x86_64`, RTX 4080 SUPER (driver 615.71.10), CMake 3.28.3, Ninja 1.11.1, CUDA 13.4, Python 3.12.3.

Passed:

- Build (CUDA backend only; the change is common code, no backend sources or `#ifdef`):

  ```sh
  cmake -G Ninja -S . -B build-tests -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
    -DSTRATA_ENABLE_CUDA=ON -DSTRATA_BUILD_CONVERSATION_TESTS=ON \
    -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=89
  cmake --build build-tests -j "$(nproc)"
  ```

- The disk-cache unit tests (CPU-only), 5/5: `conversation_cache_test` (4789 checks), `conversation_file_test` (217 checks), plus `conversation_split_failure_test`, `conversation_memory_test` and `session_save_reclaim_test`:

  ```sh
  ctest --test-dir build-tests -R 'conversation_(cache|split_failure|memory|file)_test|session_save_reclaim_test' --output-on-failure
  ```

  5/5 passed, 1.46s.

- The engine conversation tests, 3/3. `conversation_snapshot_test` uses the GPU (passed in 1.11s on an idle card; it skips with code 77 when it can't get one). `conversation_validation_test` and `conversation_transfer_test` run with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=-1`:

  ```sh
  ctest --test-dir build-tests -R 'conversation_(snapshot|validation|transfer)_test' --output-on-failure
  ```

  3/3 passed, 1.17s.

- Full suite. `ctest --test-dir build-tests --output-on-failure` on the branch gives the same result as master: 96% passed, 6 failed out of 157, 1 skipped (`expert_multi_test`). Those 6 are the usual environment/hardware ones on both branches (`ple_parity` and `tq_cpu_parity` want fixtures that aren't in the published source; `ggml_tq_overlay`, `native_hadamard_test`, `tq_cpu_parity_avx2` want AMD/trellis hardware; `isa_guard_check` is a no-ISA check). So nothing new broke. Run this on a free GPU, or `conversation_snapshot_test` OOMs on whatever else is using the card.

- Engine run on one RTX 4080 SUPER, IQ3_S pack, greedy. I launched the model the normal way from its config, adding only `--conversation-cache-disk-mib 16384` to the run-config `args`:

  ```
  .venv/bin/python serve/server.py --engine strata --config strata-iq3_s.json --port 1337
  ```

  It parked `1962 tokens to disk (266,114,352 bytes)`, I restarted it, and it took back the same 1962 tokens from disk. The next turn only read the new part (`cached_tokens 1962`, `prompt_n 17`). The guards hold too: a snapshot bigger than the whole budget is refused and the folder stays empty, foreign files and a hand-edited `conv-hacked-9.sess` are deleted at startup, and `--conversation-cache-days 0` empties the folder.

- serve suite:

  ```sh
  PYTHONPATH=. .venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s serve
  ```

  881 run, 14 skipped, 1 failed. The one failure (`test_lifeline`: "the child outlived a killed server") is a process-watcher timing race. It's not from this change: `git diff upstream/main HEAD -- serve/` is empty, so I touched no serve file, and the test fails the same on master.

Failed: nothing here is caused by this change. The 6 C++ failures above are the same environment/hardware ones master has, with or without the branch, and the serve `test_lifeline` failure is a watcher race in a file this PR doesn't touch.

Not run: HIP and SYCL, build and run - I don't have AMD hardware. The change is common code only (no backend sources, no `#ifdef`), so it should be backend-agnostic, but that's me reading the code, not a build - call it unconfirmed static analysis. Someone with that hardware should build it, and run it once on each if they can. Metal I didn't build or run. The park/restore numbers above are NVIDIA/CUDA only.

## Limits

The park/restore measurement is one pack on one card (RTX 4080 SUPER). I'm not claiming a speedup on other hardware or quants beyond the reasoning above. The disk cache is opt-in, and I didn't change the RAM cache path or how its budget is counted. HIP and SYCL are unverified because I have no hardware for them.

pulls.title: [Other] fix(setup AMD): engine probes get the engine's lib_dirs on LD_LIBRARY_PATH on Linux (the PATH-only #2372 env made strata --families exit 127, so setup falsely refused Qwen3.6)
pulls.author: xxxliqu1dxxx
pulls.body:
## Problem and result

Setup's own engine probes (`strata --families`, `strata-device --list-devices`) only got the
engine's ROCm `lib_dirs` on `PATH` (#2372), which the dynamic loader only honors on Windows.
On AMD Linux the probes exited 127 on `libhipblas.so.3`, so `./setup.sh --backend hip` Step 4
falsely said "this engine does not run Qwen3.6-35B-A3B yet" while the local HIP engine does
run it. After the change, on POSIX the `lib_dirs` are prepended to `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (existing
value preserved); on Windows the `PATH` behavior is byte-identical. The probes exit 0.

## Related discussion

Follow-up to #2372 (commit 093108c). No open issue. Focused fix, no scope agreement needed.

## Approach

`engine_env` only: on POSIX, `lib_dirs` are prepended to `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` instead of `PATH`;
on Windows the `PATH` prepend is unchanged. Mirrors `serve/server.py`'s existing
`"PATH" if os.name == "nt" else "LD_LIBRARY_PATH"` choice. Left alone: the engine binary, the
build, the server launch env, the `engine_families` fallback, `hip_lib_dirs`, prebuilt Windows
engine handling.

## Validation

**Passed:**
- `python tools/test_setup_amd.py` — revision d409ec38 (rebased on main, 0.2.0-beta), local
  Windows PC (no GPU needed): 42 tests OK. Covers `EngineLaunchEnv`: the Windows `PATH`
  behavior (pinned to `os.name = "nt"`), the new `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` test (lib dir first,
  existing value preserved, `PATH` untouched), and the two probe tests.
- Live check on an AMD Linux box (Radeon RX 9060 series, gfx1200, 16 GB VRAM, 31 GB RAM,
  local HIP engine 0.1.45): `env = setup.engine_env(Path('engine'))` +
  `engine/strata --families` → rc 0, prints `qwen4exp qwen35moe` (previously exit 127).

**Failed:** none observed.

**Not run:** multi-GPU, Windows live run (no Windows AMD box), NVIDIA/CUDA paths (untouched by
the change).

## Limits

Only affects the two setup probe commands' environment on non-Windows. No behavior change on
Windows, in the engine, the build, or the server.

pulls.title: prefill: a fixed --prefill above 65280 tokens is capped, 65536 stopped the engine at the first longer prompt (#2743)
pulls.author: ischencheng
pulls.body:
Fixes #2743.

With a fixed `--prefill 65536`, the first prompt longer than 65536 tokens stops the engine with `iq_embed_rows: invalid argument`. The prompt path launches some kernels with one grid row per token of the chunk, and a grid's y is at most 65535. The token embedding is the first one, the GDN q/k norm in `gdn_conv` (`gdn_l2_kernel`) is the next.

This caps a named `--prefill` at 65280 (the largest multiple of 256 under the limit) and prints one line at start. `auto` never gets there (32768 at most), and named chunks up to 65280 are unchanged, so default starts are the same.

I also tried tiling those two launches instead. That ran the 65536 chunk on the setup below, but other launches take one row per token too (for example the peer gather in `src/prefill/kernels.cu`), and I could only test one pack and one card. A cap in one place covers paths I could not run. Happy to switch to the tiling version if you prefer it.

One L40S 48 GB (sm_89, Linux), IQ2_XS native pack, `--max-context 131072 --kv int8`, upstream main 477ac13c. Each start reads the same 70,433-token prompt with two codes in it, one in each chunk, then a short chat:

| build | `--prefill` | prompt path loan | 70K prompt | reply |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 65536 | 21323 slots | engine exits, `iq_embed_rows: invalid argument`, HTTP 503 | - |
| main | 65280 | 21242 slots | 4422 tok/s | `BLUE-4417, RED-9052` |
| this PR | 65536 (capped to 65280) | 21242 slots | 4362 tok/s | `BLUE-4417, RED-9052` |

The capped start runs the same as main at 65280: same loan, same replies, same draft counts. The two speeds are single runs.

`generate.cpp` with this change also compiles for HIP (gfx1201, ROCm 7.0), same warnings as main.

Not tested: Windows, the NVFP4 pack from the report, HIP on a GPU, a layer split. SYCL has its own `generate.cpp` and is not touched; I don't know its limit there. Qwen3.6 (`strata-q36 --chunk`) is a separate program and not touched.

pulls.title: [Engine] serve: a request body that stops arriving is answered, not parked
pulls.author: ctr-137
pulls.body:
`_body()` is the one body read in the server with no deadline.  A peer that announces a body and then says nothing — a
silently dead client, no RST and no FIN — parks the handler thread and its fd for good, and the disconnect watcher
that would have noticed starts only *after* the body has been read.

### The three body readers, and which one was the odd one out

The two others already bound their reads, in two different ways:

```python
def _control_body(self) -> bool:
    timeout = self.connection.gettimeout()
    try:
        self.connection.settimeout(2.0)
        complete = len(self.rfile.read(length)) == length
    except OSError:
        complete = False
    finally:
        self.connection.settimeout(timeout)
```

and `_drain_body()`, which passes `deadline=time.monotonic() + DRAIN_SECONDS` to `_read_chunked()` — a parameter
`_read_chunked()` already had and `_body()` did not pass:

```python
def _body(self) -> bytes:
    ...
    if self._chunked():
        return self._read_chunked(limit)          # no deadline
    ...
    return self.rfile.read(length)                # no deadline, one blocking read
```

### What changed

- `BODY_STALL_S` (`STRATA_BODY_STALL_S`, default 120 s, `0` = wait for ever as before), beside `body_limit()`, shaped
  like the engine's own read timeouts (#1317).  Generous on purpose: this is a stopped client's deadline, not a
  slow-client detector.
- `_body()` sets it on the connection for the read and restores the previous timeout in a `finally`, exactly as
  `_control_body()` does, and answers a read that gets nothing with **408** — the status a body problem already
  carries (`BadBody` → `self._json(e.status, ...)` in `do_POST`).

It is the wait for one read that gets nothing, not a bound on the whole body: a client that is sending, however
slowly, is never cut off, only one that has stopped.  A half-read body leaves the stream unusable, so
`close_connection` is set and the connection ends with the answer.

### Why the existing test file missed it

`test_request_hardening.py` covers the two neighbours and stops just short of this one: the oversized case announces
10 TiB, which the 413 refuses *unread*, and a half-close ends the read with a 400.  A **within-limit** body that
announces a length and sends nothing is the case nothing constructed.

### How this was checked

Three cases added to `serve/test_request_hardening.py`: a within-limit `Content-Length` and a chunked body, each
announcing a body and sending none, both must answer 408 — and the elapsed time is asserted too, or a client-side
timeout would pass the test as well.  A complete body still answers 200, with the deadline set and with it off.
That file's 13 tests pass and `test_chunked_body.py`'s 12 pass unchanged, with no GPU and no engine (they run
against `MockEngine`).

A three-arm probe against the real server — announce a body, send nothing, wait 8 s:

```
deadline 1 s          -> HTTP/1.0 408 Request Timeout after 1.0 s
deadline off          -> no answer within 8 s: the handler thread is parked and its fd is held
the code before this  -> no answer within 8 s: the same
```

The two arms that reproduce the bug are the two with no deadline.

### What I left alone

The response path is the same class and wants its own change: a streamed answer to a client that stops reading blocks
`self.wfile.write()` while the generator is suspended inside `with turn:`, so the engine's single turn is held and
every later request waits (`serve/server.py:5976`).  Its `except OSError` already does the right thing —
`cancel.set()`, `chunks.close()` — and `socket.timeout` is an `OSError`, so only a *send* deadline is missing there.
That is a separate pull request.

There is no issue for this; it came out of a static audit of the tree rather than a report.  Happy to file one if you
would rather triage it there first.
