pulls.title: native dense: upload the projection matrices from 8 threads through pinned staging (1.5 s -> 0.3 s)
pulls.author: page1
pulls.body:
## Title
Issue: none

## Summary
On Windows the shard mapping is not read ahead, so one synchronous `cudaMemcpy` per matrix took its page faults one at a time: 300 projection matrices, 2019 MiB, in 1.5 s. Now 8 threads copy them in 8 MiB pieces through pinned staging: 0.3 s. The GPU holds the same bytes (checksum below).

## What changed
- `src/core/native_dense.cpp`: the matrices are allocated as before, then copied in 8 MiB pieces by 8 threads. On Windows each thread reads its piece with `ReadFile` into a double-buffered pinned staging buffer and `cudaMemcpyAsync` on its own stream. Elsewhere, or if the file cannot be opened, a piece is copied from the mapping.
- `STRATA_DENSE_UPLOAD_THREADS=N` sets the threads; `1` keeps the serial path.
- `STRATA_DENSE_CHECKSUM=1` hashes the matrices as the GPU holds them: `e2a34e261e2077dd` for both the threaded and the serial path (IQ3_S, 300 matrices, on v0.1.44.1).

## Extra Notes
Measured on an RTX 3090 24 GB, Core Ultra 9 285K, 95 GB DDR5, WD SN8100, Windows 11 26300, IQ3_S at 262K context, against a source build of v0.1.44.1 (`296b59d2`) the same day. 6 + 6 server starts in a rotated order, `/health` polled every 0.25 s:

| | v0.1.44.1 | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| projection matrices (the engine's own line) | 1.5 s (every start) | **0.3 s** (every start) |
| server start to loaded, median (range) | 17.82 s (16.91-18.23) | 16.92 s (16.43-17.13) |
| decode at 1.7K / 61K tokens (3 + 3 starts) | 89.2 / 85.4 tok/s | 89.5 / 84.9 tok/s |
| prompt at 61K tokens | 2718 tok/s | 2699 tok/s |

Built: CUDA 13.4 (sm_86) only. **Not built for HIP or SYCL** (no ROCm or oneAPI here), and the non-Windows path (from the mapping) was not run. `native_dense.cpp` is part of the HIP build, so it needs a HIP build check.

pulls.title: pinned arena (Windows): touch the pages from 16 threads before cudaHostRegister (engine start 5.1 s sooner)
pulls.author: page1
pulls.body:
## Title
Issue: none

## Summary
On Windows with 4 KB pages, `cudaHostRegister` did the first touch (zero-fill) of the expert arena itself, on one thread: 4.98 s for 46.8 GiB here. Now min(16, cores) threads touch the pages first (0.5-1.2 s), and the registration then takes 0.08 s. The engine starts 5.1 s sooner; decode and prompt speed do not change.

## What changed
- `src/core/pinned.cu`: under `#ifdef _WIN32`, for `PageBacking::NormalPages` with no shared arena file, the pages are touched by min(16, hardware threads) threads before `cudaHostRegister`. The whole arena is still registered (`cudaHostRegister PORTABLE ok`). The time goes into the arena's log line.
- `STRATA_ARENA_PREFAULT=0` keeps the old order; `=N` sets the thread count.
- The old comment (a region faulted in page by page is far more expensive to register and may fail) did not hold here, and is reworded.

What it leaves alone: large pages, the shared arena file, Linux and macOS, and everything after loading.

## Extra Notes
Measured on an RTX 3090 24 GB, Core Ultra 9 285K, 95 GB DDR5, WD SN8100, Windows 11 26300, IQ3_S at 262K context, against a source build of v0.1.44.1 (`296b59d2`) the same day. 6 + 6 server starts in a rotated order, `/health` polled every 0.25 s:

| | v0.1.44.1 | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| server start to loaded, median (range) | 17.82 s (16.91-18.23) | **12.68 s** (12.38-12.93) |
| decode at 1.7K / 61K tokens (3 + 3 starts) | 89.2 / 85.4 tok/s | 90.0 / 84.8 tok/s |
| prompt at 61K tokens | 2718 tok/s | 2705 tok/s |

Built: CUDA 13.4 (sm_86) only. **Not built for HIP or SYCL**: there is no ROCm or oneAPI on this machine. `pinned.cu` is part of the HIP build, so it needs a HIP build check; the new code is all inside `#ifdef _WIN32`.

pulls.author: jkir4n
pulls.body:
## Summary
On narrow screens (phones), an assistant reply that contains a long unbroken string (URL, code line) or a wide table stretches the whole chat view past the viewport: the right side is clipped and unreachable, and the page (heading, composer) shifts with it. Three CSS changes keep the content inside the viewport.

## What changed
`serve/web/app.css` only, 3 rules:
- `.st-msg--assistant .st-bubble { overflow-wrap: anywhere; }` — assistant text now breaks long unbroken strings, the same way the user bubble already does.
- `.view { … min-width: 0; }` — `.view` is a flex item of `main`; with the default `min-width: auto` one wide message can push the whole view past the viewport (the file already pins `min-height: 0` for the column axis — same guard, inline axis).
- `.st-bubble table { … display: block; max-width: 100%; overflow-x: auto; }` — wide tables scroll inside their bubble instead of overflowing it.

## Extra Notes
Verified against 0.1.44.1 at 390×844 with three messages (long URL / long code line / wide table):
- before: the chat column measures 752 px wide, bubbles 718 px, right edge 346 px off-screen
- after: column 390 px, bubbles 356 px, everything on screen — the URL wraps, the code block scrolls inside itself, the table scrolls inside the bubble
- desktop (1280 px) unchanged, no overflow; normal prose unaffected

pulls.title: docs(MULTI_GPU): the layer split pays most when the CPU pool is the bottleneck
pulls.author: NorwinYu
pulls.body:
## Summary

One bullet in `docs/MULTI_GPU.md`'s "Which cards and in what order" list, qualifying the
existing "decode is on par with the faster card alone" note. Docs only; no code changes.

## Why

That "on par" conclusion was measured on an RTX 5080 + 3090 over a Ryzen 9 9950X3D — a fast
CPU where the CPU pool is never the thing the window waits on. On a machine where the CPU pool
*is* the bottleneck, the same split is a large decode win, not "on par".

## Measurement

2x identical RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB, dual-socket Xeon E5-2696 v4 (AVX2 only), Strata `main`
@ v0.1.43.1, `unsloth/UD-IQ4_XS` at 131K. A plain layer split (`"gpu": [0, 1]`):

| metric | single | split |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| decode 424 / 2,944 / 11,582 tok/s | 28.4 / 29.8 / 31.3 | 52.4 / 57.9 / 57.3 |
| window | 70.06 ms | 37.96 ms |
| CPU pool | 9.52 ms | 0.79 ms |

The gain is almost entirely the CPU pool collapsing (9.52 → 0.79 ms/window): when the CPU
pool is what the window waits on, moving half the layers to a second identical card removes
that work.

## Scope

Adds one bullet and a pointer to the new benchmark report
(`bench/results/2026-10-16-community-2x2080ti-dual-socket/`, a separate PR https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/pull/2662).

pulls.title: Human and Agent Readable MAP of everything.
pulls.author: dimitri91209
pulls.body:
A map of the entire repo, sans this folder. Line references for every function in an agent readable and human readable format to allow super easy lookups for everything inside the repo. AGENTS.md contains a simple script that an agent can run to update the map between every release to keep it accurate and up to date. Honestly I made this for myself so I could add a FlyDSL backend and run nvfp4 on my R9700, but it turned out to be a great resource. But I'm also totally unwilling to maintain it beyond this point, pretty much anyone can run the script in the agents MD and bring things back up to date each release. But it really is a really really nice development reference to save you from bouncing between every file and folder trying to hunt down that one function you know you saw earlier.

The HTML files are where humans should navigate the repo. They include flowcharts for the entire repo and explain functionality. As well as a search of the tsv files that highlights results and shows exact line numbers. The reason they're as big as they are is because I bundled the necessary CSS elements and such with them (as their licenses allow) so that everything could be navigated offline. 

Bundled tsv files are grepable for agents to find exact functions without digging through code. they contain paths and line numbers, and the included script in the agents.md allows them to keep everything updated with every single release, without burning a ton of tokens. I burned a LOT having an agent make the map and then a swarm of agents to verify every single reference multiple times until every single file and reference was checked twice for accuracy with 0 errors found. It SHOULD be all good.

pulls.title: bench: community report for 2x RTX 2080 Ti on a dual-socket Xeon (split, concurrency, vLLM)
pulls.author: NorwinYu
pulls.body:
## Summary

Adds a community benchmark report for **2x RTX 2080 Ti 22 GB over a dual-socket Xeon
E5-2696 v4** (44 physical cores, AVX2 only, 94 GiB RAM, NVLink), indexed in
`docs/COMMUNITY_BENCHMARKS.md`. No code changes.

The report combines the repo's own `tools/strata_bench.py` output (`results.json`,
every request) with a hand-written A/B analysis, and fills three gaps the earlier
2x-2080 Ti report (`2026-10-06-community-r9-2x-rtx-2080-ti`) left open:

1. a **single-GPU vs layer-split** comparison on the same cards,
2. **concurrent-request throughput** with `--batch`,
3. a **same-workload vLLM comparison** on the same hardware.

## Canonical suite (`tools/strata_bench.py --long --clients 4 --runs 3`)

Final config: layer split + `--batch 4 --batch-groups 2`. Medians with ranges.

| Configuration | Prompt tok/s | Decode tok/s | TTFT s |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| short chat | — | 42.8 (31.9–49.7) | 0.67 |
| 4K / 16K / 32K prompt, fresh | 678.6 / 1102.4 / 1298.1 | — | 5.96 / 14.62 / 24.76 |
| agent session, follow-up turns | — | 50.3 (39.0–65.5) | 5.26 |
| 4 clients, 128 new tokens each | — | 41.3 total | 2.68 p50 |

## Single GPU vs layer split

| metric | single | split |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| decode (424 / 2,944 / 11,582-token prompts) | 28.4 / 29.8 / 31.3 | **52.4 / 57.9 / 57.3** |
| window | 70.06 ms | **37.96 ms** |
| CPU pool | 9.52 ms | **0.79 ms** |

The decode gain is almost entirely the CPU pool collapsing — on a CPU this slow the second
card removes expert work, it does not just add memory.

## Concurrency + `--batch`, and the power limit

`--batch 4 --batch-groups 2` packs several requests into one verify window: concurrency 4
goes 62.2 → **75.1** tok/s, concurrency 8 → **82.9** (warm-cache decode). Raising the power
limit 180 → 250 W adds +21% (75.1 → 90.8 at concurrency 4). Quality 31/31 on the 7-category
suite.

## vLLM on the same cards

| concurrency | Strata + batch (250 W) | vLLM (250 W) | ratio |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4 | 90.8 | 37.1 | 2.45x |
| 8 | 92.0 | 37.0 | 2.49x |

vLLM stays at ~37 tok/s whether the limit is 180 W or 250 W (FP8 is emulated on SM 75);
Strata fills the GPU with concurrency + `--batch` and only then becomes power-bound.

## Notes / not tested

- The engine actually run is **0.1.43.1** (the fork's project metadata says 0.1.44.1); the
  report states this. Building 0.1.44.1 was out of scope for this report.
- Thermal soak, the 128K needle cases at 250 W, and a quant-matched vLLM run (the vLLM side
  runs FP8) were not done. The `--batch` and 250 W tables are single batches, not the
  10-round protocol some other reports use. All stated in the report's Limitations.

pulls.title: serve: the Profile page (/profile, opt-in "profile": true): the last request's breakdown as it happens, and a run of tools/strata_profile.py from the page
pulls.author: qiuzan2001
pulls.body:
## What it adds

An opt-in **Profile page** at `/profile` (`"profile": true` in `strata-<model>.json`, or `serve/server.py --profile`; also a switch in the About tab's Model settings, used from the next start):

- the engine starts with `STRATA_PREFILL_TIMING=1` and `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING=1` in its environment (a value the user set for either stays), so every request writes its breakdown to the engine log;
- the page shows the **last finished request** as it happens: the prompt read's GPU time by group (experts streamed over PCIe, dequant, expert GEMM, attention, GDN, other) and the decode window's milliseconds by what the host waited for (the card, the experts computed on the CPU, the draft, the adaptive tier), with the hit rate, the PCIe share and this request's KV streaming reads. `GET /profile/last` reads the lines from the tail of the engine log with the parsers of `tools/strata_profile.py` (#2660, which this branch includes: its first commit is that PR);
- a **Tune this PC** button: `POST /profile/tune` (own page only) unloads the model (409 while a request runs, as `/unload`) and runs setup's calibration in a child process (`python -m serve.profile_page --calibrate <config>` calls `setup.calibrate_config`: tools/calibrate.py's measurements, the winners written into `strata-<model>.json` and remembered in the settings file, exactly as `setup.py --calibrate` does). When it ends, the calibrated flags and the config's `env` go into the engine's start command (`apply_to_spawn`), so the model loads with them on the next request. While it runs the server does not load its engine beside the calibration's (a request gets 503 with `Retry-After`, as when the GPU is in use by another program), `/profile/run` and the Settings view's `POST /config` answer 409, and the page asks before starting (setup's own estimate: roughly 15-30 minutes, longer on a slow card). As setup, the page offers it on NVIDIA only and not for replicas (the status says why);
- a **Run the profile** button: `POST /profile/run` (Strata's own page only, as `/settings`: JSON, no foreign Origin, the API key when one is set) starts `tools/strata_profile.py` against this server, `GET /profile/status` follows it and returns the written report (`bench/results/<date>-profile-<gpu>-<model>/`), shown as the same tables and findings. The API key goes to the tool through its environment, not the command line.

Off (the default) nothing is set in the engine's environment and the five paths answer 404, so the default path is unchanged. The page is built like `/api-monitor` (same tokens.css, no CDN, server data only as text).

## Measured (RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB, Ryzen 7 5800X3D, Linux, Strata 0.1.44.1, Swift 1.5 IQ3_S at 262K, INT8 KV, `--kv-resident 32768`)

The cost of leaving the two switches on, `tools/ab_engine.py`, 3 alternating rounds with a restart per arm, greedy, 256 new tokens:

| Request | off | on | per pair |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 8K-token prompt read (6,000 words), prompt tok/s | 2,699-2,710 | 2,582-2,592 | -4.7 / -4.3 / -3.9% (3 of 3 slower) |
| the same request's decode, tok/s | 70.4-75.6 | 71.0-75.2 | +6.8 / -1.3 / -6.1% |
| three short questions, decode tok/s (medians) | 78.0 / 79.8 / 77.1 | 78.3 / 75.8 / 77.4 | -7% to +2%, no consistent sign |

So the prompt path pays about 4% for its event marks on this card; the decode's timestamps are within the noise. The raw rows are in the PR (`bench/results/2026-10-15-timing-switches-rtx-5070-ti/`); docs/DETAILS.md says so beside the page and tells the user to turn it on while looking, off when done.

Real check on the same box: the server started with `--profile` prints the switches in its start line; `/profile/last` answered `request: null` before any request and the breakdown of a 64-token answer after it; a run started from the page (`POST /profile/run`) and `GET /profile/status` returned its lines and the report; a POST with a foreign `Origin` got 403. The run from the page (`?long=8192`, the model already loaded) took 42 s and its findings matched the command-line run's (2K read 43% + 15% waiting for expert copies; decode windows 9.5-10.2 ms of card and 11-18 ms of experts computed on the CPU). A 20-token prompt has no prefill timing line (the page says so and shows the decode window). The Tune button, on the same box from a copy of the config: a second POST while it ran got 409, `/health` said unloaded, the calibration ended after 681 s with `--pcie-frac 0.35, --spec-min-p 0.70, --adapt-every 1, --adapt-swaps 160, --adapt-decay 0.97 (96.6 tok/s)` written into the config, the server printed its "tuned for this PC" line, and the next request loaded the engine with those five flags on its command line (checked with `ps`). This check ran before the second review's guards were added; those are covered by the unit tests.

## Checked

- `python3 -m unittest serve.test_profile` 20/20; `serve.test_runconfig`, `serve.test_security`, `serve.test_monitor`, `serve.test_lifecycle` unchanged (71 together); `tools/test_strata_profile.py` 28/28. `node --check serve/web/profile.js`.
- Default path: without the key, `child_env` is unchanged and the paths answer 404 (tested).

## Not done

- The page was checked with curl and the real engine on Linux; not opened in every browser (the script uses the same APIs as monitor.js).
- Replica servers (several engines): the switches reach every replica through `child_env`, but `/profile/last` reads the primary engine's log only; not run.
- A reviewer (a sub-agent) read the diff before this was opened; its findings (the module name shadowing the stdlib's `profile`, the report path read back only from the results folder, a pump race, the server's own host for the tool, the run's end at shutdown, the unmeasured "three minutes", the A/B data not in the repo) are in this revision; a second pass on the tuning button added the no-load guard while it runs, the replica and HIP refusals, the result applied before the run is published as done, the calibration's own variables only, and the wording.

pulls.title: tools: strata_profile.py, one command that says where the time goes on this PC (prompt phases, decode window split, hit rate per turn)
pulls.author: qiuzan2001
pulls.body:
## What it adds

`python tools/strata_profile.py`: one command that says **where the time goes** on this PC. It starts the server with the user's settings plus `STRATA_PREFILL_TIMING=1` and `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING=1` in the engine's environment (the switches docs/DETAILS.md describes under "Where a decode window's time goes"), sends a few typical requests through the HTTP API, reads the engine's own lines for each one, and writes `bench/results/<date>-profile-<gpu>-<model>/README.md` + `results.json`:

- **chat**: three short questions, 128 new tokens each (a decode window at a short context)
- **2K and 16K**: fresh prompts (the prompt path's phases)
- **long**: a fresh 32K prompt (`--long N`, 0 for none), then 128 tokens (decode at a long context, the KV streaming hit)
- **agent**: the bench's agent session (six requests), turn by turn (reused / read tokens, the hit rate per turn)

The report groups the prompt read's GPU time (experts streamed over PCIe, dequant, expert GEMM, attention, GDN, other), splits the decode window (the card, the experts computed on the CPU, the draft, the adaptive tier, other) with the hit rate and PCIe share, and ends with findings in words that name the setting on each path (the ones `setup --calibrate` measures where it does). The tokens per second in the report are measured with the switches on; the report says so and points to the bench for speeds. `--verify-profile` adds `STRATA_VERIFY_PROFILE=1`; `--url` with `--engine-log FILE` reads a server that is already running (without the log the report has the API's figures and no breakdown).

It reuses `tools/strata_bench.py` (the HTTP client, the calibrated prompt sizes, the agent session's text, the machine facts, the redaction). The server starts from a temporary copy of the config (0600, deleted at the end): the config is read, never written; `--expert-profile-save` is dropped for the run as the bench does (#2088); the engine log goes to a temporary file. The KV streaming line is cumulative over the process, so the report takes the difference between two lines for the long request's own share.

## Measured (RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB, Ryzen 7 5800X3D, 76 GB RAM, Linux, Strata 0.1.44.1, Swift 1.5 IQ3_S at 262K, INT8 KV, `--kv-resident 32768`)

The example report is in the PR: [`bench/results/2026-10-15-profile-rtx-5070-ti-swift-1-5-iq3-s`](https://github.com/qiuzan2001/Strata/blob/qiuzan2001/strata-profile/bench/results/2026-10-15-profile-rtx-5070-ti-swift-1-5-iq3-s/README.md). Three runs (two with an earlier revision of the tool) agree to a few percent.

| Read | Tokens | Prompt tok/s | experts over PCIe | dequant | expert GEMM | attention | GDN | other |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2K fresh | 2,023 | 1,118 | 43% | 15% | 18% | 5% | 13% | 6% |
| 16K fresh | 16,058 | 2,982 | 5% | 8% | 30% | 18% | 25% | 14% |
| 32K fresh | 32,049 | 3,041 | 5% | 7% | 27% | 21% | 25% | 15% |

| Request | Context | Decode tok/s | Hit rate | ms/window | GPU | CPU experts | draft | adapt wait | CPU experts per layer-window |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| chat | 44 | 75.7 | 71% | 33.6 | 10.2 | 19.3 | 1.8 | 1.4 | 4.7 |
| long context | 32,049 | 82.0 | 82% | 27.4 | 10.0 | 13.1 | 2.3 | 1.3 | 3.6 |
| agent turns | 8,721 | 71.7 | 79% | 32.2 | 10.1 | 17.9 | 2.0 | 1.3 | 4.7 |

The long request's KV streaming: 96% of its 838,104 block reads from VRAM, 119 MiB from RAM. Agent session: the hit rate per turn runs from 51% (turn 0, right after the system prompt's read) to 86% (turn 4); follow-up turns read 1,469-3,380 tokens each. The run takes about 3 minutes after the model has loaded (36 s load, 2.5-3 min of requests).

## Checked

- `python3 tools/test_strata_profile.py`: 28/28 (the parsers on real engine lines, the grouping, the findings, the run against a fake server that writes an engine log; no GPU). `tools/test_strata_bench.py` 17/17 unchanged.
- Three real runs on the box above (one with `--verify-profile`, the last with the final code): every request's lines matched (prefill timing, host staging, decode timing, GPU stages, the prompt summary, the hit rate, KV streaming); the written report has no home folder, user or host name; the temporary config copy was gone at the end.
- The default path: a new tool and two docs paragraphs; no engine, server or setup file is touched, so the default is byte-identical.

## Not done

- HIP / Metal / SYCL servers are not run (the tool only reads lines; a backend that prints a different `prefill timing` line gets an empty breakdown and the API's figures, as the tests cover). `--batch` servers: the decode timing line is per request, the tool sends one request at a time, so it should work, but it was not run.
- A reviewer (a sub-agent) read the diff before this was opened; its findings (the cumulative KV line, experts vs entries, the log offset race, the wording of the findings, the temporary config's permissions) are in this revision.

The standalone companion, [Strata Profile Studio](https://github.com/qiuzan2001/strata-profile-studio) (Python standard library only), reads this tool's reports and compares runs against the noise floor of the PC, with a sign test over the agent turns.

## Title
artifact: read an all-zero `attention.compress_ratios` as absent

## Summary
Some re-quantized finetunes of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next write `qwen4exp.attention.compress_ratios` with every entry 0
(the original files have 4 on each full-attention layer). Since the geometry check in 0.1.44, such a file stops the
engine at start:

```
qwen4exp.attention.compress_ratios[3] = 0, but full_attention_interval = 4 makes layer 3 full attention
```

An array of zeros names no layer, so it is now read as if the key were missing, and the compiled pooling block
stays. Any other value is checked as before.

## What changed
- `include/strata/artifact/gguf_reader.hpp`, `read_geometry`: an all-zero `attention.compress_ratios` is skipped.
  A missing key, a valid list and every malformed list (wrong length, a non-zero entry on a linear layer, mixed
  blocks) take the same path as before.

## Extra Notes
How it was checked (CUDA build only):
- A community finetune GGUF with all-zero ratios: refused at start before, starts and answers correctly after (on a
  branch with the MXFP4 experts of #1724, which that file also needs; on `main` alone it now gets past the geometry
  check and stops at the MXFP4 expert check, as expected).
- Unsloth's UD-Q3_K_XL (valid ratios): starts and answers the same way.

Not tested: HIP and SYCL builds (the change is in a header the CPU code reads, no device code).

pulls.title: Metal: a tile for gr_down on windows of more than one token (STRATA_METAL_GR_TILE)
pulls.author: alvarorsouza-arch
pulls.body:
## What this changes

`gr_down`, one of the three dispatches of the hyper-connection read, is built with a fixed tile: 8 simdgroups per threadgroup, 8 of them splitting one row (`gr_down_q8_8_8`, `metal/src/engine/window.cpp:638` and the same line in `gr_read_m`). `gr.metal` instantiates six tiles (`GRD(8,8) (8,4) (4,4) (4,2) (16,16) (16,8)`) and the engine only ever asks for one of them.

On an Apple M3 Max that tile is the slowest of the six as soon as a window carries more than one token, and it gets worse fast. `metal/tests/gr_parity.cpp --bench` with `GR_Q8=1` (the form this pack uses) and `GR_DOWN=S_K`, median of three runs, per call:

| Tile | 1 token | 2 tokens | 3 tokens |
| --- |---:|---:|---:|
| 8_8 (the engine's) | 14.7 us | 27.5 us | 52.3 us |
| 8_4 | 12.9 us | 20.5 us | 37.0 us |
| 4_4 | 12.4 us | 19.5 us | 34.0 us |
| 4_2 | 13.1 us | 15.6 us | 20.7 us |

8_8 costs 1.88x for the second token and 3.56x for the third; 4_2 costs 1.19x and 1.58x for the same work, reading the same bytes. The two variants that split the row more ways are also the two that hold up.

The extra token is not weight traffic. One `gr_down` call reads 324 rows (hc_lr + hc) of `hc * n_embd` = 10,240 Q8_0 elements, 3.52 MB, and the tile change does not touch that. Its arithmetic is 3.32M MAC, which at the 3,729.6 Gops/s fp32 FMA rate `metal/tests/alu_bench.cpp` measures on this GPU is 0.89 us. So the marginal token, measured as the difference against one token in the table above, costs 12.8 us in 8_8 (7% of that rate) and 2.5 us in 4_2 (36%). What scales with the token count is the re-read of `xn` (10,240 floats per row, so about 13 MB per call, from cache) and the per-thread accumulation: `grd_acc` decodes each weight unit once and then loops the tokens inside it (`metal/kernels/gr.metal:62-71`), which is the right shape, but with `KS = 8` each thread holds eight live accumulators over a shorter unit run and the eight partials meet in threadgroup memory behind a barrier (`metal/kernels/gr.metal:82,94-102`). Halving KS to 2 and putting two rows in each threadgroup is where the second token stops costing 1.88x.

The same scaling is what the engine pays: a `--spec 2` window issues 96 of these calls, so the tile is worth 4.9% of the window's GPU time (below).

The patch reads the tile from `STRATA_METAL_GR_TILE=S_K`, keeps 8_8 when the variable is unset, and fixes the launch with it: the grid is `ceil((hc_lr + hc) / RS)` with `RS = SG / KS` and the threadgroup is `32 * SG`, the same math `gr_parity` uses (`metal/tests/gr_parity.cpp:106`). Unset, the engine builds the same pipeline with the same grid and threadgroup as before.

## What it leaves alone

`gr_norm` and `gr_up` are untouched. The CUDA, HIP and SYCL backends are untouched: `metal/` is its own CMake project and does not enter those builds. No kernel source changes, so the six tiles already in `gr.metal` are the only ones reachable. The variable accepts only those six and says so on stderr if given another.

With the variable unset the engine asks for the same pipeline with the same grid and threadgroup as before, and the rebuilt binary printed the same 120 output ids as a build of `main` at `296b59d` on the same prompt.

## What it buys, measured

In the engine, `STRATA_METAL_KPROF=2` on the `--spec 2` window (48 layers, 96 `gr_down` dispatches per window, one boot each):

| Tile | `gr_down` classes | whole window, GPU |
| --- |---:|---:|
| 8_8 | 2.656 ms | 27.144 ms |
| 4_2 | 1.522 ms | 25.817 ms |

That is 1.13 ms, or 4.9% of the window's GPU time. What the user sees, on the same machine, one boot per row, the fixed 449 token harness prompt with 256 out, three runs each, median first:

| Drafter | tile 8_8 | tile 4_2 | tile 4_4 |
| --- |---:|---:|---:|
| `--spec 2` plus suffix (what setup writes) | 57.3 (56.1 / 57.3 / 57.5) | 59.1 (57.9 / 59.1 / 59.2) | 59.1 (57.8 / 59.1 / 59.3) |
| drafter off | 48.7 (47.8 / 48.7 / 48.7) | | 49.7 (49.2 / 49.8 / 49.7) |
| `--spec 3` plus suffix | 49.9 (49.1 / 49.9 / 49.9) | 53.0 (52.4 / 53.1 / 53.0) | |

So +3.1% at the defaults, +6.2% at `--spec 3` (where the tile table's 52.3 us against 20.7 us per call is the whole story), and +2.1% with no drafter using 4_4, which is the tile the bench prefers at one token. Draft acceptance did not move (113 of 146 offered with 8_8, 113 of 146 with 4_2). A second boot of the unchanged default in a later session gave 57.1 (56.1 / 57.2 / 57.1), so the default's own boot-to-boot spread is 0.2 tok/s against a 1.8 tok/s difference here. A separate 200 token greedy one-shot, same session, gave 62.88 tok/s for 8_8 and 64.63 for 4_2.

## How parity looks

`GR_Q8=1 GR_DOWN=4_2 build-metal/gr_parity --ntok N` against the double precision reference, for N = 1, 2, 3, 8, both with and without the folded write: `PASS`, with the same relative errors as the current tile (`lo` 1.2e-7 against 1.4e-7, `inject` 1.1e-7 against 1.2e-7, prepared planes bitwise equal to `xprep`). The tiles are not bitwise identical to each other, since the row is summed in a different order; a greedy one-shot of 200 tokens on this machine came out with the same 200 ids for 8_8, 4_4 and 4_2, which is agreement, not proof.

## Related

#2070 found the same shape of problem on the CUDA side and fixed it for sm_75: the hyper-connection read as about 19% of an RTX 2080 Ti's decode GPU time, 96 reads per window, with a dedicated `gr_up` kernel for 3-plus tokens and the staged down kernel taking a token group, opt-in behind `STRATA_GR_UP75`. My numbers say the Metal engine has the same token scaling, and there the fix so far is only the tile choice, which is why this PR keeps it opt-in. #1775 (SYCL, three kernels instead of four for the same read) is the other thread in this area.

## What I did not test

Only the M3 Max, one pack (IQ3_S with the Q8_0 hyper-connection copies at load), one model. The M1 and M2 families and the M5 (which gets the M5 cooperative layout) are unmeasured here, which is why the tile is opt-in rather than a new default. The BF16 and F32-inject forms of the read (`gr_down_8_8`, `gr_down_q8f_*`) were benched only in their BF16 form in `gr_parity`, not in the engine. `gr_up` scales the same way with the token count (13.0 us at one token, 24.4 us at two, 35.3 us at three, and it is the larger half of the read at 2.35 ms per `--spec 2` window) and has no tile knob in `gr.metal`; that is where I would go next, and it is what #2070 built for Turing.

pulls.title: Community benchmark: Tesla V100-PCIE-32GB (sm_70), Flash-Next IQ2_XS and IQ3_XXS
pulls.author: publee
pulls.body:
Three community benchmark reports from one box, one settings set and one suite, so they read against each other: the two quants in the mode this machine serves, plus IQ3_XXS in the other expert mode as a mode comparison.

**Hardware:** Tesla V100-PCIE-32GB (sm_70, PCIe 3.0 x16), Ryzen 5 3600, 31.2 GiB RAM + 23 GiB swap, ADATA NVMe, Linux 6.8.0-147, driver 580.178.04, engine built with CUDA 12.8.

**Engine:** local v0.1.42 source build for sm_70 (`STRATA_EXPERIMENTAL_SM60=ON`), sha256 in the reports. It carries one unpushed, opt-in local patch (a conversation park that would hit the RAM floor is paged out instead of refused). The flag was passed but no parking or page-out line appears in any run's engine log and the conversations tested stay far below the 16 GiB / 20-slot limits, so the patch's path was never exercised and the numbers are what an unpatched v0.1.42 build does with the same settings. Every README states this. I have no clean release-build run to compare against; say the word and I will make one.

**Measured** (`tools/strata_bench.py --long`, 3 runs per test, medians, 262,144-token context, `--kv k8v4`):

| | IQ2_XS `--resident-experts` | IQ3_XXS `--resident-experts` | IQ3_XXS `--mmap-experts` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| chat decode | 76.1 tok/s | 66.6 tok/s | 62.5 tok/s |
| prompt tok/s, 4,019 / 16,058 / 32,049 tokens | 1251.6 / 1373.8 / 1344.9 | 1176.9 / 1355.4 / 1275.1 | 930.7 / 1180.1 / 1206.8 |
| first token, same lengths | 3.23 / 11.72 / 23.87 s | 3.44 / 11.88 / 25.18 s | 4.34 / 13.64 / 26.60 s |
| agent session decode / cache hit | 74.4 tok/s / 68.7 % | 76.1 tok/s / 68.8 % | 75.4 tok/s / 68.7 % |

The denser quant costs about 6 % on chat decode and little on prompt throughput, both in resident mode. Resident IQ3_XXS pins 20.64 GiB page-locked and its start log reports 2076 of 2076 lendable prompt-path slots resident, so answering reads no expert from disk. In mapped mode the first 4K prompt is a cold file-cache read (438 tok/s against 1015 warm) - the range is in the report rather than hidden.

**Not tested:** recall/needle checks, any coding task, concurrency (`--clients` was not used and the server was not started with `--batch`), power draw and throttling.

Results-only; no engine changes. `docs/COMMUNITY_BENCHMARKS.md` carries one entry covering the three reports.

pulls.title: calibrate: the CPU prefill share's range measured per PC (STRATA_PREFILL_CPU_SHARE_MAX 3072 against the default, into the config's env)
pulls.author: qiuzan2001
pulls.body:
For #2478's question ("Could setup measure the share once and record it when it helps?"), for the range rather than the arming.

## What it changes

- `tools/calibrate.py`: a sixth step, the CPU prefill share's range. The share is on by default for prompt chunks below 1,024 tokens; `STRATA_PREFILL_CPU_SHARE_MAX=3072` extends it, and that stays opt-in because it depends on the CPU: docs/DETAILS.md records -2% at 2,048 tokens on the Ryzen 5 7600 + RTX 5070, and on a Ryzen 7 5800X3D + RTX 5070 Ti it measured -24% / -14% / -3% at 1.5K / 2.2K / 2.9K (below). So it is measured per PC: one engine start with the variable absent and one with 3072, each reading a fresh ~2K-token prompt three times as a one-shot request (`strata_checkpoint: false`, so no checkpoint is kept and every read is from token 0; a read that reused one is not counted), the prompt tokens per second compared with the existing `pick` rule (more than 3% faster or nothing).
- The winner goes into the config's `env` (`apply_env`, the counterpart of `apply` for arguments: an older calibration's value goes when it is not chosen again), into the settings-file record, and is re-applied on a reinstall (`setup.py`).
- Every calibration start runs without the measured variables, so a value an earlier calibration wrote is not in the baseline of steps 1-5 either. A failed start or a failed read drops that arm only, as #1337 asked for the other steps.
- The step is skipped, with one line saying why, where the share is off (a HIP engine, a layer split, `--batch`) or already at 3,072 (a set `STRATA_PREFILL_CPU_SHARE`).
- docs/DETAILS.md: the fifth bullet in the `--calibrate` paragraph; the 0.1.41 paragraph's "stays opt-in" sentence gains the 5070 Ti numbers and the pointer to the calibration.

## What it leaves alone

- The engine: nothing under `src/` or `include/` changes; the default range stays 1,024 tokens. No backend to build.
- Steps 1-5 of the calibration and their tests; a config the calibration does not touch; a config's other `env` entries (setup's own, Unsloth's, AMD's) are kept as they are.
- The step adds two engine starts (about 36 s each here) to the 8-10 the calibration already does.

## How it was checked

- `tools/test_calibrate.py`: 25 of 25 (8 new: the range chosen at +15% and not at +2%, skipped without a prompt, measured with the chosen worker count, a failed start and a failed read drop that arm only, `apply_env`, `engine_env`, `share_step_applies`, the prompt builder, reads that reused a checkpoint). `tools/test_setup_choices`, `_amd`, `_hybrid`, `_qwen36`, `_unsloth` pass. `tools/test_setup_golden` has 8 failures (the unsloth UD-Q4_K_XL cases); they are the same on upstream/main 296b59d2 without this change.
- The step on the real engine, through the same functions the tool calls (RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB, Ryzen 7 5800X3D, 76 GB RAM, Linux, CUDA 13.1; Swift 1.5 IQ3_S, the setup's config, engine 0.1.44.1 from main): the prompt it builds is 2,375 tokens; two starts per arm, every read `reused=0`:

| arm | prompt tok/s, 3 reads per start | median |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| default (variable absent), start 1 / 2 | 1,292 1,379 1,380 / 1,291 1,379 1,378 | 1,378 |
| `STRATA_PREFILL_CPU_SHARE_MAX=3072`, start 1 / 2 | 1,404 1,553 1,555 / 1,321 1,546 1,551 | 1,548 |

  `pick` chooses 3072 (+12%).
- The range itself, measured the way a user feels it (fresh turns of real prose and code on a cached 57,102-token conversation, greedy, the engine restarted for every run, three alternating pairs, `prompt_ms` from the server; same box and model):

| fresh chunk | default (1,024) | `..._MAX=3072` | pairs |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 591 tokens | 1,125 ms | 1,124 ms | +0.0 / +0.2 / -2.1% |
| 1,537 tokens | 1,979 ms | 1,501 ms | -24.2 / -23.7 / -24.0% |
| 2,142 tokens | 2,041 ms | 1,748 ms | -14.6 / -14.3 / -12.8% |
| 2,848 tokens | 2,173 ms | 2,113 ms | -2.0 / -2.8 / -3.1% |
| 4,631 tokens | 2,504 ms | 2,503 ms | +0.0 / -0.3 / -0.1% |

  The decode after each turn had the same expert-cache hit rates in both arms. A second set of two rounds per arm (a build whose default range was 3,072, against the 0.1.44.1 build) gave the same figures: -24.1 / -13.9 / -2.7% at 1,537 / 2,142 / 2,848 tokens, and `=1024` on that build equal to the 0.1.44.1 build.

An independent review pass read the diff; its points (a failed read must drop only its arm, the baseline must not carry an earlier calibration's value, skip where the share is off) are in.

The standalone companion, [Strata Profile Studio](https://github.com/qiuzan2001/strata-profile-studio) (Python standard library only), reads this tool's reports and compares runs against the noise floor of the PC, with a sign test over the agent turns.

pulls.title: Metal: the routing trace of a resident window (STRATA_METAL_DUMP_ROUTING)
pulls.author: alvarorsouza-arch
pulls.body:
## What this changes

`--dump-routing` and `tools/collect_profile_traces.py --mode routing` work on the pooled backends because the routed ids reach the host through the doorbell the expert pool reads (`src/program/generate.cpp:5929` prints exactly that when you pass `--no-pool`). The Metal engine has no host pool, it reads experts in place from the mapped file, so on a Mac the flag is accepted and the trace comes out empty:

```text
routing dumped           /tmp/one.trace (0 records of layer, k, ids, weights)
verify window            wait for rings 0.000  pool 0.000  host 0.000  commit 0.000 ms/round;
                         CPU experts 0.00 distinct / 0.00 routed per layer
```

The file exists, so `tools/collect_profile_traces.py` reports success, and `tools/make_profile.py` has nothing to read. That blocks the input `tools/quant_bound.py` wants from the engine's window logs, and falls back to `--union` (default 1.0) without them: U(P), the distinct experts a pass of P tokens reads per expert a single token reads. The window logs give it on the pooled backends because they count distinct against routed experts per layer; on Metal that line reads `CPU experts 0.00 distinct / 0.00 routed per layer`.

Two files, 66 added lines, Metal only:

- `metal/kernels/moe.metal`: a `route_dump` kernel that copies one layer's `moe_route` output into that layer's own slot. It has to be a device copy because `ids_` is reused by the next layer and a resident window never hands the host a turn between layers.
- `metal/src/engine/window.cpp`: `STRATA_METAL_DUMP_ROUTING=path` opens the file, allocates one slot pair per layer, dispatches `route_dump` right after the route dispatch in `Window::layer` (the main model's window builder only, not the draft one, since both would write slot 0), and `finish()` writes the window's records in the format `tools/make_profile.py:read_trace` reads: `int32 layer, int32 k, k int32 ids, k float weights`.

## What it leaves alone

Opt-in by environment variable, default path untouched. With the variable unset no buffer is allocated, no dispatch is added to the window, `routing_write()` returns on its first line, and no file is opened. The core is unchanged. It is an environment variable rather than a flag because the core exposes no routing trace path to the backend (nothing in `include/` or `src/core/` carries one); it follows `STRATA_METAL_KPROF` next to it. Tell me where you would rather hang it and I will move it.

CUDA, HIP and SYCL builds are not affected: `metal/` is its own CMake project and does not enter those builds, and no shared file is touched.

## How I checked

Apple M3 Max, 40-core GPU, 128 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, in high power mode. Three one-shot runs of one command (`--spec 2` with the MTP draft layer, `--expert-cache 64`, `--max-context 65536`, experts resident, `--tokens-file` a 37 token prompt, `--max-new 120 --greedy`):

- a build of `main` at `296b59d` with no patch: 61.94 tok/s
- the patched build, variable unset: 61.21 tok/s
- the patched build, variable set: 60.97 tok/s

The `output  :` line is the same 120 token ids in all three, byte for byte.

The trace is 519,552 bytes: 48 layers by 123 window rows by 88 bytes. `tools/make_profile.py:read_trace` reads it as is, and walking the file gives 5,904 records, all with layer in 0 to 47, k equal to 10 and ids in 0 to 511, no malformed record and no trailing bytes, with weights from 0.0084 to 0.8066.

The cost is small but I cannot pin it down: this pair says 0.4% (60.97 against 61.21), an earlier pair on the same build said 2.9% (61.31 against 63.11), and pure decode on this machine moves about 7% from boot to boot. One extra dispatch per layer per window is the whole overhead, so it should stay under a few percent.

## What it bought

U(P) over 48 layers of a run like that, greedy, one prompt, counted as the distinct experts in the pass divided by the distinct experts of one token in it:

| Pass | U(P) mean | across layers | experts repeated in the pass |
| --- |---:|---|---:|
| 2 tokens | 1.684 | 1.543 to 1.950 | 15.8% |
| 4 tokens | 2.822 | 2.288 to 3.765 | 29.5% |
| 8 tokens | 4.615 | 3.301 to 6.773 | 42.3% |

Worth one caveat about the rows: they are the window's proposals, so a draft that was rejected still shows the experts it routed. For a cache profile that is the useful view; for accepted token accounting you would filter them.

The machine and the unmodified binary numbers are in the report PR #2649. Related but different: #1547 puts routing counts on `/metrics` in the server, which is not what reads a per window trace, and nothing open covers the empty trace on Metal. If you would rather have `collect_profile_traces.py` fail on a 0 record trace than accept it, that is a one line change I can add here or in an issue.

pulls.title: Community benchmark: Apple M3 Max (Metal), Flash-Next IQ3_S
pulls.author: alvarorsouza-arch
pulls.body:
Report from hardware the maintainers do not have: an Apple M3 Max (40-core GPU, 128 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6) on engine 0.1.44.1-metal built from source at `296b59d`, original Flash-Next IQ3_S resident, 65,536-token context, setup defaults otherwise.

The folder adds one `README.md` plus the index bullet above. No engine code and no other docs change in this PR.

## Headline numbers

Decode 55.0 / 58.8 / 58.8 tok/s at the defaults, where the drafter is on (`--spec 2` with the MTP draft layer). With no drafter at all the same build gives 48.2 / 48.6 / 48.8 tok/s, and prompt ingestion 504 tok/s at 16,388 tokens. `docs/MAC.md` shows 94 to 102 tok/s for IQ3_S on an M5 Max, so this chip lands about 1.6x slower, close to the 400 against 546 GB/s bandwidth ratio.

## What else the report carries

- The repo's own Metal benches on this GPU: `rt_bench bw` reads 381.8 GB/s best (five runs, 381.8 to 394.9) and 365.7 GB/s for the 1 MB chunks the experts arrive in; `gridbar_bench` reads a 48 phase layer shaped chain at 379.4 GB/s; `mm_bench` reaches 12.0 to 13.3 TFLOP/s fp16 at 4096 cubed and 2.0 to 3.1 TFLOP/s at a 16 token batch.
- The byte inventory of one token (5,159 MB: 982 MB routed experts, 4,177 MB dense) put beside the measured step, which makes pure decode 255 GB/s, or 70% of a plain streaming read of the same bytes.
- A per class breakdown from `STRATA_METAL_KPROF=1`. The LM head, attention and SSM gemvs run at 363 to 430 GB/s; the hyper connection read at 242 and the expert path at 275 are the laggards.
- A power finding: the same build and config ran at 24.1 / 24.4 / 24.3 tok/s before I moved the machine to high power and 57.4 / 57.6 / 58.1 after. That is larger than every tuning result in the report, which is why the doc asks ask reports to quote the power mode.
- Settings measured one boot each that do not beat the defaults on decode: a larger `--expert-cache`, `COOP_K4=1`, `STRATA_METAL_MATH=fast`, `STRATA_METAL_GEMV_NR=2`, `STRATA_METAL_PROMPT_EXPERTS=v3`, `STRATA_METAL_PROMPT_QSA=flash`, `STRATA_HC_Q8=0`, and four drafter configurations. `COOP_K4=1` also produces wrong output on this GPU, so the probe is right to keep it off.
- Broken or absent on this backend: `--kv int8` and `--kv-resident` abort at boot with no Metal implementation for `kv_block_bytes`; `--expert-cache` at 1024 and above fails every prompt request until `--no-prefill-borrow`; `--no-fused-gr` is inert (the fused gr entry points are `missing()` stubs); `--dump-routing` writes a trace with 0 records because the Metal engine has no host expert pool; and `--batch 2`, `3` and `4` are accepted at boot, build 1.73 GiB of slots each, then exit the engine with code 86 on the first request that runs two sequences together (with `STRATA_METAL_STUBS=log` the batch route reaches 17 entry points that have no Metal implementation), now filed on its own as #2715.
- The resident prompt chain, measured. The matrix units carry a 16K prompt 5.9x faster than the 8 row window path (`STRATA_METAL_PROMPT=window`: 79.5 tok/s against 475 and 466), and the shipped tiles are already the good ones, the alternatives costing 3 to 5% on the dense GEMM and 3% and 15% on the grouped expert GEMMs. A longer `STRATA_METAL_PROMPT_CHUNK` costs 11% at 4,096 and 21% at 8,192 here, where docs/MAC.md measures 2 to 4% on Q2_0, and `STRATA_METAL_PROFILE` shows why: GPU time falls 5% while the chain's host rows work triples. The budget is 239.4 TFLOP of matmul in a 16,383 token prompt, 27.9 s of its 34.1 s on the GPU, 8.6 TFLOP/s, against the 23.7 s `mm_bench` prices the two GEMM classes at. The report also notes that `STRATA_METAL_PROMPT_GEMM` and the dense tile in `Window::prompt_chunk` belong to the streaming path, so on a resident pack they do nothing, and it corrects its own element count from 6.67 G to 7.31 G per token.
- A measured U(P) for `tools/quant_bound.py`, 1.684 at two tokens and 4.615 at eight, which needed a small local patch to reach the routed ids on Metal. That patch is a separate PR and is not part of this folder; every other number here comes from an unmodified 0.1.44.1 binary.

## Doc asks

Twelve of them, listed at the end of the report. They are documentation only: the Metal limits for `--kv`, `--expert-cache` and `--no-fused-gr`, a note that a Mac in a low power mode runs at roughly half, a paragraph for `STRATA_METAL_KPROF`, having `collect_profile_traces.py` reject an empty routing trace instead of accepting the file, naming `--batch` rather than the old `--parallel` in the Mac limits, which prompt variables belong to the streaming path rather than the resident one, and a paragraph for `STRATA_METAL_PROFILE` beside the KPROF one.

## Not tested

The guide's 4,096 / 32,768 / 128,000 token sweep, vision, any context above 65,536, `--spec` above 2, `--parallel`, soaks, and concurrency. The pack and the MTP draft layer were copied from an existing 0.1.40.3 install rather than freshly built, so a clean first install on 0.1.44.1 on this hardware is unverified and no hashes are included. I can add `provenance.json` and `REPRODUCE.md` the way some other reports here do, if that is wanted.

pulls.title: batch: repetition / frequency / presence penalties apply in the batch windows (a slot counts its own conversation's tokens)
pulls.author: qiuzan2001
pulls.body:
docs/BATCHING.md lists, under "Limits (for now)": *Repetition / frequency / presence penalties are not applied in batch windows.* This applies them.

## What it changes

- `Verifier::sample_rows` (src/core/verify.cpp) cleared `penalty_last_n` for every slot row and handed the sampler no history, so a request with `repetition_penalty` / `frequency_penalty` / `presence_penalty` decoded in a slot as if it had none. It now samples a row whose slot has penalties on the host side with that row's history, greedy or not (the graph's argmax pick is replaced, as the solo path does for a greedy request with penalties).
- `batch_step` (src/program/generate.cpp) stages one history row per window row from the slot's own tokens, `ids` followed by the token the row feeds, and with `--batch-mtp` the proposal row follows the fed token too. The rows are built by the same `strata::kernels::penalty_rows` the solo path uses, so a slot counts exactly what plain decode of that conversation would count. A new `Verifier::set_slot_history` hands them over (it reaches the last stage of a layer split, where the rows are sampled; the buffer is on that device, next to the solo path's).
- `BSlot::penalty_last_n`, set at admission from the request's sampling.
- docs/BATCHING.md: the limit is reworded; the `tools/batch_test.py` row says how to check it. docs/DETAILS.md: one sentence in the penalties paragraph.

## What it leaves alone

- A window in which no active slot has penalties hands the verifier no rows and takes the old code path; a slot without penalties in a window where another has them leaves its rows at -1 and is sampled as before (its `penalty_last_n` is 0).
- The pipelined slot groups (`--batch-groups` above 1) never stage rows and are unchanged. The docs say so.
- The SYCL tree has its own `verify.cpp` / `generate.cpp` and is not changed; its batch windows still skip penalties (the docs say so).
- The solo path, the drafts (the draft layer still guesses without penalties) and every request without penalties.

## How it was checked

RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB, Ryzen 7 5800X3D, Linux, CUDA 13.1 (arch 120); Swift 1.5 IQ3_S; `tools/batch_test.py --batch 2 --n 2 --max-new 64 --extra "--max-context 32768 --pcie-frac 0 --adapt-every 1000000"` (the script sets `STRATA_IQ_MT_MIN=1`), on the binary before this change and after it, the engine restarted for every arm:

| arm | binary | `--keys` | slots vs their solo tokens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| plain | before | none | identical (both slots) |
| plain | after | none | identical, and the same solo and batch tokens as "before" |
| penalties | before | `penalty_repeat=1.5 penalty_last_n=64` | **differ** at token 3 (slot 0) and 22 (slot 1); the batch tokens equal the plain arm's, i.e. the penalties were ignored |
| penalties | after | the same | identical (both slots) |
| penalties + `--batch-mtp` | after | the same | identical (both slots) |
| penalties, sampled | after | `... temperature=0.7 top_k=20 seed=11` | identical (both slots) |

The solo tokens with penalties are the same on both binaries. An independent review pass read the diff (row/slot mapping across stages, the history contract against the solo path's `consumed` + `window`, buffer bounds, the no-penalty path) and found nothing to change beyond the docs wording above.

Not built: HIP (no AMD card here; `src/core/verify.cpp` and `src/program/generate.cpp` are the shared sources), Metal (no Mac). SYCL not touched.

pulls.title: [Engine] Metal: opt-in fp16-slab expert path (mpp) for streaming prompt chunks
pulls.author: catalinb13
pulls.body:
Adds the measured M1 Max streaming-decode work on top of the mpp prompt path and the v0.1.45 merge (see commits; the earlier description covered mpp only):

## Device-flag cut handshake, now the default (`STRATA_METAL_CUT=event` opts back)
The decode window's 48 per-layer cuts used an MTLSharedEvent signal+wait pair inside the window's command buffer. On the M1 Max that costs 230-400 us per cut because the queue stops and re-arms at every wait (worst around indirect dispatch chains: +170 us, measured with `metal/tests/dispatch_lat`, rows `seg ...` vs `flag ...`). `Context::run_graph_flag` replaces it with two tiny kernels shipped in `metal/kernels/units.metal` (`cut_seq` bumps a shared-buffer counter after each cut, behind the window's own barriers; `cut_spin` at each segment start waits for a plain host store) - the queue never stops and propagation measures ~90 us/cut.

Measured on Apple M1 Max 64 GB, IQ3_XXS 47 GB pack, 40K ctx, t357, `--spec 2` MTP, 33 GB pinned arena (`gap/gap.sh`, arms `gap/arms-round25.txt`/`26.txt`, results in `gap/results/1018-1534` and `1018-1545`): 3x3 interleaved flag/event + a default-vs-opt-out sandwich. Decode 19.5-20.3 -> 29.97-30.49 tok/s; T=2 window 87.8 -> 56.0 ms, at the busy+miss floor (~55.5 ms: kernel busy 48.6 + 8.6 misses x 0.8 ms). All eleven arms produce byte-identical outputs (128-token output line md5 `956dbac3e10818130ee6a82d3327f688`).

## Read-ahead depth 12 for big-expert packs (default; `STRATA_METAL_PREFETCH` opts out)
`stream.cpp` default `big ? 6 : 10` -> `big ? 12 : 10` (big = experts >1.5 MB). 7 candidate vs 7 anchor arms (rounds 21+22, `gap/results/1018-1318`/`1329`): decode misses 15.9 -> 8.6/window, window GPU 88.8 -> 83.0 ms, 19.0 -> 20.3 tok/s, +63 MB read/window overlapped behind the GPU, same md5. Depth 24 measured worse (aheads collide with urgent reads).

## Also in this push
- `docs/DETAILS.md`: the two measured changes with their numbers, per the repo rules.
- Gap harness: pinned 33 GB arena per arm (the dynamic `vm.vm_page_filecache_min` floor moved the arena between arms and faked drift), per-arm filecache/free-page logging, progress output; dispatch_lat grows seg/flag/indirect handshake rows.
- Stream stats fix: the decode line's MB/reads now report decode-only (they were cumulative since boot).

What it leaves alone: the prefill path's timing (one big streamed chunk, handshake-free; warm prefill 49.5-49.99 event vs 50.9-51.1 flag tok/s, within drift), all CUDA/HIP code, and every non-stream default. Not tested on Apple hardware other than the M1 Max: the event-pair cost is a driver/queue property, so the win's magnitude may differ elsewhere; `STRATA_METAL_CUT=event` is the instant revert.

pulls.title: Add community benchmark: RTX 4060 Ti 16 GB + RTX 3060 12 GB, IQ3_S — plus a layer_split sweep
pulls.author: Tworks25
pulls.body:
Community benchmark on an asymmetric dual-GPU pair, plus a `layer_split` sweep that may be worth upstream attention.

## Hardware

RTX 4060 Ti 16 GB + RTX 3060 12 GB (28 GiB total VRAM), Xeon E5-2696 v3 (18c/36t, AVX2, no AVX-512), 125.6 GiB DDR3, Linux 5.15, driver 595.91.07. Strata 0.1.44.1 (`296b59d2`), original Flash-Next IQ3_S, 262,144-token context, `--kv int8 --kv-resident 32768`, `--vision`, both cards at their **default** power limits.

## Results

Measured with the project's own `tools/strata_bench.py`, 3 runs per test, medians:

| Configuration | Prompt tok/s | Decode tok/s | TTFT |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| short chat | — | 50.4 (45.4-60.0) | 0.74 s |
| 4K prompt, fresh | 488.2 (486.5-488.2) | — | 8.27 s |
| 16K prompt, fresh | 835.0 (730.7-866.2) | — | 19.28 s |
| agent session, follow-up turns | see README | 36.2 (27.1-55.8) | 8.45 s |

Conversation cache hit over the agent session: 68.6 %.

## The finding: `layer-split auto` costs a lot of prefill on this pair

`auto` gave the **RTX 3060 3 of 48 layers**, leaving 12 GB of its VRAM idle and the card drawing 17 W through an entire prefill while the 4060 Ti sat at 100 % utilisation. Sweeping `layer_split` on an identical cold 14,564-token prompt, fresh server per point:

| `layer_split` | 3060 layers | 4060 Ti layers | prefill tok/s |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `auto` | 3 | 45 | 452.6 |
| 12 | 12 | 36 | 581.8 |
| 18 | 18 | 30 | 693.0 |
| 24 | 24 | 24 | 761.7 |
| **28** | **28** | **20** | **802.1** |
| 32 | 32 | 16 | 803.2 |

**+77 % prefill at split 28**, plateauing at 28-32. Decode improved too (41.8 → 50.4 chat median; 25.1 → 36.2 agent median), since fewer layers per card lets the expert cache cover each layer better.

I understand from the log that the engine chose this deliberately — it cites avoiding a stage whose tiny expert cache would clamp the prompt chunk of every card (#1616). That caution is reasonable in general, but on a pair this asymmetric it costs 44 % of prefill throughput, and the clamping case did not materialise at any split I tested.

## Two things that may generalise

**A mis-set split shows up as a flat prefill-vs-length curve.** Under `auto`, prefill barely moved with prompt length (491.7 tok/s at 4K, 512.1 at 16K — no batching benefit). At split 28 it becomes a slope (488.2 at 4K, 835.0 at 16K). The 4K figure is unchanged, so a 4K-only benchmark cannot detect this at all.

**Memory bandwidth, not SM count or FP32 TFLOPS, tracked the optimum.** The 3060 has 360 GB/s against the 4060 Ti's 288 GB/s, making it the better host for expert-heavy layers despite fewer and slower SMs. The intuitive rule — give the *faster* card proportionally more layers — predicts the opposite direction, and I got it wrong twice before measuring.

## Also observed

The below-512 MiB VRAM warning (#2065) fires at the **low** split values, where the 4060 Ti carries 30-36 layers, and disappears at 24 and above — the tight card is not necessarily the smaller one. `--vram-reserve-mib` was raised 700 → 1024 alongside the split change.

## Limitations

Speed only: no correctness, needle or concurrency tests. The sweep points are single cold-prompt runs; the suite results are 3 runs. Absolute throughput drifts roughly 10-15 % with server age (expert profiles adapt after start), so the sweep is comparable within itself rather than against unrelated runs.

Full per-request data is in `results.json`. Note that `layer_split` is a top-level config key rather than an `args` entry, so it does **not** appear in the engine command line recorded in the report — the README states the split explicitly for that reason.

pulls.title: bench: community report - GTX 1080 Ti (sm_61 Pascal), 2x Xeon E5-2696 v4, IQ3_S at 262K
pulls.author: MrKop-git
pulls.body:
## Summary

A community benchmark on a **GTX 1080 Ti (sm_61 Pascal)** - [TEST_REQUESTS.md](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/blob/main/docs/TEST_REQUESTS.md) asks for Pascal and the earlier answers it lists are Tesla P40s. A consumer card shares the fp32 compute path but has a different memory subsystem (GDDR5X, higher clocks), so it is a useful second data point for the row.

**Strata 0.1.44.1 official release engine** (the installed server - a release binary, not a source build), the standard `tools/strata_bench.py --long --runs 3` suite against the running server, so model loading is not timed.

## Results

| Configuration | Prompt tok/s median (range) | Decode tok/s median (range) | TTFT s median (range) |
|---|---|---|---|
| short chat | — | 27.4 (23.1-31.9) | 1.28 (1.08-1.32) |
| 4K prompt, fresh | **202.4 (201.1-202.8)** | — | 19.92 |
| 16K prompt, fresh | **194.6 (193.5-196.7)** | — | 82.59 |
| agent follow-up turns | ~115 (resent history) | 23.6 (19.1-24.5) | 25.60 |

Prompt throughput is flat from 4K to 16K and reproducible to better than 1% across the three runs of each.

**Conversation cache on agent turns:** 66.0% (63.2-68.8) of the resent history reused, **3 tokens a session read again** - the cache holds almost all of it. That part of the prompt runs at ~115 tok/s against ~202 tok/s fresh.

## What failed, honestly

The **32K prompt test has no numbers**: one agent session and all three 32K requests failed with the server down (the guard script restarted it). The engine log shows healthy requests up to the last successful one and no crash line. The report gives the likely cause without claiming it is proven: the agent sessions park their conversation snapshots (the log's last parking line: `bytes=3911781620` - 3.9 GiB against the configured 8 GiB budget) and the 32K fresh prompts need large buffers on top of that on an 11 GiB card. Worth a look for anyone with a small-card setup.

## Hardware and settings

GTX 1080 Ti 11264 MiB, 2x Xeon E5-2696 v4 (44c/88t, **no AVX-512** - the engine runs its expert kernels on AVX-2), 125.8 GiB RAM, NVMe. **PCIe Gen3 x8** although the card negotiates x16 elsewhere - nvidia-smi reports `pcie.link.width.current 8`, matching the link-tier observations in #2099. Stock 250 W power limit. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next GSQ-RCO **IQ3_S** native pack at **262,144** context, `--kv int8 --kv-resident 32768`, `--expert-cache auto --prefill auto --spec 4 --spec-min-p 0.5`, MTP on.

## Not tested

Contexts past 32K (the 32K test failed, above), `--batch` concurrency, the layer-split path, KV formats other than `int8`, and any correctness check - this is a speed suite. No thermal or clock capture.

Results only, no engine change. `README.md` and `results.json` (per-request data, sanitized by the tool and re-checked for host names and paths before pushing).

pulls.title: [Other] serve: a tool's picture starts the elastic encoder, and its turn counts
pulls.author: jerry78424
pulls.body:
## Problem and result
`_note_unreadable_tool_images` - the method that promises "a picture a tool returned that this server cannot read becomes a short note in its place instead of a 400" - encodes the picture without starting the elastic encoder first. Once the idle sweep has stopped the encoder (`elastic_idle_s` without a picture, default 120 s), the tool's picture writes to a pipe that no longer exists: the `AttributeError` on the `None` proc escapes the `except (ValueError, OSError)` filter and the route's body-shape filter, and the request dies as a **400 "the request is malformed (AttributeError...)"** - the opposite of what the method exists to do. And because clients re-send the whole history every turn, every later request of the conversation dies the same way at this method's own line: the conversation stays broken until a picture from another conversation (or a restart) starts the encoder.

Reproduce: `"elastic": true` + `"vram_elastic": true`; send one picture, let the encoder idle-stop (log: `[strata] images: the image encoder stopped after N s ...`); then send a `tool` message whose content carries an `image` block (Claude Code's Read of a picture - the exact input 3709c15f added this method for). Expected per the method's own docstring: a `[image omitted: ...]` note. Actual: `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'stdin'` (inside `Vision.encode`'s `self.proc.stdin.write`) surfaces as a 400.

After the change the tool picture starts the encoder first, the note is written as documented, and the conversation survives.

## Related discussion
Fixes #3171. The prepare() path does not have this problem - its encode block calls `_vision_up()` inside the FIFO turn; the tool path (3709c15f, wrapped into `_turn` by 873a0d66) never got the wake, and the elastic idle stop made the missing wake fatal. Related: #2435 (the sibling: a start that fails on the prepare path), #2343 (MCP picture results will send more traffic through this exact path). Independent of #2455 (its `cached()` skip lands in this same method later - textual overlap only). #3174 is a parallel PR with the core wake alone; this one is the same fix plus the two sides that adding a wake to this path brings.

## Approach
- `serve/server.py`: inside the tool path's turn, `_vision_up()` before the encode (the caller holds the FIFO, as prepare does); the turn's end updates `last_image_at` in a `finally` - without it the idle sweep judges the just-started encoder by the previous picture's timestamp and reclaims it at once, and a tool-picture-only conversation never moves the timer; `start()`'s `RuntimeError` joins the filter, so a failing start becomes the documented note, not a dead request.
- `serve/test_vision_elastic.py`: two cases - a tool picture wakes a stopped encoder, and the turn holds it across the idle check; a start that raises becomes the note.
- Compatibility: the widened filter matches what can still raise (`encode()`'s own pipe death already becomes ValueError/OSError internally - #1317's read timeout raises ValueError, a write to a dead pipe is OSError - and `ClientGone` is a bare Exception, so a client that left still propagates). No native files touched.

## Validation

**Passed:**
- Both new cases fail on the base tree at the fake's "a picture reached an encoder that was not started" assert (the bug's exact signature), and a real `Vision` with the proc unloaded raises the `AttributeError` verbatim.
- `python -m unittest serve.test_vision_elastic serve.test_vision_busy` (CPU-only, no engine): 13 OK; `python -m unittest serve.test_images`: 19 OK - at `e88ee39d` (v0.2.0-beta-12), rebased 2026-10-20, Windows 11 26200, Python 3.12 venv. On the previous base `f57c0adc` the same files were 9/9 + 32 OK.
- With #2455 on top (cherry-picked, auto-merge clean): the three files stay 19 + 19 OK - the two PRs conflict in neither order.

**Failed:** none observed.

**Not run:** CUDA/HIP/SYCL builds (no native files touched); the live GPU end-to-end is #3171's reporter's log, reproduced here by the two CPU tests' fail-on-base/pass-after signature.

## Limits
- The wake reuses the same FIFO turn the encode already runs in, so a tool picture now costs the encoder start (~seconds, logged) on an idle-stopped encoder - the same cost the user-picture path already pays; it is what the note path cannot afford to skip.
- No native files touched; nothing here changes non-elastic behavior.

pulls.title: generate: --prompt-cache-policy log keeps checkpoints on a geometric grid (opt-in, default lru unchanged; #2431)
pulls.author: qiuzan2001
pulls.body:
For #2431 (TwoAnts' point there that the retention should thin out with distance rather than keep only the newest points).

## What it changes

A new engine argument, `--prompt-cache-policy lru|log`, default `lru`.

With more checkpoints than `--prompt-cache`, the current rule keeps the root and the most recently used points. A 256K conversation with the defaults (`--prompt-cache 6`, `--prompt-cache-every 16384`) therefore holds the root (~30K) and 192K–256K, and a request that branches anywhere between them (an agent compacting its history, an edited early message, a sub-agent that shares the first half) reads everything after the root again.

`log` picks the victim against a geometric grid behind the newest point instead: targets at `every × (2^k − 1)` behind it (0, 16K, 48K, 112K, …), the root pinned as before, the targets that would fall behind the root spent halving the widest remaining gap. The tail checkpoint (`--prompt-cache-tail`) and `pin=N` prefixes are treated exactly as before. The function is pure (`eviction_victim_log` in `include/strata/program/conv_cache.hpp`); the one call site in `src/program/generate.cpp` passes the chain's lengths to it only when the flag is on.

Simulated growth with the defaults (`conv_cache_test`): at 256K `lru` keeps 30/192/208/224/240/256K, `log` keeps 30/80/128/224/240/256K; the largest gap is 96K against 162K. At 1M it is 674K against 930K.

## What it leaves alone

- The default path calls the same `eviction_victim` with the same arguments as before; the new branch is only entered with `--prompt-cache-policy log` and `--prompt-cache-every > 0`. A chain with no more points than `--prompt-cache` is the same either way.
- With more than 64 checkpoints the `log` rule falls back to `lru` (its scratch arrays are fixed; the help text and the docs say so).
- `sycl/src/program/generate.cpp` is not changed. The header is shared and additive, so the SYCL build is unaffected, but the flag is an unknown argument there until that port is re-migrated.

## How it was checked

- `src/program/conv_cache_test.cpp`: 37/37 (16 new: the simulated 128K/256K/1M growth, root/newest/pinned never the victim, the tail rule first, `--prompt-cache-every 0` / no lengths / one slot / more than 64 items fall back to the plain rule, the root not the shortest, the root the longest).
- An independent review pass read the diff and fuzzed the policy with 300,000 random chains under ASan/UBSan: no out-of-bounds, never the root or a pinned item.
- CUDA build (RTX 5070 Ti, CUDA 13.1, arch 120). Not built: HIP (no AMD card here), SYCL (not wired, see above), Metal (no Mac).
- A/B on the machine below with `tools/checkpoint_branch_test.py` (included): four greedy requests against the server, 4 output tokens, thinking off. Three rounds per arm, alternating order, the engine restarted for every run. Every run of an arm reused the same token counts; the prompt time below is the median.

RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB, Ryzen 7 5800X3D, 76 GB RAM, Linux, CUDA 13.1; Swift 1.5 IQ3_S, 262,144 context, `--kv int8 --kv-resident 32768`, `--prompt-cache 6`, `--prompt-cache-every 16384`; engine built from this branch, 0.1.44.1 otherwise.

| request | prompt tokens | lru: reused / read / prompt time | log: reused / read / prompt time |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| cold read | 178,823 | 0 / 178,823 / 62.5 s | 0 / 178,823 / 62.5 s |
| retry of the last turn | 178,823 | 165,035 / 13,788 / 5.7 s | 165,035 / 13,788 / 5.7 s |
| branch at 90,104 | 90,104 | 16,384 / 73,720 / 23.9 s | 66,731 / 23,373 / 8.2 s |
| return to the full conversation | 178,823 | 81,920 / 96,903 / 34.4 s | 83,115 / 95,708 / 34.1 s |

The branch request is the only one where the two differ. (In this run the root the engine kept was the periodic 16,384-token checkpoint, which lands before the ~30K system prompt ends; the gap the `log` rule closes is the same either way.)

Docs: one paragraph in `docs/DETAILS.md` ("Which checkpoints stay") with these numbers, and the flag in the engine options list.
