pulls.title: serve: the keep-alive while a prompt is read is a real SSE frame, not a comment
pulls.author: rebuilt
pulls.body:
## What

The streaming keep-alive (the heartbeat while a long prompt is read, or while a tool argument is held back) is written as an **SSE comment** (`: keep-alive`). A client that resets its stream idle timeout on parsed SSE **frames** drops comments before that accounting, so a slow prefill times out and the client retries from scratch every time.

This changes the two writers whose clients time out this way:

- **OpenAI** `/v1/chat/completions`: an empty `chat.completion.chunk`, reusing the last real chunk's `id`/`created`/`model` (`choices: [{index: 0, delta: {}, finish_reason: null}]`).
- **Anthropic** `/v1/messages`: a real `event: ping` / `data: {"type":"ping"}`.

`/v1/responses` already sends a real `response.in_progress` event every 15 s, so it is unchanged.

## Why not the comment

Reported from a live OpenCode session against a local Strata (gfx1201, IQ3_S 128k): 72k–100k-token prompts, 1–4 minute prefills. OpenCode applies its `chunkTimeout` (default 300 s) to the parsed frame stream and ignores comments, so it aborted mid-stream with `"Timed out waiting for response data"` / `"Connection lost while reading the response"` and retried, each retry re-reading the prompt. The engine log showed the abandoned turn:

```
strata serve: prompt 72822 tokens = 0 reused + 4096 of 72822 read in 17866 ms (229.3 tok/s), 0 generated in 0 ms ... (cancelled)
```

After the change, ~5.5 h of the same traffic: **0** client timeouts/retries, 301 requests served, 0 stalls, 0 engine faults.

## Related

- #1619 (a queued request sends no bytes) and #1666 (a held-back tool argument) suggest the same comment. The queue wait and the held-back argument still send real frames now; please use frames, not comments, in those paths too — a comment will not reset a comment-dropping client.
- Fixes the client-side half of #1951.

## Tests

- New `serve/test_server.py::KeepAliveFrames` — `test_chat_keepalive_is_a_frame`, `test_anthropic_keepalive_is_a_ping_event`.
- `PromptProgress.test_a_client_that_does_not_ask_gets_a_keep_alive_frame` now expects the empty chunk instead of the comment.

pulls.title: cpu(bug): the AVX2 dot kernels keep their accumulators in registers (2.1x router; +20-24% expert rows at 4 tokens)
pulls.author: maxious
pulls.body:
## Title

cpu(bug): the AVX2 dot kernels keep their accumulators in registers (2.1x router; +20-24% expert rows at 4 tokens)

Issue: none — no existing issue covers this (I searched upstream for router dot / AVX2 / spill / kq_avx2; the open CPU-pool ones, #921 #1549 #1913 #1923, are about other problems). Happy to file one and link it.

## Summary

`bf16_rows_dot_multi` (the routing-aware prefetch's router dot, `kq_avx2.cpp`) held its per-token sums in `__m256 acc[MAXT]` indexed by a variable. With eight 256-bit accumulators live, **neither GCC nor clang keeps them in registers** — the array-indexed accumulator is a shape no mainstream compiler undoes by itself: GCC unrolls the column loop and leaves the whole array in memory, and clang spills it too (its object carries the same stack-slot FMA plus a per-row `memset`/`memcpy` call). Every token's FMA then read and wrote a stack slot. On a Ryzen 7 5700X3D that made the AVX2 kernel **slower than the AVX1 copy written for pre-Haswell CPUs**, and every AVX2 CPU calls the AVX2 one (`expert_source.cpp:2271`). The same effect measures on a Zen 5 Ryzen 7 9800X3D (2.06x on GCC, 3.2x on clang), so this is every AVX2 CPU on both compilers, not one GCC version's codegen on one core.

Same sums, same tokens, four named accumulators instead of the array:

Ryzen 7 5700X3D (Zen 3, AVX2, no AVX-512, no AVX-VNNI), one layer's router `[512 experts x 2560 embeddings]`, 4 tokens, one thread pinned to core 2, `router_dot_parity --cpu 2`, median of 3:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| AVX2 kernel `bf16_rows_dot_multi` | 0.400–0.401 ms | **0.185–0.188 ms** (2.1x faster) |
| AVX1 kernel `bf16_rows_dot_multi_avx1` (untouched) | 0.248–0.249 ms | 0.248–0.252 ms |
| AVX2 against AVX1 | 1.6x slower | 1.3x faster |
| stack slots in the inner loop | 21 memory ops per iteration | 0 |
| output bits (FNV-1a over `out[]`, nt 1/2/4/8 x cols 2560/5120) | — | identical, 8 of 8 |

Ryzen 7 9800X3D (Zen 5, AVX2 + AVX-512), same bench, GCC 15.2.0 (the build's default compiler on this PC), one thread pinned to core 0, median of 3:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| AVX2 kernel `bf16_rows_dot_multi` | 0.255–0.274 ms | **0.124–0.125 ms** (2.06x faster) |
| AVX1 kernel `bf16_rows_dot_multi_avx1` (untouched) | 0.165–0.198 ms | 0.146–0.150 ms |
| AVX2 against AVX1 | 1.5x slower | 1.2x faster |
| `router_dot_parity` failures | 0 | 0 |

The compiler is not the variable — the array-indexed accumulator is. Both spill before the change (9800X3D, this file's exact flags `-O3 -DNDEBUG -mavx2 -mfma -mf16c`, 4 tokens pinned to core 0):

| compiler | before: AVX2 | before: AVX1 | after: AVX2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| GCC 15.2.0 | 0.256 ms | 0.171 ms | 0.124 ms |
| clang++ 21.1.8 | 0.401 ms | 0.372 ms | **0.124 ms** (3.2x faster) |

clang's unpatched object shows the same shape at the instruction level — `vfmadd213ps 0x60(%rsp,%rsi,1),%ymm0,%ymm1` followed by `vmovaps %ymm1,0x60(%rsp,%rsi,1)` — so neither compiler recovers the registers itself, and on the Zen 5 box the clang build is slower still because of the per-row `memset`/`memcpy` call. With the accumulators in named registers both compilers land on the identical 0.124 ms, which is the point: the source shape, not the compiler, was the limit. It is not a flag problem either: the build carries no `-march=native` (the CPU kernel files get explicit per-file ISA flags), and adding it would not change `kq_avx2.cpp`'s codegen.

## The expert-row dots: the same shape, the same fix

`q5_1_dot` and `q8_0_dot` (the Q5_1 and Q8_0 down-projection rows, `kq_avx2.cpp`) held their per-token sums in the same runtime-indexed `__m256 acc[MAXT]`. Both are now `template <int NT>`, dispatched 1..4 and chunked four tokens at a time past that - the same idiom the router change and `kq256_gu_rows` already use. Measured the same way (9800X3D, GCC 15.2.0, `native_expert_parity --synthetic` with ggml-quantized weights and activations, one thread on core 0), at the verify window's four tokens:

| kernel | format | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `q5_1_dot` | Q5_1 down rows [2560 x 640] | 190-197 us | **155-156 us** (1.24x) |
| `q8_0_dot` | Q8_0 down rows [2560 x 640] | 135 us | **104 us** (1.30x) |

Sums unchanged: 0 of 36 token-sets differ in any bit against ggml's own `vec_dot` over 1..8 tokens, both before and after; `native_expert_parity: 0 failures`.

**Why `q4k_dot` is left alone.** The Q4_K gate/up dot keeps its runtime-nt array on purpose. Its token accumulators are not what spills - the unpatched function carries 8 ymm stack ops for the sums, against 24 (`q5_1`) and 59 (`q8_0`); what it spills is its weight-side unpack arrays (`q4l`/`q4h`/`scale_l`/`scale_h`), which token chunking does not touch and re-does. The same change measured +5% at four tokens and -4..-7% at six to eight, so it is a wash at the window and a small regression above it, and q4k is the gate/up format that runs most.


## What changed

`src/kernels/cpu/kq_avx2.cpp`: `bf16_rows_dot_multi` (the router), and `q5_1_dot` + `q8_0_dot` (the Q5_1 and Q8_0 down-projection rows); plus one comment line in `kq_avx1.cpp`.

- The row loop is chunked four tokens at a time (`for (int t0 = 0; t0 < nt; t0 += 4)`), the same idiom `kq256_gu_rows` already uses in this file, and each pass keeps its sums in four named `__m256` accumulators (`a0..a3`) instead of a variable-indexed `__m256 acc[MAXT]`. Four live accumulators fit in registers alongside the weight vector, so the column loop can unroll without the array going to memory — under GCC and clang alike.
- A window longer than four tokens reads a row a second time, from L1, so the extra pass costs nothing measurable at nt=8 (0.37 ms, the same as the spilled form, in a micro-benchmark of the two shapes compiled with each file's exact flags).
- `#pragma GCC unroll 1` on the column loop is **not** part of the change: it changes nothing. GCC keeps the column unroll and the spills either way; the variable-indexed array is what forces the array into memory.

**What it leaves alone.** The arithmetic and the reduction. Each token's FMA chain still runs over the same columns in the same order and ends in the same `hsum_float_8`, so every sum is bit-identical. The AVX1 kernel's code, `q4k_dot` (see above), the other expert row kernels (`iq_avx2.cpp`, `q2_avx2.cpp`, `kq256_gu_rows`, `kq256_rows`) and the engine's dispatch are untouched — the single `kq_avx1.cpp` line is its comment only, which had said the AVX1 kernel reads its rows "exactly as the AVX2 kernel does" and is no longer true once the AVX2 kernel chunks its row loop four tokens at a time. The router stays what it was — an estimate for which experts to prefetch, not part of the model's output.

## Extra Notes

How I checked:

- **Both CPUs:** the 5700X3D (Zen 3) table above, and the 9800X3D (Zen 5) table — 0.256 → 0.124 ms, 2.06x, from the same source build and the same commands as the reproduction below.
- **Both compilers:** GCC 15.2.0 and clang++ 21.1.8 spill on the unpatched source (the compiler table above, and clang's object disassembled); the change removes the array-indexed accumulator, so the codegen question disappears either way — both compilers end at the same 0.124 ms.
- **Bit-exact:** the whole `out[]` hashes the same (FNV-1a) before and after for nt 1/2/4/8 at cols 2560 and 5120, 8 of 8. `router_dot_parity` reports 0 failures with the AVX2 rel error against the double reference unchanged at 3.16e-07.
- **Tests:** `ctest -R 'router_dot|iq_avx|q8k_quant|q2_bitplane'` — 100% tests passed, 0 failed out of 8.
- **No router regression in the expert path:** the `iq_avx2_parity --bench` run over four format pairs x 1..8 tokens (255 MB of experts streamed from DRAM, one thread) moved within 1.6% across all 64 medians, which is noise; the expert path does not call this function.
- **The expert rows:** `native_expert_parity --synthetic q4_K/q5_1` and `q4_K/q8_0` report `0 of 36 token-sets differ` in any bit and 0 failures over 1..8 tokens; `iq_avx2_parity`, `iq_avx1_parity`, `q8k_quant_parity` and `router_dot_parity` all exit 0. One thread pinned to core 0 throughout.
- **Backends:** CUDA and HIP do not compile this file. The SYCL port does (`sycl/CMakeLists.txt:176`), and `strata_kernels_cpu` builds there under icpx 2026.1 (exit 0, no new warnings, and its object has no spills either). The expert-row change added since has not been through that SYCL build (no icpx on the measuring machine); it is the same file and the same kind of change.

The benchmark, from a source build (CMake fetches the pinned llama.cpp commit for ggml-cpu when `STRATA_GGML_DIR` is not given):

```
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSTRATA_BUILD_TESTS=ON
cmake --build build --target router_dot_parity iq_avx2_parity
```

This change, one thread pinned to one core (the first table is core 2 on the 5700X3D, the second core 0 on the 9800X3D; any core works, the medians move a little):

```
taskset -c 2 ./build/router_dot_parity     # 5700X3D: avx2 0.19 ms, avx 0.25 ms (was 0.41 ms)
taskset -c 0 ./build/router_dot_parity     # 9800X3D: avx2 0.124 ms, avx 0.171 ms (was 0.256 ms)
```

Both print `router_dot_parity: 0 failures`. The compiler comparison, in a second build folder with the same file flags:

```
cmake -S . -B build-clang -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
      -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++ -DSTRATA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
cmake --build build-clang --target router_dot_parity
taskset -c 0 ./build-clang/router_dot_parity   # before the change: avx2 0.401 ms, avx 0.372 ms
```

The expert rows, for the no-regression check:

```
taskset -c 2 ./build/iq_avx2_parity --bench --cpu 2
```

`--cpu N` pins inside the tool as well, `--reps N` (default 5) sets the repetitions behind each median, `--pairs iq3_s/iq4_nl,...` picks the format pairs and `--mb 256` the expert bytes streamed from DRAM per pair.

pulls.title: Add files via upload
pulls.author: kxyct
pulls.body:
```markdown
Results-only submission (no engine changes): `bench/results/2026-10-11-community-rtx-5070ti-laptop-12gb/`.

The two 5070 Ti rows already in the index are desktop cards. This is the **12 GB laptop** part, and I
believe it is the smallest-VRAM row in the table running a 262K context.

- **Hardware**: RTX 5070 Ti Laptop GPU 12,227 MiB (driver 616.64, 140 W limit, AC), Ryzen 9 9955HX
  (Windows reports 8C/16T for this part), 61.7 GB RAM, YMTC PC411 1 TB NVMe, Windows 11 build 26100.
- **Software/model**: engine 0.1.41 release (CUDA 13.0); Flash-Next IQ3_XXS, 262,144 context,
  `--kv int8 --kv-resident 32768 --vram-reserve-mib 700 --expert-cache auto --spec 4`, plus this
  machine's own `--calibrate` values. Expert cache filled 1585/1585 slots (2.61 GiB) at startup.
- **Method**: 3 fresh runs per tier (unique nonce first, server reports `0 reused`), 256-token cap.
  Prefill, decode and the expert-cache hit rate are read back out of the engine's own log lines, not
  timed by the harness. Script and per-run JSON in the folder.
- **Results (medians)**: 4K: prefill 788.5 / decode 63.8 tok/s; 32K: 901.4 / 64.1; 128K: 886.8 / 64.4;
  192K: 869.4 / 61.2. Expert cache hit 56-58 % throughout.
- **The point**: decode is **flat** from a 4K prompt to a 192K prompt (63.8 → 61.2 tok/s). Context
  length on this card costs prefill *time* (231 s for a 197K prompt at ~870 tok/s), not decode speed.
  I put this down to `--kv-resident`: the same card at 204800 **without** it held only 207 expert slots
  and decoded at 2.3 tok/s.
- **Limitations**: single laptop, English prose prompts only (prefill is content-sensitive), no clock
  or power capture, non-streaming so no separate TTFT. The 204800-without-streaming figure is 2 replies
  from an earlier session — a direction, not a measurement.
```

pulls.title: bench: ROG Flow Z13 Windows HIP, Huihui IQ4_XS 256K tuning and placement
pulls.author: xszwow
pulls.body:
## Summary

Records a reproducible configuration search on a 128 GiB ASUS ROG Flow Z13 (Ryzen AI Max+ 395 / Radeon 8060S gfx1151, 96 GiB GPU allocation), Windows 11, Strata 0.1.42 at 61b3fb5, with Huihui Qwen3.8-Flash-Next unsloth-UD-IQ4_XS and the official Qwen MTP draft layer.

The final same-machine six-case comparison improved weighted harmonic decode throughput from 46.41 to 48.87 tok/s (+5.31%). It uses two repetitions per case and 512-token output prefixes. The report distinguishes these from completed xhigh answers and near-256K input tests.

## What changed

Adds one community-results folder with 18 files:
- Portable original, selected text, and later vision configuration snapshots; exact per-profile configurations and selection decisions.
- 809 per-request records: 780 formal throughput requests, 10 complete quality answers, four full-context requests, 12 coding conversation turns, and three fresh-process startup checks.
- Exact deduplicated prompts, full response/timing/grade/memory records, a CSV index, model/pack/engine hashes, matching Windows hipBLASLt tuning table, replay/analysis script and checksums.
- Audited placement log: all 24,576 experts in a 55.43 GiB GPU cache, effective host expert residency zero, mapped embeddings, MTP/head/verify allocations, worker affinity and startup free-memory counters.

The recorded selected text profile uses spec 6 / floor 0.4, prefill 16,384, int8 KV, MTP window 8,192, eight pool workers, and 262,144 total context capacity. Daily prompt cache is six; scored comparisons disable prompt reuse. Server fallback is high; xhigh tests explicitly override it. Thinking budget/cap behavior is documented.

## Validation and limitations

- Offline report verification passes: checksums, exact message references, 809 unique records, 780 formal requests, and independently recomputed final medians/score. Each uploaded Git blob matches the local file. Diff whitespace check and config-render smoke check pass.
- Completed coding checks: 94 per quality profile; full-context BFS 41; 12-turn conversation 376. Three fresh-process starts: 92.531 / 91.407 / 91.281 seconds, each with a complete 26-test check.
- Exact-count reasoning failed under both profiles (expected 601380693). Failed allocations, an earlier unbounded-thinking run and explicit stored-reply regrades are retained.
- TTFT, sustained power/temperature and aggregate peak VRAM were not measured. Windows commit headroom fell to about 0.16 GiB. Two repetitions and this small quality set do not establish broad equivalence, a global optimum or a win over different online conditions.

Related vision warm-up change #1946 remains separate. The later vision config is labeled as outside this text search's measurement coverage. No engine defaults, kernels or headline performance claims change in this PR. No model weights or private user paths are included.

pulls.title: fix(vision): scale GPU warm-up for image caps above 4096
pulls.author: xszwow
pulls.body:
Issue: Fixes #1945

## Summary

With `--gpu --max-tokens 8192`, `strata-vision` still warms a fixed 2048 × 2048 bitmap, which produces only 4096 image tokens. On a Radeon 8060S/Vulkan run, encoding an 8160-token 4K image subsequently allocated another 605,757,440 bytes after `READY`, when the language engine may already have sized its expert cache.

Scale the dummy bitmap for explicitly configured caps above 4096. The tested 8192 cap now warms at 8100 tokens and reaches its observed 2.1474 GiB encoder allocation before `READY`; the same 4K image adds no further allocation in this test.

## What changed

Only `tools/vision/strata_vision.cpp` changes:

- Add `<cmath>` and use `32 * ceil(sqrt(max_tokens))` for caps above 4096, matching the Qwen merged-token pixel size.
- Retain the 2048-pixel square for an omitted cap and caps up to 4096. CPU mode continues to skip warm-up.
- Correct the comment: mtmd rounds the square's patch grid, so prewarm approaches the cap rather than guaranteeing its exact token count.

The model, encoder math, CLI defaults, language engine, installer and server settings remain unchanged.

## Validation

Same-day source builds against `main` at `61b3fb5dd3f1e8ec09cf7e4e05208bc6d3c46406`, with llama.cpp pinned at `3cf03257f219afbe7334045ff7c6a06ac68c627d`. Tested on Windows 11 Home build 26200, Ryzen AI Max+ 395 / Radeon 8060S (gfx1151), 128 GB RAM / 96 GB GPU assignment, AMD driver 32.0.31032.1003, LLVM MinGW 23.1.3 (20261006), Vulkan SDK 1.4.350.0. Both builds used native CPU kernels.

- CPU-only and Vulkan Release build/link passed for baseline and patch.
- Vulkan: caps 300, 4096 and 8192 all reached `READY 2560`, encoded valid finite SVE embeddings and exited cleanly.
- CPU: cap 8192 kept the no-warm-up path and produced valid finite embeddings.
- All six paired SVE files were byte-identical: a 1200 × 720 Chinese-text fixture at all three Vulkan caps and CPU 8192; a synthetic 3840 × 2160 fixture at Vulkan 4096 and 8192.
- The published source blob matches the locally compiled file; `git diff --check` passed.

| GPU image cap | Baseline warm-up tokens | Patched warm-up tokens |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 300 | 289 | 289 |
| 4096 | 4096 | 4096 |
| 8192 | 4096 | 8100 |

For cap 8192, Windows dedicated-GPU-memory counters were:

| Snapshot | Baseline bytes | Patched bytes |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| At READY | 1,699,991,552 | 2,305,748,992 |
| After the 8160-token 4K image | 2,305,748,992 | 2,305,748,992 |

Measured prewarm was 8.2 s before and 33.2 s after at cap 8192. This intentionally moves the larger allocation/encode cost to startup. These are single functional observations, not a throughput benchmark or an established end-to-end speed improvement.

Reproduction:

```text
strata-vision --mmproj <mmproj-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-BF16.gguf> --model <first-text-GGUF-shard> --gpu --threads 16 --min-tokens 1024 --max-tokens 8192
ENC <3840x2160-image.png> <output.sve>
QUIT
```

## Extra Notes

Draft because CUDA encoder build/runtime validation is still outstanding under the repository's backend-validation requirement; this AMD machine has no CUDA toolkit. HIP/SYCL language-engine files are untouched. Other GPUs, caps above 8192 and unusual aspect ratios were not tested, and no OOM/paging failure is claimed to have been reproduced.

Both local builds needed an explicit `<functional>` include in the external pinned llama.cpp Vulkan header when using libc++; that identical build prerequisite is excluded from this Strata PR.

Related Windows AMD image work: #1155, #1287, #1789. This change can accompany those build/installer changes.

pulls.title: hip: opt-in exact gfx1100 QSA scorer for long prefill
pulls.author: 2jztricks
pulls.body:
Large fresh prompts on gfx1100 spend substantial time in QSA block scoring. This adds an **opt-in, HIP-only exact scorer** that reduces fresh request latency by about 10–23% on an RX 7900 XTX in the measurements below, while keeping the default scorer selected.

This ports the four-lanes-per-query method and original FP32 reduction tree from **xrip's #1825**, pinned to `14bf32150490bb9f5fc4d9c7c5dcfdc96dd98797`. That PR currently excludes HIP. Credit for the algorithm belongs there; this contribution adds the guarded gfx1100 implementation, hardware validation, and reproducible measurement evidence.

### Scope

- Enable with `STRATA_SCORES_THREAD=1` at process startup; **off by default**.
- Exact gfx1100 device check; at least 64 queries and an actual live bound of at least 16,385 index blocks, within allocation capacity. A reserved 256K context alone never engages it.
- Four wave32 lanes per query, all four heads in registers, keys reused through LDS; 64 queries / 32 key-block tiles / 256 threads. Original tail scorer and top-k remain intact.
- Decode, expert placement, CPU kernels, PLE storage and sampling are unchanged by the patch. No extra persistent weights or conversation state are allocated.
- Adds a standalone HIP score/ID parity target, available even when the published tree omits `tests/`. CUDA does not compile the new HIP kernel.

### Before/after on the RX 7900 XTX

RX 7900 XTX 24 GiB, Ryzen 9 7950X3D, 64 GiB installed RAM, Nobara 44, ROCm 10.0.0, observed PCIe 4.0 x16, fixed 272 W cap. OrcaRouter Flash Next IQ3_S; logical context 262,144; int8 KV / 32,768 resident cells; 15 CPU expert workers; prefill 16,384; MTP6/floor0.70; same balanced profile and 8,144 GPU expert slots in every arm. PLE stayed on ext4 SSD with direct I/O. Experiment swap limit zero.

Fresh numerical-source prompts, zero reused prefix tokens, greedy sampling, reasoning disabled, **one generated token**. Values are non-streaming **request latency**, excluding model loading; this is not a sustained decode or streaming-TTFT benchmark. New private worker for each fresh case; OS file cache not flushed.

| Engine family | Actual prompt tokens | Paired trials | Before mean | After mean | Less elapsed time |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Tuned 0.1.40.3 control/candidate | 130,978 | 3 | 66.741 s | 59.769 s | 10.45% |
| Tuned 0.1.40.3 control/candidate | 239,906 | 3 | 142.718 s | 110.407 s | 22.64% |
| Current main, **same binary**, flag off/on | 130,978 | 1 | 68.872 s | 60.020 s | 12.85% |
| Current main, **same binary**, flag off/on | 239,906 | 1 | 142.843 s | 111.828 s | 21.71% |

The repeated family used off/on, on/off, off/on and includes the same local prefix-reuse/budget-loan changes in both arms. The separate current-main engine was built from `61b3fb5dd3f1e8ec09cf7e4e05208bc6d3c46406` plus this patch. Its only arm difference is the scorer flag. These families are **not pooled**. All fresh input/output hashes and output counts matched.

At the actual 256-query batch size, the submitted CMake microbenchmark measured the **scorer stage**:

| Live context | Original scorer | New scorer | Stage speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 131,072 | 3.065300 ms | 0.742917 ms | 4.126× |
| 240,000 | 5.264949 ms | 1.389344 ms | 3.790× |

Warmed GPU-event timing, interleaved ABBA, four trials / ten calls per trial. The stage speedup is not presented as whole-task speedup.

### Correctness and build validation

- Submitted HIP CMake test passed **35 cases: 223,664,777 bitwise-equal score values and 11,895,800 equal ID buffer entries**, including padding and allocation guards.
- Boundaries, partial tiles, 256-query batches, one/six-query fallback, capacity versus actual live extent, invalid/absent bounds, ties, signed zero, NaN/Inf, wide exponents and cancellation covered.
- Tuned-model 4K/131K prefill plus first token matched main state byte for byte; separate 64-token output and STOP/resend output checks matched. Full speculative state after 64 MTP tokens can vary even across repeats of the original binary; this is documented rather than claimed as full-state equality.
- Current-main full HIP engine and standalone CMake test target built and ran. The touched CUDA module compiled with CUDA 13.0 for sm_89; no CUDA GPU test or full CUDA-engine build. No SYCL source changed.
- Current-main off/on requests passed, matched output hashes, kept the same 8,144 expert slots, and maintained the 8 GiB available-memory floor; minimum observed 12.249 GiB, experiment swap zero.

### Limits: no default or general agent-speed recommendation

Cached follow-ups processing 2,085 new tokens had only a modest/flat repeated gain: 2.829→2.658 s at 128K; 3.418→3.417 s near240K (two pairs each). The single current-main continuation results are included in the report but do not establish a repeatable large gain.

A separate correction-inclusive 192K-source-archive pilot used xhigh/8,192 reasoning tokens, T0.3, matched seeds and automatic full-suite checks:

| Task | Original | New scorer | Outcome |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Go alphametics | 209.136 s | 400.318 s | Both passed; 3 versus 5 turns |
| Rust xorcism | 473.734 s | 304.906 s | Both passed; 6 turns each |
| **Total** | **682.870 s** | **705.225 s** | **New scorer 3.27% slower** |

One pair per task, not an official Aider leaderboard score. The Go repair-path divergence remains unexplained. An earlier 240K archive attempt exceeded the context limit during Rust repairs and is preserved separately as a protocol failure. The general promotion gate failed; no full24 run, no production promotion, and no Luna/frontier/overall quality superiority claim.

Only gfx1100 was validated on hardware. The model comparison used the same locally patched prefix-cache frontend in both arms; the stock latest Python frontend was not benchmarked. The one-token screen cannot establish generation quality. Broader task qualification is needed before any default change.

### Reproduction and artifacts

[Full report, medians/ranges, per-request JSON, exact prompt fixture, configuration/provenance and benchmark script](https://github.com/2jztricks/Strata/tree/hip-gfx1100-exact-qsa-scores/bench/results/2026-10-11-gfx1100-qsa-scores).

```bash
cmake -S . -B build-qsa -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DSTRATA_ENABLE_HIP=ON -DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1100 \
  -DSTRATA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF -DSTRATA_PARITY_GFX1100_QSA_SCORES=ON
cmake --build build-qsa --target qsa_scores_gfx1100_parity -j 6
ctest --test-dir build-qsa --output-on-failure -R '^qsa_scores_gfx1100_parity$'
```

The report provides request-screen commands and all tested settings. The script reproduces the frozen fresh/follow request hashes, refuses to overwrite attempts, and rejects accidentally reused prefixes in a fresh case. No credentials, private conversation history, model weights or large profiling traces are included.

pulls.title: serve: the image encoder can run on a second PC over ssh (#1404)
pulls.author: TraceRecursion
pulls.body:
Issue: Resolves #1404

## Summary

The image encoder is already a separate process behind a line protocol (`ENC <image> <out>`), and it is not tied
to the server's machine, so it can run on a second PC over ssh. That takes its VRAM off the card running the
model: 1383 MiB measured, and the engine's own startup line goes 3112 -> 3641 experts (+1.00 GiB of expert
cache). 2.8 s per 1024-token picture against 15.27 s on this CPU (5.4x), and 1.2 s a picture slower than a
local GPU encoder. It does not make text faster: long-context text is the same in all three modes, because
+1 GiB against a ~47 GiB expert set is ~2% coverage. A picture-latency and VRAM trade.

## What changed

- `docs/REMOTE_VISION.md` (new): the page asked for in #1404 - the exact command, the config line, what happens
  when the second PC is down, and the measurements with what they were measured on.
- `README.md`: one line under "Pictures" pointing at it.
- `docs/DETAILS.md`: the `"remote": true` paragraph in "Images (vision)", next to the other vision settings.
- `tools/remote-vision/` (new): `strata_vision_remote.py` (the wrapper - the protocol passes paths, not data, so
  the picture and the embeddings cross one ssh connection), `strata-vision-remote.cmd` (the `vision.exe` shim;
  `Popen` cannot start a `.py` directly), `make_vocab_stub.py` (an 11 MB vocabulary-only stub - `strata-vision`
  opens the text model with `vocab_only = true`, so the vision host does not need the 51 GB shard),
  `remote-build.sh` (builds the encoder on a Linux host), `remote-vision-watchdog.sh` (reaps the encoder when the
  server's port stops answering), and `test-wrapper.ps1` (the check in the notes below).
- `serve/server.py`: the two changes I asked about in #1404. `"remote": true` keeps the encode out of the request
  FIFO: a local encoder shares this machine's GPU with the engine and must stay serialised, a remote one shares
  nothing, and holding the FIFO across the upload to a starved host freezes the API, text requests included - a
  text request sent during one encode waited 13.30 s with the turn held against 0.56 s or less with
  `"remote": true` (measured below). `Service.ensure_vision` lets the server start and serve text when the
  encoder cannot, answering `400 the image encoder is not available: ...` on the first image and asking again on
  the next one. Without it, a boot-order race dropped the connection and told the client nothing at all
  (measured: `status 0`).
- `serve/test_server.py`: 4 tests (`RemoteVision`). The FIFO one counts the engine's turn, so it fails if the
  remote path ever takes it (0 entries, against 1 for a local encoder), and it asserts that the client's cancel
  event reaches the encoder (#1999).
- `.gitignore`: `tools/remote-vision/*.gguf`, so the generated stub cannot be committed by accident.

## Extra Notes

**Rebased on the current `main` (`477ac13c`).** The conflicts were with #1999 (the engine's turn is a cancellable
`Service._turn(cancel)` now), with the `"elastic"` encoder's `Service._vision_up` / `last_image_at` in the
picture path, and with the `"elastic"` paragraph that now sits where the vision settings are documented. The
resolution keeps all of it and only skips the turn for a remote encoder: `encode_all(images, cancel)` for a local
one, the same call without the turn for a remote one, and the paragraph follows the `"elastic"` one.

**It composes with the neighbouring vision options.** `"elastic": true` (#2189) starts the GPU encoder on the
first picture and gives its VRAM back when it sits idle; `"remote": true` moves the encoder off this card
entirely, so there is no local VRAM to make room for and the encode skips the turn. Upstream now points
pictures at the CPU encoder on NVIDIA cards under 24 GB (#2406, measured there at 15.27 s for a 1024-token
picture against 2.7 s here), so the two answer different points of the same trade: that one keeps the card's
VRAM and pays in seconds per picture, this one keeps the seconds and pays a second PC over ssh.

**Default path.** `"remote": true` is the opt-in and nothing without it behaves differently - including the
startup tolerance, which is gated on the same key: a LOCAL encoder that fails to start is still fatal, and still
names the cause (#1445), because that is a broken install and not an absent host. Only a remote one starts
text-only and retries.

**What I checked.** `python -m unittest discover -s serve -t . -p "test_*.py"`: 852 tests, OK (15 skipped) on
this branch, rebased on `477ac13c`. Real-machine checks on engine 0.1.45 (server from this branch; an RTX 5080
plus an RTX 3060 over ssh, the encoder rebuilt from this branch's `tools/vision`):

- the picture path: the log has `[vision-remote] encoder up: READY 2560`; a text request answered in 0.87 s; one
  fresh 1600x1600 picture (1024 image tokens, none of it cached) answered in 5.23 s with the right answer, and
  the wrapper logged `...img: OK 1024 in 2.71s (10.00 MB back)`;
- the encoder's host gone (same config, `STRATA_VISION_SSH` at a host that does not resolve): the server still
  started and served text (0.70 s), and the first image answered `400` with `the image encoder is not available:
  the vision encoder did not start: ERR the remote vision encoder could not be started` - a readable error
  instead of a dropped connection - and so did the next one (7.97 s and 7.95 s, the ssh attempt's cost);
- the FIFO, isolated: the same fresh 1024-token picture through the LOCAL CPU encoder (about 15 s of encode, so
  the window is unambiguous) - with the turn held, a text request sent while the encode ran waited 13.30 s (the
  image request itself 20.9 s); with `"remote": true`, nine text requests spread over the same encode all came
  back in 0.17-0.56 s against a 0.17-0.19 s baseline (the image request 19.3 s).

Only Python and `tools/` are touched, no C++/CUDA/HIP/SYCL file, so no backend rebuild is involved.

**What I did not test.** The server side was only exercised on Windows; the wrapper's Linux side
(`remote-build.sh`, the watchdog) was built and smoke-tested on the vision host but not against a Linux Strata
server. `STRATA_VISION_MUX` is off by default because ssh multiplexing fails on Windows (`getsockname failed:
Not a socket`). The translated READMEs are untouched. The FIFO A/B above uses a local CPU encoder to make the
encode long enough to measure; the turn it takes is the same object a remote encoder would take. The encode
above was the first picture after a fresh encoder start (2.71 s); a warm encoder measured 1.71 s for the same
1024 tokens.

**The table is from engine 0.1.40.2** (the release current on 2026-10-07/08, when it was taken): the three modes
were measured the same day on one build, which is what the deltas need. The encoder binary and its mtmd path are
unchanged since, and the config gives `--vram-reserve-mib 700` explicitly, so 0.1.42's Windows auto-reserve floor
(#1376) does not apply to these numbers either. The branch itself is rebased on 0.1.45, which is what the checks
above ran on.

**Left out on purpose:** my own deploy helper (a PowerShell script that pushes the sources to my vision host and
rebuilds there - it hardcodes my two machines and my model paths). Happy to add a generalized version if you
want one.

**Happy to split** the `serve/server.py` behaviour and its tests into their own PR if that is easier to review;
the page and `tools/remote-vision/` need each other to be usable.

pulls.title: Add Arc native Windows support
pulls.author: K8-and-a-half-1000
pulls.body:
### Author's note:

This PR adds support for running Strata on Arc on Windows **natively**, tested on a Pro B70. No WSL2, no docker.
This work was done over the course of a week in an offshoot project at first, but I've decided to contribute upstream based on the project activity and direction.

In short: I like what I see, so here's a contribution to help support the project.

## AI disclaimer
Fable 5.1 ultracode and max used heavily throughout.
I've been critical and culled as many temp files, tools and journey notes that are not relevant for this project. 

## Summary

The SYCL port builds and runs natively on Windows 11 with the Intel oneAPI compiler (`icx`), the Visual Studio Build
Tools and the Intel Arc driver. Written for and measured on an Arc Pro B70 (32 GB) dedicated to the model. The Linux
build is unchanged: everything lives in `sycl/` under `#if defined(_WIN32)` or in new Windows scripts.

Full description, measurements and open questions: `docs/INTEL_WINDOWS.md`.

## What it adds

- **Build**: `sycl\tools\build_windows.bat` finds Visual Studio and oneAPI, configures `sycl\CMakeLists.txt` with
  Ninja, builds the engine, `strata-device` and the probes, and packages `engine\` with the oneAPI runtime DLLs and a
  `BUILD.json` (`sycl\tools\package_windows.py`). CMake: MSVC-style flags for `icx`, `/Qmkl:sequential`, the dynamic
  CRT, the AVX flags.
- **Install and serve**: `sycl\setup_intel.py` and `sycl\serve\server_intel.py` on Windows (cards numbered by
  `strata-device --list-devices`, the engine's environment, Sysman telemetry through `ctypes` in
  `sycl\serve\xe_telemetry.py`); `setup.py` hands `--backend sycl` over on Windows. Tests without a GPU:
  `tools\test_setup_sycl_windows.py`.
- **Engine**: the card choice and capability gate (`device.dp.cpp`); a chunked VRAM arena that tries one allocation
  first (`core/device.hpp`); the DXGI video-memory budget folded into the free-VRAM figure (`sycl_mem.hpp`); a VRAM
  heartbeat against WDDM eviction on a card that drives no display (`sycl_heartbeat.hpp`); `prepare_for_device_copy`
  on the pinned expert arena; overlapped `ReadFile` for `--stream-experts`; the `windows.h` macros that collide with
  identifiers in the kernels (`IN`, `OUT`, `near`, `far`, `small`, `hyper`) dropped after the dpct headers;
  `_putenv_s` in the two parity programs that call `setenv`.
- **Probes** (`sycl/probe/`): doorbell, allocation, bandwidth and graph probes, each ending in a `VERDICT` line that
  names the engine setting it decides. All under Strata's MIT license (the two that derived from XeStrata's LGPL files
  were rewritten from their descriptions).
- **Tools**: `report_windows.py` (a one-shot bug-report bundle) and `benchy_windows.bat` / `.py` (the Linux port's
  benchy on Windows; not yet run).

## What ran

Arc Pro B70, driver 32.0.101.8976, oneAPI 2026.0.0, AOT `bmg-g31`, 2026-10-10 and 11: the build (0 errors), the
probes, and Swift 1.5 IQ3_XXS at `--max-context 262144` with INT8 KV and 32,768 resident cells, used from qwen-code for
an evening: prompts read at 630-890 tok/s, decode 50-76 tok/s, 97-99.3% of the KV block reads from VRAM, 2.1 GiB of
VRAM free with everything loaded. On the 0.1.38 base before this: Coder IQ1_M at 60 tok/s sampled, and Swift served
for several days.

## Two things worth knowing upstream

1. **`sycl/src/kernels/cuda/qsa_decode_attn.dp.cpp` is the 0.1.38 migration, kept in place of the 0.1.41 one.** The
   0.1.41 copy adds the opt-in lane-cell scoring variant (`STRATA_ATTN_LANECELL`) as a second template parameter of
   `attn_chunk_kernel`. Compiled that way by icx 2026.0.0 for `bmg-g31`, the INT8 instantiation's batched output is
   inf and NaN (`qsa_prompt_attn_parity`, "vs FP64 old": 78.5 on an output scale of 3.7) while the fp16 instantiation
   is exact; the 0.1.38 copy, otherwise the same code, measures 2e-6 in both. Since 0.1.41 routes SYCL prompts
   through this kernel, every reply on Windows was token 0 until the swap. `kv_stream_parity` cannot catch this
   class of defect: it compares the kernel's streamed output with its resident output, both through the same kernel.
   Whether the Linux build is affected was not measured.
2. **The opt-in XMX prompt attention** (`STRATA_PROMPT_ATTN_XMX=1`) measures 2e-3 absolute (5e-4 of scale) on this
   Windows build, where `docs/INTEL.md` reports 1e-6 of scale on Linux. Off by default; not understood.

## Known limits

One card per model on Windows (`--gpus` / `--layer-split` is refused); images are not wired on Intel; only the Arc Pro
B70 has run this (other Battlemage cards need `STRATA_SYCL_AOT=bmg-g21` or a JIT build); the greedy benchmark and the
heartbeat's idle test have not been run. Details in `docs/INTEL_WINDOWS.md`, "Known limits and open questions".

## Extra Notes

On Windows there is a RAM eviction on idle timeout that affects Intel Arc cards, which will happen if the card is not driving any displays. This can be avoided by adding a small heartbeat every 10 seconds to poke the card. Check the heartbeat files for more info.

pulls.title: [Engine] serve: parked conversations on the disk, optionally across restarts (--conversation-disk-dir, --conversation-disk-persist)
pulls.author: xrip
pulls.body:
## Problem and result

A conversation the RAM conversation cache evicts (its slots or its byte budget full) is dropped, and a client that comes back to it reads the whole prompt again: an agent that switches between its main conversation and sub-agents too large for the budget together reads ~150K tokens again on every switch. Every restart of the engine (an update, a settings change, a reboot, a poweroff) also reads every conversation from token 0 again.

- **Before:** an evicted conversation, and every conversation at a restart, costs a full re-read (73.3 s for 165,558 tokens on the box below).
- **After, with `--conversation-disk-dir DIR`:** the evicted conversation goes to `DIR` and comes back from there when a request continues it. With `--conversation-disk-persist on|exit-only` the conversations outlive the engine: the same 165,558-token conversation came back after a restart in 8.4 s, with the same answer.

## Related discussion

The maintainer said in #1090 that one disk-persistence design will be chosen; this is one of them. It was closed in the 0.2.0-beta reset and is rebased here onto 0.2.1. #3404 (separate, in the conversation cache) drops stale parked copies of a conversation, which the disk tier would otherwise write out.

## Approach

Off by default (opt-in options, help text and `docs/DETAILS.md`):
- `conversation_disk.hpp/.cpp`: the tier. Each image (one per stage with `--layer-split`) is one session file, written and read with the session files' own code (size, header and hash checks, the free-space preflight). A background writer (nice 10 on Linux) means a switch never waits for the disk, and queued images can be read back from RAM. Every checkpoint is kept, as in RAM. `--conversation-disk-mib N` (default 32768): oldest out first.
- `conversation_cache.hpp`: `set_on_evict`, so an evicted conversation goes to the tier instead of being dropped. A park that does not fit the cache's byte budget is also sent to the disk.
- `generate.cpp`: options, wiring, the read back when the disk holds a longer prefix than the session / a batch slot / the RAM cache (it needs RAM for the whole image above `--conversation-cache-min-free-mib`, else the prompt is read again), and the request line says when it was reused from the disk.
- `--conversation-disk-persist on|exit-only`: the files are bound to the session files' identity (model, engine version, settings), with an index per conversation, so the next start takes them in. Files of another identity are removed at start. On QUIT the engine saves the current conversation and the parked ones; while persist is on it ignores SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP and ends through its stdin, so a poweroff's SIGTERM does not cut the save short. The server waits up to 300 s for QUIT (`serve/server.py`, 4 lines). `exit-only` writes nothing while running and saves only at QUIT.
- A file is read back only when that is faster than reading the tokens it adds, by this run's measured disk and prompt speeds (the match reports its files' bytes; the prompt path's parts of 2,048 tokens or more are timed). A new conversation that shares only the system prompt with a saved one no longer reads that one's whole file. Until both speeds are measured the file is read; a skip is logged as `not read`. Second commit.
- `conversation_disk.cpp` is added to the CUDA/HIP, SYCL and Metal engine lists (all three compile `generate.cpp`).

Compatibility: with no `--conversation-disk-dir` nothing is written or read. One change stays in the parking path: before the RAM admission evicts a conversation, it calls glibc's `malloc_trim(0)`, so freed images count in MemAvailable. Output is unaffected.

## Validation

**Passed:**
- Rebased onto 0.2.1 (`90767252`) as two commits: `65a79b51` (the tier) and `c6b99976` (the read check). CUDA build in Docker (`nvidia/cuda:13.3.0-devel-ubuntu24.04`, GCC 14, `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=75 -DSTRATA_ENABLE_CUDA=ON -DSTRATA_BUILD_TESTS=ON -DSTRATA_BUILD_CONVERSATION_TESTS=ON`): `strata` and the tests build; `conversation_disk_test` 69 checks, `conversation_cache_test` 4,772, `conversation_file_test` 201, all pass.
- `python -m pytest -q serve/test_server.py serve/test_parallel.py serve/test_parallel_yield.py serve/test_request_accounting.py`: 392 passed, 3 skipped, 444 subtests passed (Windows 11, Python 3.14).
- Hardware end to end on my fork's main `342185bd`: that is 0.2.0-beta plus this disk tier, plus one diagnostic log line and fork-only serve/tool patches (the disk-tier code is otherwise this commit). Box: 2x CMP 50HX 20 GB (sm_75, layer split), 2x Xeon E5-2670 v2, 64 GB, NVMe ext4, Ubuntu 24.04.4, driver 610.43.03, Flash-Next IQ3_XXS; `exit-only`, `--adapt-swaps 0`, greedy, 48 tokens.
  - Three conversations that share no prefix (41,839 / 41,846 / 165,558 tokens, cold 22.5 / 23.3 / 73.3 s), then SIGTERM to the server: saved for the next start in 17.0 s (5,786 MiB).
  - The next start took in all three. Each came back from the disk with the same answer as before the restart, in 2.6 / 2.9 / 8.4 s.
  - The disk tier has been in daily use on that box since 2026-10-11. Since 2026-10-20 on a 12 TB 7200 rpm HDD with `on` (my fork on 0.2.1 with both commits and #3404): a 304,364-token conversation came back from the disk in 47.6 s (5,465 MiB read in 44.1 s, then the restore) and a 286,199-token one in 41.7 s, where reading them takes ~140 s.
  - The read check, live on the same box: after a 124,097-token conversation came back from the HDD in 19.6 s (2,856 MiB at 169 MB/s), a new sub-agent that shared only the 16,384-token system prompt with a saved 2,018 MiB conversation skipped that file: `not read: its 16384 more tokens read in ~9.4 s, its file (2018 MiB) in ~12.5 s`. On the NVMe days the same case read whole files: four reads of 4-6 GB for 13,764-16,384 tokens (6,033 MiB in 11.4 s for 16,384 tokens).

**Failed:** the same end-to-end check with adaptive expert swaps on (the live config) gave one restored conversation a different first token. Swaps make decode non-repeatable on this box even without a restore; with `--adapt-swaps 0` the check passed (above).

**Not run:**
- HIP, SYCL, Metal and Windows builds and runs: I have no environment for them.
- The restart check on these exact commits: it ran on my fork (above), whose disk-tier code is the same, and that code has served the box live since.

## Limits

- Linux, one box.
- With RAM this short, a park waits for an evicted conversation's write before it has room: 28.6-31 s for 5.5-6 GB on the HDD, 7-8 s on the NVMe.
- The streamed park/restore of the earlier version of this PR (used when RAM is short) is left out to keep this one smaller; it can follow as its own PR.

pulls.title: mtp_pack: Q2_0 scale search over 0.15 to 1.0 x max|w|, either sign
pulls.author: gputier
pulls.body:
`tools/mtp_pack.py` picks each Q2_0 block's scale among 17 positive values between 0.5 and 1.0 times the block's max |w|. The levels are -1, 0, 1 and 2, so they are not symmetric, and a negative scale is often closer: it puts the level 2 on the side where the block's largest weights are. This PR searches 0.15 to 1.0 times max |w| for both signs. It keeps the previous 17 candidates in the set and rounds each scale to fp16 before measuring it, so no block ends up with a larger error than before. The file format does not change, and neither does the engine: the kernels already read a signed scale.

Relative RMS error of the packed draft experts, on synthetic blocks (`tools/test_mtp_pack.py`): 0.855 of the previous search on normal weights, 0.824 on Laplace, 0.833 on Student t3. The test also checks every block, and that the packed bytes decode, through `tools/gguf_writer.dequantize_q2_0`, to the values the search measured. A scale too large for fp16 now raises an error. One that rounds to 0 keeps the previous behaviour.

`expert_multi_test` now gives half of its Q2_0 scales a negative sign and compares the kernel with the scalar oracle. `s2_expert_grouped_parity` already drew signed scales. On an RTX 5090 with a Ryzen 9 9950X3D (AVX-512), both pass, and the whole ctest gives the same 106 of 107 as v0.1.42.

On that machine (IQ3_S, a French draft vocabulary of 46,587 tokens, served with `--spec 4 --spec-min-p 0.5`), I rebuilt the draft head from the same inputs with this packer. Only `experts.bin` changes. Against the current head, 8 interleaved pairs on fresh servers: draft acceptance 0.732 against 0.716, and output speed on a 22,785-token prompt +9.4% (8 of 8 pairs). Short prompts and a 99K-token cold read stayed within noise. That head was built before the commit that adds the previous candidates back to the search, which can only lower each block's error.

Python suite: `tools/test_mtp_pack.py` adds 5 tests. Everything else gives the same results as on v0.1.42, including 8 `setup.py` tests that fail in a plain container on both.

pulls.title: serve: aggregate batch request timings
pulls.author: constantindjonkam
pulls.body:
## What this fixes

A request that moves through solo generation, batch admission, batch windows, and possibly back to solo was reporting only the final native segment. This produced inflated prompt rates and single-step decode rates for concurrent requests.

This change:

- accumulates prompt/decode clocks and native counters across all DONE/BDONE phases of one API request;
- avoids double-counting the batch admission token when BDONE's generated count includes it;
- accounts for a queued BDONE when a stop token/string closes the generator;
- derives `timings.prompt_n` and Prometheus prompt totals from the engine's `prompt_read` field when available;
- adds regression coverage for cumulative batch stats and slot-reused prompt timing.

Fixes the behavior described in issues #1869 and #1870.

## Validation

- `python -m py_compile serve/server.py`
- `python -m unittest serve.test_server.BatchRequestStats serve.test_request_accounting -v`
- `python -m unittest serve.test_parallel -v`
- `python -m unittest discover -s serve -p 'test_*.py' -q` (692 tests; one existing order-sensitive sampler-thread test was flaky in the full run and passed in isolation)

pulls.title: fix(hip): add opt-in stability profile for reset reports
pulls.author: CC-David-CC
pulls.body:
Long HIP inference can stress host-memory transfers, prompt cache refills, and PCIe traffic. Add an opt-in conservative profile to reduce overlapping host-memory and GPU operations while preserving the requested context and model settings.

Set `STRATA_HIP_STABLE=1` in the server environment to use owned 2K prompt buffers, pageable resident experts, CPU expert misses, checked prefill stream drains, and conservative verify synchronization. Set `STRATA_HIP_STABLE=2` to additionally reserve the full KV cache in VRAM and disable elastic KV remapping and adaptive expert swaps.

Remove the variable and restart the engine to return to normal behavior.

Related to #872: https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/issues/872

pulls.title: bench: community report, RX 6900 XT (gfx1030) x1 and x2 on 0.1.42 - Unsloth UD-Q4_K_XL beside GSQ-RCO IQ3_S, stock and with the gfx103x PRs
pulls.author: Vop3p
pulls.body:
## Summary

Community benchmark folder `bench/results/2026-10-11-community-rx-6900xt-ud-q4_k_xl-iq3_s-0.1.42/` from the machine of the 0.1.41 report (2x RX 6900 XT 16 GB, gfx1030, PCIe 4.0 x8 each, Ryzen 5 5600X, 128 GB, ROCm 10.0). It adds Unsloth UD-Q4_K_XL to that machine's numbers, next to GSQ-RCO IQ3_S, on 0.1.42 built with `-DSTRATA_MMQ_KQUANTS=ON` (the flag #1897 proposes for setup).

Eight arms (format x one card / layer split x stock / the three open gfx103x PRs + switches), 4K / 32K / 128K, two runs each, zero stalls:

| | prompt 4K / 32K / 128K | decode |
|---|---|---|
| one card, IQ3_S, stock -> prs | 476 / 504 / 488 -> 959 / 1,153 / 1,129 | 45-47 -> 47-53 |
| one card, UD-Q4_K_XL, stock -> prs | 471 / 505 / 489 -> 676 / 1,117 / 1,087 | 30-32 -> 32-33 |
| split, IQ3_S, stock -> prs | 464 / 766 / 873 -> 985 / 1,792 / 2,046 | 71-72 -> 75-82 |
| split, UD-Q4_K_XL, stock -> prs | 462 / 763 / 873 -> 756 / 1,748 / 1,981 | 43-47 -> 45-51 |

What the folder says beyond the table: stock prompts are the same for both formats (the dense FP16 route is the limit, not the experts); 0.1.42's stock split equals 0.1.41's on this machine (464 / 767 / 869); UD-Q4_K_XL decodes 30-35% slower (experts 53% larger, 40% fewer cache slots); the 8K / 16K one-card arms match #1897's x16 numbers from an x8 slot (1,085-1,093 / 1,121-1,122 over three starts); and the llama.cpp RDNA2 MMQ patches that help the dense 27B do nothing for Strata's expert GEMMs (+-1% prompt, measured with and without `GGML_CUDA_MMQ_Q8K` compiled into `strata_mmq`), so the K-quant MMQ flag is the lever for this format on RDNA2.

Per-arm `config.json`, `summary.json`, `results.json` (every output text) and `BUILD.txt`, plus `benchmark.py` (unchanged from the earlier reports). Paths are rewritten (`/work/stock`, `/work/prs`, `/m`, `/bench`).

Developed with an AI coding assistant; every number above was measured on 2x RX 6900 XT (gfx1030, PCIe 4.0 x8 each) / Ryzen 5 5600X, ROCm 10.0.

pulls.title: Add optional GPU electricity cost display to Power card
pulls.author: hash13
pulls.body: Minimal version without electricity pricing: https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/pull/1876 # Add opt-in GPU energy and electricity cost monitoring to the Power card ## Summary This PR adds opt-in GPU energy monitoring and optional electricity cost calculations to the existing Power card, based on Strata v0.1.42. The implementation reuses Strata's existing GPU telemetry, multi-GPU support, and Monitor refresh infrastructure. No additional services, dependencies, or persistent storage are required. The changes are intentionally limited to cumulative GPU energy consumption and total electricity costs. There is no request-level energy attribution, token cost calculation, or additional details dialog. ## Screenshot ## Configuration GPU energy monitoring is enabled by adding an `electricity` block at the top level of the existing Strata JSON configuration. **Energy monitoring only:** ```json "electricity": {} ``` An empty object is sufficient to enable cumulative energy monitoring. **Energy monitoring with electricity costs:** ```json "electricity": { "price_per_kwh": 0.32, "currency": "EUR" } ``` - `price_per_kwh`: Electricity price per kWh in the configured currency (e.g. `0.32` = €0.32/kWh). - `currency`: Currency code used for displaying electricity costs (defaults to `EUR`). - Both settings are optional. Without a valid price, only energy consumption is displayed. Without an `electricity` block, GPU energy monitoring is disabled and the existing Power card remains unchanged. ## Power Card The existing Power card continues to display: - Current GPU power consumption (W) - NVIDIA power limit (W) - Power history sparkline When electricity pricing is configured, the card uses a compact two-column layout: | Left | Right | |---|---| | Current GPU power (W) | Accumulated electricity cost | | NVIDIA power limit (W) | Accumulated GPU energy (Wh/kWh) | **Example:** | Power | Electricity cost | |---|---| | **278 W** | **0.155 €** | | of 520 W limit | 483.0 Wh | The layout reuses the existing Speed card styling, without introducing additional CSS or increasing the card height. When only energy monitoring is enabled, cumulative energy consumption is displayed alongside the existing power limit. All values update automatically through the existing Monitor refresh cycle. ### Value Formatting **Energy consumption:** | Consumption | Display | |---|---| | Below 1 kWh | Wh, one decimal place | | From 1 kWh | kWh, three decimal places | **Electricity costs:** | Cost | Display | |---|---| | Positive values below 0.001 | < 0.001 € | | Below 10 | Three decimal places | | From 10 | Two decimal places | The currency symbol is displayed in a smaller font, matching the existing unit styling. Number formatting follows the browser's locale. ## Energy Measurement The implementation prefers NVIDIA's cumulative NVML hardware energy counter (`nvmlDeviceGetTotalEnergyConsumption`). This provides accumulated energy directly in millijoules and avoids estimating consumption solely from periodically sampled power values. If the hardware counter is unavailable, energy is estimated by integrating the existing GPU power samples over time. For multi-GPU configurations, energy consumption is aggregated across the monitored GPUs. Energy accumulation starts with the telemetry sampler and resets when Strata restarts. Electricity costs are calculated from accumulated energy: **Cost = GPU energy (kWh) × configured price per kWh** No additional NVML reads are required for the cost calculation. Measurements cover GPU energy only. CPU, RAM, motherboard, storage, fans, and PSU losses are not included. ### Operating Modes | Configuration | Power Card Display | |---|---| | No `electricity` block | Current GPU power (W) and power limit only | | `"electricity": {}` | GPU power, power limit, and cumulative energy consumption (Wh/kWh) | | `electricity` with `price_per_kwh` | Two-column layout: GPU power and power limit on the left; total electricity cost and cumulative energy consumption on the right | ### Configuration Examples **Energy monitoring only:** ```json "electricity": {} ``` **Energy monitoring with electricity costs:** ```json "electricity": { "price_per_kwh": 0.32, "currency": "EUR" } ``` - `price_per_kwh`: Required to calculate electricity costs. - `currency`: Optional, defaults to `EUR`. Explicit configuration is recommended. - Without a valid electricity price, only cumulative GPU energy consumption is displayed. - Without an `electricity` block, energy monitoring remains disabled. Electricity costs are calculated as: **Cost = accumulated GPU energy (kWh) × price_per_kwh** ## Scope Cumulative energy consumption is exposed through the existing `/metrics` hardware data. The optional electricity price and currency are provided through the existing static telemetry data. Request-level energy attribution is deferred to a later PR, initially limited to serial requests to avoid double counting energy during overlapping requests. ## Changed Files The complete implementation, including the optional electricity cost extension, affects three files: | File | Changes | |---|---| | `serve/telemetry.py` | Cumulative GPU energy measurement, NVML fallback, and optional electricity price configuration | | `serve/server.py` | Pass the optional `electricity` configuration to telemetry | | `serve/web/app.js` | Display cumulative GPU energy and optional electricity costs in the Power card | The electricity cost extension itself only modifies `serve/telemetry.py` and `serve/web/app.js`.

pulls.title: Community benchmark: 5070 Ti + 2x 5060 Ti (one on a USB4 eGPU), UD-IQ4_XS, engine 0.1.42, Ryzen 7 7700X, 46 GiB RAM in an LXC
pulls.author: chiangww
pulls.body:
**Notes for maintainers:**

- This is the 3+ stage case for `--pipeline-windows 2` (#1656): with the third stage behind a USB4 dock (probe 3.8 GB/s vs 28.9/14.4 GB/s internal), overlapping the stages recovers decode to ~67 tok/s — matching the same machine's two-internal-card IQ3_S config at a heavier quant.
- **The finding that reframed this whole benchmark**: `--pipeline-windows` decodes a request serially whenever it carries `penalty_last_n > 0` — so our first pass (server `repeat_penalty 1.03`) silently ran the flag as a no-op. The headline is now the pipeline-active arm; the serial-vs-pipeline A/B (+3.4–6% decode) and a suggested consideration (skip penalty history when the penalty is exactly 1.0) are in the README.
- **Negative result** for `STRATA_SPLIT_RING` (#1600): 384 costs **−16% prefill median** (887 vs 1,056 tok/s; per-length gaps up to +44% against it), decode unchanged. The extra borrowed slots come out of a 42%-resident expert tier; the R9700 gain does not transfer to a USB4-eGPU split with tight RAM. Data in `results-long-split-ring-384.txt`.
- Cold vs warm, noted as a limitation: first 165K prompt after boot measured ~1,690 tok/s cold vs ~2,000+ warm; these runs are warm.

Per `docs/COMMUNITY_BENCHMARKS.md`: README + startup logs + per-run result files + needles.json in `bench/results/2026-10-11-community-3gpu-5070ti-5060ti-usb4/`; measurement scripts described but not attached; no model/pack files.

The full report is inlined below so reviewers do not have to open the file.

---

# Community benchmark: RTX 5070 Ti + 2x RTX 5060 Ti (one on a USB4 eGPU), Ryzen 7 7700X, 46 GiB RAM in an LXC

Measured on 2026-10-11 by **chiangww** (GitHub). Unsloth UD-IQ4_XS on Strata v0.1.42,
3-GPU layer split `32,41` with `--pipeline-windows 2`, resident RAM mode
(32 GiB page-locked expert complement) on a machine whose third GPU hangs off a
USB4/Thunderbolt dock.

Headline (pipeline active, no repetition penalty): **prompt 852–1,281 tok/s at
30K–120K fresh tokens** (single stream, thinking off), **decode median 75.9
tok/s** on the short suite (67.1–86.7), **needle 6/6** at 32k/128k.

The transferable finding: **`--pipeline-windows` silently decodes serially
whenever a request carries `penalty_last_n > 0`** — so a llama.cpp-style
default sampling set (`repeat_penalty 1.03`) leaves the flag a no-op with only
a once-per-reason log line. We measured both arms on this rig: pipeline ON is
worth **+3.4–6% decode median** here (the decode bottleneck is expert file
fetches, not hand-off, so far from the +33% measured on 4x R9700); what the
overlap does hide is the per-window hand-off across the USB4 stage.

Main limitations: two engine sessions (one per arm), one repetition per
long-context length; the arms also differ in generated text (no penalty vs
1.03), so the A/B is regime-level, not strictly single-variable.

## Hardware and software

- GPUs (all three selected, layer split):
  - GPU0 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB — PCIe 5.0 x8, direct to CPU, probe 28.9 GB/s host→device
  - GPU1 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB — PCIe 4.0 x8, direct to CPU, probe 14.4 GB/s
  - GPU2 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB — **USB4/Thunderbolt eGPU** behind a TBT4 dock
    (`00:02.2-[12-79]` AMD USB4 host → 3 downstream bridges → card, link reports
    PCIe 4.0 x4 after the dock), probe **3.8 GB/s**
- CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 7700X (8C/16T, AVX-512 capable, max 5.58 GHz); Strata pool:
  7 workers + host thread (`--host-core first`), 24 tasks/phase automatic
- RAM: 46 GiB usable by the container (host is a Proxmox node; Strata runs in an LXC)
- Storage: KLEVV CRAS C930 1 TB NVMe (models and packs on local NVMe)
- GPU power limits: set to **90% of spec** — 270 W on the 5070 Ti (of 300 W),
  162 W on each 5060 Ti (of 180 W)
- OS: Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS inside LXC (Proxmox host kernel 7.0.14-15-pve)
- Driver 595.91.07; CUDA 13.3 toolkit (`/usr/local/cuda-13.3`)
- Strata **v0.1.42** (`61b3fb5`), engine binary installed by setup/update
  (`engine/BUILD.json`: version 0.1.42, arch 120, src `1e0c97588848ea0f`;
  vision engine src `1fb2b3fb797ec402`) — not a manual source build
- Background load: the Proxmox host ran its usual other VMs/LXCs during the
  runs (~5% host CPU load); the LXC itself had no other Strata instances.
  No clock capture.

## Model and configuration

- Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF` @ revision `766911a6b7369840a91dbcd95f9f997acaab6cd6`,
  `UD-IQ4_XS/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-IQ4_XS-0000{1,2,3}-of-00003.gguf` (~93.7 GB),
  sha256:
  - 00001 `5ce89370720f8bf90890f439361282104c1aa1482d4013bb9a50923e758e71a4`
  - 00002 `577a38a2392b40ca2193cea502e1d92f60b8cd370675d308e0ec21885d9daaa7`
  - 00003 `d4634e6d84f0ebb0940be15c90d3790bf6464e3dea3a1cddc567dc0e83ad8833`
- Vision encoder `mmproj-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-BF16.gguf` loaded (`--vision`) but not
  exercised — all runs are text-only
- Native-experts pack `unsloth-ud-iq4_xs` (setup-built, experts served natively
  from the GGUF, largest blob 3.48 MB); shipped `expert-profile.bin`
  (sha256 `8f59b4aa8873209dff11c11e37bcda9529a1335b724a1afeea37bf6388975baf`)
- MTP draft head from setup (`Strata-data/mtp/rt`), `--spec 5 --spec-min-p 0.5`
  (verify window grows to 7 with the default suffix drafter; web panel: "MTP
  drafts up to 4 + extensions")
- Context 204,800; KV `k8v4`; expert cache auto (GPU0 2,960 / GPU1 4,370 /
  GPU2 3,348 slots); low-RAM mode `--resident-experts --resident-budget-gib 32`
  (30.9 GiB expert complement, 32 GiB page-locked); `--vram-reserve-mib 750`;
  `--pipeline-windows 2`
- Conversation cache 5,120 MiB / 8 slots in the serial arm, 6,144 MiB in the
  pipeline arm (raised between sessions; not expected to affect decode)
- Abliterated behavior via control vector:
  `Huihui-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-refusal-direction-r.gguf:1.0`, project, per-layer,
  layers 1..47 (47 steered)
- Sampling:
  - **pipeline arm (headline)**: server defaults temp 0.7, top_p 1.0, top_k 64,
    min_p 0.08 — **no `repeat_penalty`** ([config-rep-off.json](config-rep-off.json));
    clients sending `repeat_penalty: 1.0` did not trigger the serial fallback
  - **serial arm**: same plus `repetition_penalty 1.03` server-side
    ([config.json](config.json))
  - `reasoning_budget_tokens` 5120 (unused here, thinking off)
- Environment: `STRATA_PREFILL_HELP=1`, `STRATA_SSD_KEEPALIVE=0`,
  `STRATA_IO_PREFETCH=1`, `STRATA_PREFILL_CPU_SHARE=auto`
- No `--calibrate`, no experimental speed projection, no `--batch`.

```text
strata --serve \
  --pack Strata-data/packs/unsloth-ud-iq4_xs \
  --native models/unsloth-UD-IQ4_XS/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-IQ4_XS-00001-of-00003.gguf \
  --expert-profile data/expert-profile.bin \
  --expert-cache auto --prefill auto \
  --spec 5 --spec-min-p 0.5 \
  --mtp Strata-data/mtp/rt \
  --max-context 204800 --kv k8v4 \
  --resident-experts --resident-budget-gib 32 \
  --vision --vram-reserve-mib 750 \
  --pipeline-windows 2 \
  --conversation-cache-mib 6144 --conversation-cache-slots 8 \
  --control-vector-scaled models/IQ3_S/Huihui-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-refusal-direction-r.gguf:1.0 \
  --control-vector-layer-range 1 47 --cvec-mode project --cvec-dir per-layer \
  --layer-split 32,41        # GPUs 0,1,2; CUDA0 layers 0-31, CUDA1 32-40, CUDA2 41-47 + head
```

Startup logs: [engine-log-rep-off.txt](engine-log-rep-off.txt) (pipeline arm,
headline; contains **no** "decodes serially" line across 20 requests) and
[engine-log.txt](engine-log.txt) (serial arm, `repeat_penalty 1.03`, warning
present).

## Method

Two Python 3 stdlib clients against the OpenAI-compatible streaming API over
LAN (scripts not attached; the workloads are fully described here):

- **Short suite** (`results-short*.txt`): 10 general questions in Traditional
  Chinese (TCP handshake steps, birthday probability for 30 people, quicksort
  without built-in sort, REST vs GraphQL + N+1, a two-pipe reservoir equation,
  the uncertainty principle, a monthly top-3 SQL window-function query,
  self-attention math, a knights-and-knaves logic puzzle, PostgreSQL MVCC).
  One user message each, thinking off (`chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking:
  false`), `max_tokens` 2,048, sequential single stream.
- **Long fresh-prompt ramp** (`results-long*.txt`): targets 15,000→120,000
  tokens in 15K steps. Context = a long system-design document in Traditional
  Chinese built by cycling 12 fixed technical paragraphs (order rotated per run
  by a seeded RNG) until the target length, with one needle fact planted at
  ~50% depth; the question asks to extract the needle and summarize the
  document. `max_tokens` 512. **Every request carries a random 32-hex salt at
  the front**, so no run reuses a prefix — engine logs show `reused = 0` on all
  runs. Character counts are resized to hit targets using measured
  `prompt_tokens` from earlier runs.

Both suites send one warm-up request first (absorbs CUDA graph capture / KV
allocation; model loading is not in any timed run). Timing is client-side:
TTFT = first non-empty streamed content delta; `prefill tok/s = prompt_tokens / TTFT`;
`decode tok/s = completion_tokens / (total − TTFT)` using the usage counters the
server reports (`stream_options.include_usage`). LAN latency is sub-millisecond.
The engine's own log lines agree with the client numbers to within ~1%.
Expert cache state: warm sessions in both arms — the adaptive tier and pinned
complement were trained by prior production traffic (long agent conversations),
not reset for these runs; the ramp's own fresh prompts kept the page cache hot
as it went.

## Results

### Pipeline arm (headline; no repetition penalty, `--pipeline-windows 2` active)

Short suite (`results-short-rep-off.txt`, 10 questions, prompt 36–69 tokens,
output 514–2,048):

| Configuration | Decode tok/s median / range | TTFT s median / range |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| UD-IQ4_XS 3-GPU split, pipeline ON, thinking off, ≤2,048 out | **75.9** (67.1–86.7) | 2.03 (0.57–2.49) |

TTFT on 36–69-token prompts was erratic (0.6–2.5 s; first eight requests ~2 s,
last two ~0.6 s) — prefill at these sizes is overhead- and noise-dominated;
listed for completeness, not as a throughput figure.

Long fresh-prompt ramp (`results-long-rep-off.txt`, one run per length,
`reused = 0` on all):

| Actual prompt tokens | Reused | Generated | Prefill tok/s | Decode tok/s | TTFT s | Total s |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 13,777 | 0 | 283 | 545.4 | 69.1 | 25.3 | 29.4 |
| 30,038 | 0 | 229 | 851.8 | 69.1 | 35.3 | 38.6 |
| 45,097 | 0 | 347 | 1,020.1 | 67.5 | 44.2 | 49.4 |
| 60,134 | 0 | 174 | 1,048.1 | 71.0 | 57.4 | 59.8 |
| 75,062 | 0 | 241 | 982.4 | 68.6 | 76.4 | 79.9 |
| 90,110 | 0 | 123 | 1,262.1 | 61.4 | 71.4 | 73.4 |
| 105,076 | 0 | 141 | 1,281.3 | 64.9 | 82.0 | 84.2 |
| 120,080 | 0 | 219 | 1,262.4 | 66.6 | 95.1 | 98.4 |

Decode stays 61–71 tok/s across 13.8K→120K context; draft acceptance 62%.

### A/B: the `penalty_last_n` serial fallback

With `--pipeline-windows 2`, the engine decodes a request **serially** if it
carries `penalty_last_n > 0` (the once-printed line: `a request with repetition
penalties (penalty_last_n) decodes serially`). Sending `repeat_penalty: 1.0`
does **not** trigger it — the fallback keys on the history window, not on the
penalty value. Both arms are full 20-request sessions on the same machine and
engine config, one session each:

| Arm | Short decode median | Ramp decode median | Engine-side decode median | Acceptance |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| serial (`repeat_penalty 1.03`) | 71.6 (65.1–83.2) | 65.8 (60.8–71.5) | 67.5 (60.3–83.1) | 0.65 |
| pipeline (no penalty) | **75.9** (67.1–86.7) | **68.0** (61.4–71.0) | **69.8** (60.5–86.6) | 0.62 |

Pipeline overlap is worth **+3.4% to +6% decode median** on this rig. Modest
because the decode bottleneck here is expert file fetches (engine-side stats
show decode waited 10–20% of wall time in fetches), which overlap does not
remove; what it does hide is the per-window hand-off across the USB4 stage.
Caveats: dropping the 1.03 penalty also changes the sampled

pulls.title: serve: run Codex's client-side tool_search
pulls.author: msola-ht
pulls.body:
Fixes #1917.

Codex (CLI and Desktop, Responses wire API) declares its deferred tool discovery as
`{"type": "tool_search", "execution": "client"}` with no `name`. `serve/responses.py` listed `tool_search` in
`HOSTED_TOOLS`, so the declaration was dropped and the model never saw it: a Responses client could not reach the
tools it keeps in reserve, and the search that same client runs itself had no way to start.

## What this changes

- `tool_search` is declared to the model as the ordinary function `tool_search`. The model can only call it, the
  client runs the search and answers, and the call goes back as a `tool_search_call` item (`execution: "client"`,
  `arguments` as an object, no `name`, no argument deltas, `incomplete` if the turn runs out of tokens).
- `tool_search_call` and `tool_search_output` are read back from `input`: the call is replayed as the `tool_search`
  call it was, and the tools the search found are declared for that prompt the same way an `additional_tools` item is
  read (#782) - a `namespace` of found tools included.
- A `tool_search` a client marks for some other host to run is still left out, like the other hosted tools.

## What it leaves alone

Web search and the other hosted tools are still left out (this server cannot run them) and `tool_choice` still cannot
force a tool. Nothing changes for a request that does not declare `tool_search`: no new config key and no new
default - the client's own declaration is the opt-in, as it is for `additional_tools` (#782) and the
`namespace__name` mapping (#812).

## How I checked

- `python -m unittest serve.test_responses`: 40 tests, 1 skipped, no failures.
- Every new path observed through the Responses API: the declaration, both input items, a search result whose tool
  is then called, `execution: "server"` still dropped, and a request with a repeated tool declaration unchanged.
- End to end against a real Codex 0.160 client and an engine: `tool_search_call` -> `tool_search_output` -> the model
  calling a tool that only the search had returned.

Not covered: the suite has no test for `tool_search`, and the wire shapes come from measured Codex traffic rather
than a published specification.

pulls.title: OpenAI logprobs on /v1/chat/completions for the CUDA/HIP engine
pulls.author: gt50
pulls.body:
## Title
OpenAI logprobs on /v1/chat/completions for the CUDA/HIP engine

## Summary
`"logprobs": true` (with `"top_logprobs": 0..20`) on `/v1/chat/completions` now returns `choices[0].logprobs.content`, as OpenAI and llama-server do. Until now only the SYCL port had it (835d30b); the CUDA/HIP engine and `serve/` accepted the field and returned nothing. A client that marks values the model was unsure of (the weakest token of a value under 50%) needs it.

## What changed
- **Engine (`src/program/generate.cpp`):** the GEN key `logprobs=K` writes `LP <logprob> [id:logprob ...]` after each `T <id>`, from the verify window's head logits (`Verifier::copy_logits`), before penalties, temperature and sampling. It is the SYCL port's code, placed at both token outputs (the plain and the pipelined path). Without the key, no LP lines and nothing else changes.
- **`serve/server.py`:**
  - `sampling_keys` sends `logprobs=K` only when the request asks; an engine without LP lines ignores the key and the reply has no `logprobs`.
  - `StrataEngine.generate` reads a token's LP line before it yields the token (the engine writes both in the same flush), so the logprobs belong to the right text chunk. When nothing follows a token within 0.5 s, it is yielded without one. A line read this way is handed to the early-stop drain, so a `DONE` read after the last token is not waited for again (tested).
  - Each content / reasoning chunk carries the entries of the tokens that spell its text. `token` is the text the token completes (an incremental UTF-8 decode, as the reply's text is made): a character split across tokens is in the token that finishes it, so the tokens, joined, spell the reply. `bytes` are the token's own bytes. Tokens that make no text (`</think>` and the newlines after it) and the stop token are left out.
  - `openai_collect` merges them into `choices[0].logprobs` (`content`, `refusal`, and `reasoning_content` with thinking on).
  - `response_format` `json_schema`: with `logprobs`, the answer is returned as the model wrote it (validated as before, the same value) when its tokens spell it, including the JSON inside a ```` ```json ```` fence; otherwise the canonical JSON without `logprobs`. Without `logprobs`, the canonical JSON as before.
- **`docs/DETAILS.md`:** a "Logprobs" paragraph after the sampling one.
- **`serve/test_logprobs.py`:** the request keys, the engine line pairing (with and without LP lines, not asked, early stop), the API streamed and not (multi-byte characters, `top_logprobs`, the stop token), thinking, `json_schema` with a fenced answer, and the span helper.

## Extra Notes
- **Default path:** a request without `logprobs` sends the same GEN line, reads the same lines and returns the same reply (tested). The engine prints LP lines only when asked.
- **Measured** on a Radeon 8060S (Ryzen AI Max+ 395, Windows 11, UD-IQ4_XS, `--spec 4 --mtp`), this branch built with `tools/hip/build_windows.bat` (gfx1151, engine 0.1.42):
  - A greedy 255-token answer: the same text with and without `logprobs`, 38.5 and 38.1 tok/s; 254 entries (the stop token left out).
  - `{"rent": "$1,250", "quote": "Rent is $1,250 a month."}` from a two-field `json_schema` at temperature 0: 26 tokens that spell the content.
  - Thinking on: `content` and `reasoning_content` each spelled by their tokens. A streamed `json_object` answer and a sentence with `café`, `東京` and `€5`: spelled too.
  - The same patch on 0.1.40.2 gave the same results; that build is what I run day to day.
- **Not covered:** the Responses and Anthropic APIs, and `--parallel` batch slots (their `BT` lines get no LP lines). The legacy completions form `"logprobs": N` is taken as `top_logprobs` N.
- **Tests:** all `serve` test files pass on `main` 61b3fb5d (704 tests).
